So I made it from Nuernberg to the Alps in 3 days in ~35-41C. That was a little nuts in retrospect. It taxed my body a lot, but I made it. I met Klaus in Landeck, Austria. It rained that afternoon and evening, we went for an Italian dinner and had great talks between the two of us. I tried local Austrian Tiramisu and I have to say, it was really good. The chef prided himself with making it all from scratch. The portion was more meant for 3 people, but I did not care and ate it all. Klaus and I met up in the morning, not too early as the weather did not demand it. I quickly felt my legs, not in a good way. Clearly the last days demanded their toll. We managed to take the scenic, less-traveled route up to Reschenpass. ==> 5km more and about an extra 100-200m of climbing. But the benefit was a whole lot fewer cars and riding in 3 countries in an hour or so. We came up to almost 1600m in great weather. We followed the "Via Claudia Augusta" path for some sections. I followed this path for a lot of km already days before. Going up Fernpass it was a true blessing to have it as the alternative, riding on the main road" now is a stinky mess and borderline dangerous. It's steep, gravel road and you need to push at least one section of Fernpass. On Reschenpass it is much more ridable, even with skinnier tires. Here are some details of the route built in ~15BC-47AD by the Romans, you guessed it, the son of [Augustus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustus). [LINK to the road](http://www.viaclaudia.org/it/via-claudia-augusta.html).

\

Klaus turned around back down the pass as the weather was supposed to turn for the worse in a hurry that day. And he got wet on the way down, soaking wet.

![DSC01236-S](/photos/dsc01236-s.jpg)

Not for me though, I tried to recover my weak body with some lunch and then ride along the really stunning Reschensee with hundreds of Kite surfers jumping about. Quiet the scene. The way down the Italian side of the pass was a TRUE treat. The people of South Tirol created a jewel of a cycle path. Completely separate from the road for the cars, they established a safe and truly enjoyable pass experience. What a treat. I was not here at least 25-30 years. The difference is amazing. It is so well established and safe, I found myself wondering when the 1st rest station just for Bikes would show up. But oops, there it was already. Complete with on-ramp and parking, self-service or catered. I was blown away. And on top of it all, the next 150km I passed more apples than I think I ever did. Fields and fields without end full with Apples.

![d764ceffb791fa0ced41db2bf9d61b91d29f5f57592b8be6227c1b00ede47206](/photos/img_20190729_112754806_hdr-s.jpg)

I held a rest day the next day and only rolled down to Milano that day (32km) it rained on and off but it was just what I needed. I managed to get a very interesting accommodation in Merano. [Castel Pienzenau](http://www.pienzenau.com/#pic/thumbs/schloss_0.jpg). A little gem on the outskirts of Meran towards the hills. It has private rooms that looked quite stylish and I was the only one in a Dorm of up to 6 people. Any time I can, I would like to stay there again.

The following day was one of tailwind coupled with a slow and long downhill on a supercycle path. It seemed like the whole world is on bikes, racers young and old, families, couples - fast and slow, e-bikes and traditional. The weather could not have been any better. The Sun is out and the temperatures are very reasonable. I had 95km down at lunchtime in Trento and only started at 9.00. The only climb of the day was a real one, going up to Lago di Caldonazzo. A tip I got from Kurt. It is one of his favorites in the Alps it seems. Simple and beautiful. People and things seem to be in order here. A community centered on tourists and trying to take care of them the best way they know. I slept in a tiny tiny BnB Casa D Arte, run by a Russian family from Moscow. The young daughter let me in and we quickly had an interesting conversation going. What a delight to talk to. Open, friendly, knows rules and knows to appreciate. On the other side the room was decorated in a really old and kitschy style, the stuff that was on the breakfast table the next morning must have been the worst attempt at breakfast for me, maybe ever. EVERYTHING was wrapped in Plastic. The attempt at a Pain O Chocolate, plastic, the cookies (3 types), the jam, the yogurt..... No bread. Oh, there was coffee and it came out of a Bialetti type machine, no plastic. I did not know what to eat and just walked out, no food. The following 70-80km prooved to be one amazingly scenic set. Valstagna is one beautiful place on earth. Go there and ride it down, not up. Or either way, ride it but bring a set of GPX files to make sure you find all the nifty little intersections. I managed NOT to find one and decided one exit on a "**car only**" street could not be so bad. I just could not find where else to go. I was in for a scary experience. ~2.5km of two-lane Freeway (Autobahn) style road, with Italian style narrow lanes, no emergency lane and big Semi-trucks passing me. On the right side, 2-meter high guard rails made sure I can't just escape the misery. Stefan happy to be off, was not happy with his last decision at all!!! The valley is really worth a journey. Here some details [LINK.](https://www.lifeintravel.it/en/valsugana-cycle-path-from-pergine-to-bassano-del-grappa-by-bicycle.html) The second 1/2 of the day was a slightly different story. Like crossing a line, when I rolled out of the Alps, then there was flat. Long and wide, flat. The Poo Delta. It's moist, hot and wide just as it is long. Think about the CA central valley, just with water and humidity. After lunch in Bassano del Grappa, I headed for this THING. It surely made sure the reputation is kept up. Truck traffic on pretty small roads. I tried to escape on others, sometimes with success, sometimes without. 2/3rds into the 55km stretch, I finally found a cool Oasis. A pub and I got more than 2 liters of water into me, without a flinch. By the time I arrived in Padova, my decision was sealed. I am taking the train for the next day's distance. Padova seemed like a traffic hub of the area. I did not really find anything that sparked my interest. But to be fair, I did not look very long. I just needed some food and needed to be out of the sun.

The next morning I rode the Station and bought a E 18.00 ticket to Forli, for me and my bike. I met two Italian riders on the platform and we hooked up for the train ride. A really nice French-Italian couple that just set out on their bike trip to Greece. Lea and Filippo. They seem to know how to live and know about travel, plan less ==> experience more. Out of all that I also heard a recent and locally pretty embarrassing story for an Italian city they traveled through [LINK .](https://www.repubblica.it/cronaca/2019/07/10/news/_niente_acqua_andate_via_la_parrocchia_di_restena_caccia_i_turisti_assetati-230890270/?refresh_ce)

# "No water, go away", the parishioners drive out thirsty tourists. [LINK](https://www.repubblica.it/cronaca/2019/07/10/news/_niente_acqua_andate_via_la_parrocchia_di_restena_caccia_i_turisti_assetati-230890270/?refresh_ce)

They were denied water in a little town. As a cyclist, I cannot understand what can cause this type of behavior. As a resident of the current USA and Mr "T"s hatred of anything and anyone that does not look like you, I sadly can. Read this article and the impact the two made by getting it published. Bravo!! This is the only way to fight ignorance and fobia. Thank you.

**Forli**, not the center of the universe, but it is an old place, kept up well, in the area of the Adriatic coast and also in the are of the Poo Delta. ==> It is really hot and humid in the summer, not cooling off much at night. The little cool off there is, happens only really after 21.00 h. I found it interesting to feel the pulse of a place, at least a little. For me, it starts with how people live their lives, where they do and when they do it. Here, the town was pretty much on slow motion since the time I arrived. Just after noontime. This is a climate where SIESTA makes sense. I have no idea where it was invented, but I can imagine it was in a place with similar climate than this. You don't want to go out on the street from 11.30 till maybe 16.00 . Forget about socializing before 21.00 . Chasing young girls, hanging out with friends from the city, leading a social life seems to start again at around 21.00 . It makes total sense. I caught the starting part of it all as I needed to get to bed for my early rise and start of the ride at ~ 6.00 if I want to avoid the intense midday heat.

![IMG\_20190731\_205922339\_HDR-S](/photos/img_20190731_205922339_hdr-s.jpg)

Goodnight, wish me lowish temperatures tomorrow and a good set of legs.

![](/photos/photo661210320218_inner_117-98-668-98-103-898-647-914_thumb2.jpeg) I want to start off with the main message of this post. My Mom is dead. My Mom is now done with this somewhat absurdity we call life. And I can say, I am glad for her, she now is done with this phase on this planet. It was no longer her type of life, her quality of living and giving. _**Life**_ is really an absurd construct. We are born, it is hard to learn all these new things, touches, smells, looks, behaviors, movements. We learn about our family, about other people we decide to like, and learn what we can do to please them, upset them, get them to do what we want and so much more. None of this is easy, some things are pleasant, most are not so pleasant. Unless we learn to sprinkle highlights into this thing called life, it will most likely just plot along, on its own terms, we just do what is needed at the time, some are fun, some not so much. So my Mom is now done with this thing called life. And if I can be the judge, she managed to sprinkle plenty of meaningful parts into these almost 84 years. Truly meaningful, as I am not talking about owning this house or that car, this new toy or that fancy dress. Meaningful for Marita was to have a family that knows the true meaning of family, to have friends that truly deserve being called a friend. It was also to do things no one has really done before, being an ancor and an innovator as well.  _**Style**_ was big for Marita. She seems to have had style since she became around 18-20 years old. The earlies pictures I see of her being young, she dressed to fashion and took care of herself. I think my Mom was HOT. Her appartement always was maticulously decorated. Not cold, but a style that was lived in and modern. Flower arrangements done so creatively, you could place them in any flower store. The decoration and color combinations were always well tuned and thought through, nothing was left to chance. _**Sports**_ were always big for Mom and Dad, meeting on a Ski vacation was just the start. It was 1974 where they decided to take my sister and me on a bicycle tour. You know, one with pannier bags on the rack and a map in your hands, having a destination for the day and trying to make it there, rain or shine, with hills or without. None of our friends could tell us which bikes would work best, what clothes to wear, how to be safe on the roads. We met exactly one other group of cyclists in our 1st week of riding.  Marita also went to a school for Ice climbing after being scared on a Glacier while hiking and did not know what to do to be safe. During class she had to jump into a crevasse and getting pulled back out. It was part of the drill, yes, Marita did it and yes she felt better on the next alpine hiking trip. _**Skiing**_. It brought Mom and Dad together in Salbach. We did it together as a familyThe bug was implanted in us kids with 5-6 yeas of age. A local park with a little hill is where I started skiing, and I have not stopped since. Summer vacations were kept small to be able to afford a week of skiing. Marita made herself the communication and care center of the apartment house she lived in for almost 50 years. She gave life meaning by helping others in the house through some rough times, or just to sit down and having a casual and community-building chat with them. That could be almost any time of the day and as long as it was needed to get the other person in a better state of mind. The Nordkapp, Australia, California, were some of the remote travel destinations of her. But it did not take distance for Marita to create meaning and substance in life. A simple walk or bike ride could evolve into something you might never forget with her. She did anything and everything for others, she directed her decisions to what others would like more and did that with fun and passion. There was always a friend that needed some special time of her, some extra words, some certainty of love and she was always there to deliver. She taught me so much, she shaped me and guided me. I think she knows how grateful I was and am. I am still in awe and amazement about the way Marita dealt with the news of her Tumor last March. But really, I am more amazed how she dealt with her own experience of aging and capabilities being removed from her tool belt. She fought many of them with fervor and unrelenting attitude. She fought others with grace, on her own terms. I am certain she was nearly 100% aware of what this Tumor does to her and at what speed. She almost never talked about it though. Any form of negativity around her would not be acceptable. Positive vibes and a good outlook on life would continue. She seemed to manage to create so much of a positive bubble around her, she was truly a little surprised when we had to break certain facts to her about her true state of health. She seemed shocked how we saw her and what we felt are the upcoming steps. She was smart, and focussed inwardly in this regard, not letting the devastating news affect her outlook on life. Giving up riding her newly acquired bicycle just like driving a car was never a done deal, it was just not in the cards at this point in life. Death as a concept could be discussed to a certain degree, but she would only contemplate her own state in her own head. Not shutting us out, but dealing with it as a truly private matter and discussing matters only on an “_as needed_” basis.  _**She is done**_ with this strange thing called life, I think she was happy to call it an end, finding herself in the conditions she was. She could and should have rocked our world for another few years. I would have enjoyed another few sessions of joy with her, of fun with her, a few sessions of enjoyment with her.

I really could not imagine how far, wide and dry it is in this area. It really is a dessert here. Small grass bushels everywhere, some areas have some trees, most make do with bushes. I was riveted to the window of the bus… I think I mentioned this in my last post. I still cannot understand how people draw curtains, sleep, read, watch movies when the best show is going on right outside right next to you. Whatever.

WIND

I think to this day I had no idea what really strong wind means. I thought I did, but now I know I did not.

When the wind comes and

  • you are still standing
  • your eyes are still open
  • you are breathing normally
  • your bicycle is not literally flying away from you like a flag in the wind
  • you are still riding and not pushing your bicycle into the wind on a flat road
  • water is not whipped off the almost waveless lake and bursts into mist instantly

THEN, I don’t think you are looking at a strong wind. I don’t think you experience it in Patagonia. Go back and try again.

As the next day (Friday) was supposed to be a good and warm day, Mumu and I took the chance to go and see the Glacier in El Calafate area. Perito Moreno Glacier, right at the end of the amazing Lago Argentino. The lake has an amazing pale blue / Aquamarine color and pretty long in size. Well, we did not get disappointed, to say the least. A good hour drive on the bus and we were there. The glacier is huge, the wall of ice breaking into the lake is 40-70 meters tall. That is at least a 12-22 story building. Huge. The colors go from white to shades of blue, to dirty grey. And the ends of this glacier keep falling into the lake. in smallish or huge huge chunks. No picture can describe the feeling to stand within 300m of this. It is surreal.

Ice, and more ice and it’s beautiful.

Eis und noch mehr Eis und es ist wunderschön.

After the amazing stretch to and through Big Sur we knew the scenery would change.... A lot. What I did not see coming was the number of cars passing iys at 65mph, at a distance that was way under my comfort zone and the constant noise level I would have around me. For the next three days we rode ~230 miles and from that at least 70 miles under these conditions. I was not prepared for that and did not like one minute of it. Call me a whiner or what ever. This is not my type of riding. Adding 5 flat tires in 24 hours and me the German softy was done with. As we rolled into Santa Monica at 5.30pm in the dark, the beautiful sites we have seen could no longer outweigh the mental stress I felt under. I had to tell Chris I was done with riding this tour.

I do not want to overshadow the amazing accommodation and hospitality we got through Warmshower.org . What a super treat we received during our stay in Santa Barbara. An amazing place and view, great conversations and super people. Thank you so much.

### Print edition | International

Oct 25th 2018 | GORAKSHEP

“TAKE ONLY memories, leave only footprints” is more than a clichéd hiking motto at the Sagarmatha National Park in Nepal. The large box of rocks sitting next to the metal detector at the local airport is a testament to that: tourists departing from Mount Everest have to dispose of material they have collected before stepping onto the dauntingly short runway. Fulfilling the second half of this mantra, however, is harder. Tens of thousands of tourists leave more than just footprints. They have created a mountain of feces, which is becoming an environmental problem. In 2017, 648 people reached Everest’s summit, more than seven times the number two decades ago. Many more make it to base camp. Currently, toilet waste is carried and dumped into pits near the town of Gorakshep, an hour’s walk down the mountain. The amount of waste is increasing fast, says Budhi Bahadur Sarkhi, a porter who has been carrying poo from base camp to these pits for 12 years. When Mr Sarkhi started there were seven porters hired for the job. Now there are 30. Dumping sites are filling up quickly, and the run-off is infiltrating the region’s water channels, some of which feed into wells that supply drinking water. When tests were done at nine water sources in the region, seven were contaminated with significant levels of E. coli. The presence of human by-products in the water, like nicotine and sunscreen, suggests that the contamination came from human feces, rather than that of the many local yaks. One innovative solution could help. The Mount Everest Biogas Project, led by two mountaineers, hopes to install a biogas reactor in Gorakshep at the start of next year. All of the feces from base camp would then be converted into two by-products: fertilizer and methane gas, possibly for cooking. In which case the mountain would be a little less brown and a little more green. This article appeared in the International section of the print edition under the headline "A mountain of waste"

So we moved to Italy in May 2020. We had the experience of 3 real winter times in this area. Don't get me wrong, there is a lot of beauty there. But it also is really cold, really dark, really windy and for me the worst of it is that not much is happening. Very very few events are happening, people stay at home, before and after work. This is hard for me. I thought it would grow on me again. After all, I spent 30 years in Germany. And Germany has even stronger winters than we have in Casentino. But NO, nO, No, no, it did not grow on me. Sicily So, during the summer Muriel and I decided what to do about this trouble. After bouncing around some ideas, looking at a lot of data, stories, and pictures. After looking at endless accommodation sites and making choices, we ended up in Catania Sicily. Downtown Catania, 20min by foot to the beach, coffee shop in front of the house, Etna visible almost all day kind of Catania. We wanted the stimulation of a city, a variety of different foods, warmer temperatures, and proximity to the sea. CHECK. We are here now for 1 week and I like it. I have been in the sea 2x already, walking for hours on the beach 2x, riding a bike 3x, riding a unicycle 2x, found fresh, local oranges for juice, have eaten well so far and have eaten international (cucina non tipici).

The SAD part. What did not seem to have stopped is the political insanity around the world. Wars are being fought in what seems every part of this planet. There seems to be a growing number of people acting in complete disregard of any human standards. Whether it is Israel, slaughtering Muslims, and not giving them the decency of being considered human, if it is Putin's Russia picking up a territorial fight with Ukraine and using methods that are thought to be outdated and impossible in and around Europe. Whether it is China trying very successfully to pick up territorial gains in the South China Sea and more importantly Taiwan, defying any human standards and decency, only looking out for its own (RMB) gain and gain of this so super important POWER. I even see it in France, Italy, and Germany. Not war directly but that people follow populists in ever-growing numbers, being blinded by short soundbites and simple "truths". Incompetence has reached far far up in Governments. I just have to look at the current pathetic puppet show in Germany where one of the engines of the EU is being grounded to an almost standstill. I even previous Chancellor Merkel as part of this team of incompetent leaders. How can any leader worth his/her name be led around by the nose like she did? A complete lack of leadership seems to spread. I think everyone knows about the USA and the fact that the path is being made to have a narcissistic, populistic cult leader as a president (again) of the still most powerful country o the world. And no one is crying foul. This highly degraded remnant of a democracy, fueled by institutionalized corruption will cease to exist. It will happen just as it was announced by the man himself. Just like Hitler announced all he wants to do in "Mein Kampf" Mr. "T" will do away with all checks and balances in this Government. Sorry this got a little long, but I had to vent. Have a good winter.

Art islands in Japan - a lesson in Science Fiction

Google Photos [LINK](https://photos.app.goo.gl/pNjUEe9v5fvW9bsVA)

We heard a lot about the ...shima Islands in Japan, thank you, Cassandre, for priming us with this info. We decided we will finish off Japan with visiting them for two days. What a great decision that was.

Naoshima, Teshima, Inujima, and Megijima. All are located close to each other and located between Okayama and Takamatsu is the Osaka Bay. There are long stories on why, how, where and who made all that ART happen on these islands. You can read up on all that. Pretty interesting. The result, for us as travelers are installations in odd places, different settings and vastly different in depth and meaning. The art museum on Teshima is by far my favorite. The most unique and impressive structure I have ever been to. Impressive on a number of levels. _**I want to give a spoiler alert**_. If you plan to go there sometime soon, please skip the next section.

<!--more-->

![](/photos/architecture4587620514651217411.jpg)

![](/photos/teshima_museum_top-thumb-1440x967-4861668175532021459834.jpg)

From the outside, this thing looks impressive. A white and flat elliptical blob made from concrete. Reminded me of a drop off water, just on its side. It's got two giant holes in it, right on the top. That's all you see from the outside. Scifi. Ok. What's going on inside? It takes a ticket and walk and a speech and your shoes off till you can find out. It comes down to, not much else. One giant flat surface, concrete, and the sun 🌞 coming in through the two big holes. People are sitting around on the floor in no order. Really really cool and impressive and touching and space ship like. But again close to and in the middle of nature at the same time. This giant concrete blob felt human at the same time. Two thin strings hang across the holes. With no wind, they seem to resemble a drop style shape as well. Hmmm. Then I was told to watch where I step on that flat concrete floor. There are art installations in there I hear. Hmmm, where are they, I ask myself. Then I see something moving. Drops of water on the ground are moving sideways, combining with others, then stopping again. Others join in and there is movement in the drop again. Then it gets bigger, accelerates and forms a snake-like shape, growing thicker then thinner, then running into a bigger puddle. You see them joining and see the waves this event joining event causes in the puddle. I am completely fascinated and taken in by little drops of water. What the hell is going on here? Next, I see what looks like a golf ball on the ground. Once in a while, tiny drops of water escape it and join the water game, but with much faster horizontal speeds than the others. Tiny streams are created and then they disappear. They disappear into tiny holes in this concrete floor that looked 100% flat to me 7 minutes ago.

![](/photos/artist6065183727613553091.jpg)

I detect more and more minuscule gradients on the floor. I see the source of the water. Little holes in the concrete are emitting water at different rates and intervals in different ways. It is all a huge water playground with almost no water at all. You look back up and see the glaring bright Sun casting its shadow on the ground and I am trying to take in this as well. Then the is the septation with nature again and still being so close and present. In the meantime, none says a word. There are 20-30 people in this structure and it's almost completely quiet. Only in Japan! This is amazing. I am fascinated.

If I have not made it Cristal clear yet. This thing is amazing and I will never ever forget it. Mumu loved it so much, she said she cried in the middle of the experience, among all the people, it was so beautiful. It was a lot to take in.

Thank you, Rei Naito and Ryue Nishizawa, artist and architect of this impressive structure and piece of art.

I think it is best to just rent a bike and tire from one at installation to the next. Teshima island has actual hills, so if you are tall like me I recommend the e-bike option. I felt like on a kiss bike, it was so small. There are free shuttle buses as well. None of them are far apart and the views are great with good weather. Teshima seems to have smaller and more private feeling sites whereas Naoshima has some heavy hitters in the mix as well. Do not miss the [Chichu at museum](http://benesse-artsite.jp/en/art/chichu.html). They are two really amazing rooms you don't want to miss.

![](/photos/screenshot_20190518-1458348431786133850279163.png)

![](/photos/artist_turrell8854211156364461684.jpg)

To top it all off, we managed to meet a lovely NZ artist lady in line to the ferry. She seems to use bees to install social change and is involved or leading a whole lot of interesting projects. I am looking forward to hooking up with her to learn more about it.

Mumu and I have a quick dinner before we head back to Okayama by train then I slip into my little sleeping compartment. So small and unusual for me. Good thing I brought ear plugs. It was a valuable experience to have, I am in no rush to do it again. I had more space than when camping, has power outlets, TV.

![](/photos/41820191511509144852615729819734.jpg)

![](/photos/41820191512529013216824708331738.jpg)

**Shinkansen** is pretty awesome. Yes, it's a Tain. But it clearly takes a huge amount of little things to be in place, every day to get all these trains to be there, clean and on time, every time. And if you miss one, like us, we waited 9 minutes till the next one came. As a comparison. Trying to take a "train" from San Jose to San Francisco you will be hard pressed to find two trains leaving for the same destination in less than 20-30 minutes intervals. Usually, we have 1-hour intervals. Caltrain takes 1 hour for 76km. It's noisy, everything vibrates, it smells, it's dirty.

Okayama to Osaka took 50 minutes for a distance of 179km. We left the station on time to the minute, smooth, quiet, food service provided.

In my view it is an insult to use the same name for these two connections. They feel worlds apart.

A Train

![](/photos/download1912234567424631553.jpeg)

does not equal Tain.

![Shinkanses](/photos/shinkanses.png)

Japan has the trains down and brought the whole public transportation to a level that I have seen nowhere else. Dedication to your customer, dedication to efficiency, and dedication to the strive for perfection.

Back Country Skiing in BC Canada

![SKI.png](/photos/ski.png)

After many months of planning, literally thousands of e mails and a few gave to face meetings with the team 14 guys made their way to Golden BC. By car, by plane, stopping en route as part of his winter skiing extravaganza. Most of us had one or two warm up days, skiing at kicking horse ski resort right outside of Golden. What a treat that was. Small, personal and amazing; the resort really has only two usable lifts, but the terrain, runs and possibilities are almost endless, while the crowd are really really small. Many of the runs can only be accessed by short hikes, the others go from regular groomer runs to rope rappels through rocks and trees to get to the actual decent of choice. We where welcome to what locals described as the best day of skiing in several years. Snow and weather as well as visibility where good. There was a freestyle ski competition the weekend before and we were treated to a couple amazing lines being skied in front of our eyes. Canadian audience was in no way shy to respect the Achievent with a complete lift line applause. We adjusted to the much lighter snow and had a great day. The to of my list was skiing the T1 as one of the 1st 20 people after the recent storms. I heard from two group members "best run  **EVER** ". On the way back to the lift I managed to slowly fall on a small tree stump and bruised my ribs. Not bad, but I will get rimming of this little fall for a number of weeks, every time I bend to close my ski boots or twist. Apres ski 🎿 it was easy to link up the team with the needed supply of"organic gardening" products, in the so so strict Canada. Canadians are so friendly, fulfilling common expectations.

Six more Californians joined us that evening and so we only missed 3 more for our departure Saturday to the helicopter flight to our but and home for the next week. Sunrise Chalet of GAH, Golden Alpine Holidays. All food had to be packed into big banana boxes and taped securely. The vans FULLY loaded with gear and people we heard to the launch pad about 45min West of Golden. My 1st time being this close to a helicopter and then actually flying with it was an amazing experience. I did not know what to feel when it took off. Thrilling to say the very least.  On less than 10 minutes flight we already touched down on the snow helicopter of next to our hut. The precision of these machines is amazing people are sitting within one meet left and right of the landing gear and the pilot touches down right on the middle with complete confidence.

The hut is at 2100m elevation and send to be the hut with the biggest selection of mountains, aspects, elevation, terrain and runs. We had the great fortune to get Brad as our custodian on the hut. He actually built this and the other 3 GAH huts in the 1980ties. He has guided people for 30 years in these mountains and is a hell of a guy to have around. Especially in the snow conditions we where facing. Right from the start the avalanche danger was up on#4 of 5. After unloading we received our safety speech and went humbly on our 1st route.

Wet snow fell on a complex snow base. We choose the safest of save routes, Toro, Brian and me. South facing, low angle, on the trees. We where safe but what we heard during the 1st climb back up was nothing short of a firework. Or team mates on the south side saw one of them being released just above them. Nothing happened other than all of us ended up back in the hut with the tail between our legs and hugely humbled. 4th of July fireworks in Canada in March. WOW!

#01# PLÖTZ' EINSICHTEN  
  
Wann war Ihnen das letzte Mal schlecht? Nicht, weil Sie zu viel oder das falsche gegessen hätten. Nicht, weil Sie krank geworden wären. Nein. Sondern weil Sie Dinge gesehen haben, die Ihrer inneren Einstellung, Ihrer Vorstellung widersprochen haben, was richtig ist.  
Vor zwei Tagen war mir schlecht. Zwei Stunden im straffen Schritt durch die Hallen der größten deutschen Bäckerfachmesse Südback haben gereicht, um mich ins Wanken, Zweifeln und Kopfschütteln bringen zu lassen. Sechs Stunden lang habe ich zuvor am Stand des Knetmaschinen- und Ofenherstellers Salva aus Mehl, Wasser, Salz und etwas Hefe Kleingebäcke gebacken. Alles, was danach kam, war an Kontrast nicht zu überbieten: Vormischungen; Fertigmischungen; Tiefkühlbackwaren in Hülle und Fülle; Konditorennationalmannschaften, die von einem der größten Backmittel- und Vormischungskonzernen gesponsert werden; funktionelle Mehle, "verfeinert" mit exogenen Enzymen; Urkornbackwaren und 2ab-Weizen für den "Handwerksbäcker", ein wenig vorbehandelt und mit freundlichen Grüßen zur Verfügung gestellt von Ihrer Backmittel- und Mühlenindustrie; aus dem Ei gepellte Vertreter, die Backwarenkataloge präsentieren, als ginge es um Mode für die moderne Hausfrau, aber von den eigentlichen Inhalten Ihrer Produkte keine Ahnung haben...  
Nach der dritten Halle musste ich raus, frische Luft, Mut und Hoffnung fassen für die nächsten Hallen.  
Ich bin kein Bäcker und mir steigen dennoch auch jetzt noch die Tränen des Unverständnisses in die Augen, wenn ich an diese Messe denke. Wie muss es dann einem Bäcker gehen, der noch mit Ehre, Demut und Ehrfurcht sein Handwerk lebt?  
Ich habe heute in einem Interview für die Presse von der Südback erzählt. Und auch dort hatte ich mit Tränen zu kämpfen. Wer einmal über eine solche "Bäckermesse" gegangen ist, ist entweder geheilt und bäckt anständig oder er ist "messioniert".  
Aber es gab auch Lichtblicke. Nicht wenige Bäckermeister haben Halt am Stand des Vereins "Die Freien Bäcker e.V." bei Salva gemacht, für den ich am Sonntag gebacken habe. Und viele davon kannten mich, meine Arbeit und meine Brote. #01# PLÖTZ’ EINSICHTEN

Wann war Ihnen das letzte Mal schlecht? Nicht, weil Sie zu viel oder das falsche gegessen hätten. Nicht, weil Sie krank geworden wären. Nein. Sondern weil Sie Dinge gesehen haben, die Ihrer inneren Einstellung, Ihrer Vorstellung widersprochen haben, was richtig ist.
Vor zwei Tagen war mir schlecht. Zwei Stunden im straffen Schritt durch die Hallen der größten deutschen Bäckerfachmesse Südback haben gereicht, um mich ins Wanken, Zweifeln und Kopfschütteln bringen zu lassen. Sechs Stunden lang habe ich zuvor am Stand des Knetmaschinen- und Ofenherstellers Salva aus Mehl, Wasser, Salz und etwas Hefe Kleingebäcke gebacken. Alles, was danach kam, war an Kontrast nicht zu überbieten: Vormischungen; Fertigmischungen; Tiefkühlbackwaren in Hülle und Fülle; Konditorennationalmannschaften, die von einem der größten Backmittel- und Vormischungskonzernen gesponsert werden; funktionelle Mehle, “verfeinert” mit exogenen Enzymen; Urkornbackwaren und 2ab-Weizen für den “Handwerksbäcker”, ein wenig vorbehandelt und mit freundlichen Grüßen zur Verfügung gestellt von Ihrer Backmittel- und Mühlenindustrie; aus dem Ei gepellte Vertreter, die Backwarenkataloge präsentieren, als ginge es um Mode für die moderne Hausfrau, aber von den eigentlichen Inhalten Ihrer Produkte keine Ahnung haben…
Nach der dritten Halle musste ich raus, frische Luft, Mut und Hoffnung fassen für die nächsten Hallen.
Ich bin kein Bäcker und mir steigen dennoch auch jetzt noch die Tränen des Unverständnisses in die Augen, wenn ich an diese Messe denke. Wie muss es dann einem Bäcker gehen, der noch mit Ehre, Demut und Ehrfurcht sein Handwerk lebt?
Ich habe heute in einem Interview für die Presse von der Südback erzählt. Und auch dort hatte ich mit Tränen zu kämpfen. Wer einmal über eine solche “Bäckermesse” gegangen ist, ist entweder geheilt und bäckt anständig oder er ist “messioniert”.
Aber es gab auch Lichtblicke. Nicht wenige Bäckermeister haben Halt am Stand des Vereins “Die Freien Bäcker e.V.” bei Salva gemacht, für den ich am Sonntag gebacken habe. Und viele davon kannten mich, meine Arbeit und meine Brote. Peter Kapp, seit geraumer Zeit als “Brotrevolutionär” in den Fachmedien gefeiert, meinte gar, er würde sich vor Bewunderung meiner Arbeit drei Tage lang nicht mehr die Hand waschen, mit der er mich begrüßte. Diese positiven Gespräche und Eindrücke muss ich nun langsam wieder aus der Erinnerung hervorziehen, um das Entsetzen in mir über einen Großteil der Bäckereibranche ein wenig abzufangen.

Die Messe hat mich noch einmal darin bestätigt, weiter daran zu arbeiten, das Verständnis für gutes Brot nach außen zu tragen. Einen Schritt auf diesem Weg gehe ich morgen gegen 17.20 Uhr als Gast in der Sendung “Leichter leben” im MDR-Fernsehen. Mit dabei habe ich dann ein Rezept aus meinem neuen Buch “Brot backen in Perfektion mit Sauerteig”, das vor vier Tagen das Licht der Welt erblickt hat. Auf www.brotbackbuch.dekönnen Sie es, wie alle meine Bücher, versandkostenfrei bestellen (ein Blick ins Buch ist hier möglich: http://www.book2look.com/book/9783954531394&biblettype=html5).

Ich wünsche Ihnen im kommenden Monat bessere Eindrücke und Erlebnisse rund ums Brot, als ich sie am Sonntag habe aufnehmen müssen und verbleibe mit herbstlichen Grüßen aus Cranzahl,

Ihr Lutz Geißler

#### So we were in Bamberg,

a small town 60km north of Nuernberg. It is not super well known, but a good amount of tourists and locals from Frankonia make their way to this Gem of an old, stylish, livable and human-sized town.

It has three major waterways through it. The Main, Regnitz and then there is the "Rhein-Main-Donau Kanal".  The center of town is sliced up nicely by the water and it makes for a truly great experience for a walk through town. You always seem to have a great view of some part of town, involving water.

![Bamberg-3waterways](/photos/bamberg-3waterways.png)

### Bamberg - no bicycle needed

We ended up "stranded" in a nice coffee shop, run by a German-Italian guy (born in Germany, living most of his life in Rome and northern Italy) he decided a few years ago to settle in Bamberg and roast his beans and brew some awesome coffee for his customers. No "TO GO" cups are coming from him, ever. He is opposed to the runaway culture that spilled into the coffee scene thanks to Starbucks. No good words from him about that trend as you can imagine. We ended up talking to him a while in-between his runs to serve coffee and clean tables. He decided to live in Bamberg and still prefers it to Nuernberg because of its size. Nuernberg, it's so big, he said. You need a bicycle to get around; Nono, that is not good for him. In Bamberg, you can walk everywhere and find everything you need and want. I had to laugh, but I also had to agree. It is a very charming town and is even more human size than Nuernberg is. I just found it so amazing to be able to compare between these two modes of transportation, car not even being an option. No Car ! No Car ! No Car ! No Car ! No Car ! No Car ! No Car ! No Car ! I managed to meet up with my kinda long term friend Oliver this week. I mean loooong term. Since 7th grade long. When we meet, it's like no time has passed at all. We have pretty different lives, but we align well, somehow, every time and instantly. After building himself and his wife a house ~50km south of Nuernberg he seems really content with the life they built themselves together. We went from one place in town to the next, drinking some great coffee, beer, get some food and exchange stories and experiences. What a treat. One of the highlights was to sit on the cobblestone plaza next to the Duerer House and have some beer, sitting on the street with 100-200 others, similar minded people. The place selling the delicious selection of beer there is called "Bier Amt" translated "department of beer". It's a truly unique setting where they decided to have it, they employ unique characters of the Nuernberg scene. Friendly and welcoming, but with a fast whit I have not heard in a while. Oliver asked what type of finger-food they would have for us. Looking around there was no food to be seen. The bar-keeper was quick with a reply. I can offer you some "Bauchspeck and Huehnerbrust" (belly fat and chicken breast) pointing to the belly of his partner behind the counter and then squeezing his own breast. It took me a second. Everybody had a great laugh, we walked away without food today but with great beer and a smile.

\

### Marita is getting back on the bike

Last year my Mom got herself a new Bicycle. At the age of 81. Congratulation. The only bad thing was that the ground came closer than wanted and faster than wanted in one of the 1st rides with the new beauty. Needless to say, the bike stood in the garage most of the time since then. I took out my training hat and we did 3 trips so far training and getting the confidence back that was with her not too long ago. It's hard work but she seems to make great progress. Riding slow, on singletrack, one-handed, emergency braking. All the lectures you need to get back on that horse. Good job Mom.

Stay we started from echo Lodge going along the story gentle ridge towards Becker Peak and Talking mountain [LINK](https://caltopo.com/map.html#ll=38.83398,-120.05741&z=15&b=mbt&a=sf), then heading down to echo lakes. 2nd lap was 80℅ back up to the ridge, the runs were so smooth, amazing fun. Back over the lake, it ended up being pretty cold. A quick climb up to the road and smooth gliding asking the road back to the car. 2 ND day we got a late 11 am start and headed to Carson pass parking lot. Several groups were active there. We headed east towards Red Lake area to get three more amazingly fun descents 6km 650m elevation. The snow started off to be little sticky for skinning, but it cooled down ascents as well as descents worked out to be great. Back along the road to get back up to the pass. Great day(s).

Really a LOT of work has been done since I last wrote, a lot of water went down the Arno River, a lot of applications filed, documents translated, holes punched in the house we worked on getting for so so long. Two project managers at work, Mumu and Stefan. Let me tell you, things got moving.... fast.

### House and grounds

After arriving in Casentino, Quarantine, and an awesome welcome by our host family, followed by House cleaning and making the immediate yard operable we could get to the place where the actual work of getting our new home in the shape we wanted could begin. 3 weeks after we signed and bought the house, the construction workers moved it and we can now say we have more of a swiss cheese of a house that we ever thought. Decisions are made every day, tiles selected, floor coverings selected, radiator locations selected, sizes and shapes selected, fireplaces removed and and and. Application for our pool is submitted for a 4 months processing time. We found ways to open all the gates on the hillside of the property so we could finally get access to all parts and see what we actually bought. This sounds silly and maybe pretentious. It's not. Just to be able to make it into one part, I had to work on clearing the gate from Blueberry bushes for 2 hours, then cut the metal chain with my hand saw, then use the hulk of a mower to cut a trail in the 1.5 meter high grasses, just to get closer to the area of the 40 walnut and 7 hazelnut trees we bought but never saw. Finding the way in was not trivial, cutting it and making it accessible for the regular person was another 4 hours of cutting grasses and whacking bushes and trees. Now we could SEE the trees, we still could not walk there easy. The light into this orchard was truly magical, soft, and fresh in the morning. I loved it. So, I got to work to get the area cleaned out and made accessible. Blackberries gone wild, extra trees growing everywhere, Wasps in the ground. 4 days of mowing and I was through. Then some more cleaning of the dead branches and this area looked somewhat like an orchard. Next in line is the second access gate tot he area, 1,5h of mowing and cutting the gate clear of the vines and and and the gate was open. Then the future vegetable field needed a second clearing, making it ready for tilling and planting next year. We still have an area on the bottom of the house, it is so steep and overgrown and speckled with rocks, no regular machine could clear it, not even close. So Mumu hired a mini excavator with a DINGBAT at the end of it. In a little over a day, all was whacked down and we could at least see what we have. Then we had the pleasure of uprooting all the little blackberries, or they would come back in a few months, similar to what they were like as we started. We got some help from our friends Medi and Marko, but then we were left alone with it. We now need to find a willing and able helper again with all this. We are not 21 years old anymore and the body shows signs of limits. This is really wearing on us. One morning, Mumu could not even lift up her cup of tea in the morning. Too much.

I ventured in the lower part of the property the 1st time a few days ago. One gate opened, and then making my way down-hill for 2 hours, cutting and whacking and getting a little lost and finding my way again.... I still could not make it to the end of the property.![Macia-2-street-path](/photos/macia-2-street-path.png)

### Residency

Meanwhile, we did a lot and a lot of work to gain residency in Italy. It is not a simple thing to do and you need it for pretty much everything. Just to be able to buy a car and insure it, residency is required. And I have to say, the Italians came for the rescue. The people are so overwhelmingly helpful and kind as well as understanding. We went to the city of Pratovecchio-Stia commune and wanted to find out what we need to bring. the first kind lady told us as we live in the rea of Porciano, we needed to go to the Stia office of the commune. She said it in the nicest way and even described to us in detail how to find it. It's not that hard. Turn left on the main street, drive to the beautiful grand villa on the left, park and you are there. But you could see she cared for us to make it there. And this was still in the pretty crazy COVID times. You follow the rules of distance, mask, and polite behavior ==> you get all the politeness and help you want. At the new location we find out which documents we will need, we get them printed and come again the next day. Well well well, stupid Stefan. You need these in the Italian language, not in German and/or English. Well well well. This is where the action started. Getting them translated and certified - sworn - and stamped was a different matter. The Tribunale needed to be involved, they are open only 2 days in the month, due to COVID. What do we need to bring, who translates them, who can swear for their accuracy.... so so many questions and few answers. We managed to get a temporary and limited residency document so I could buy my little dream car. Fiat Panda 4x4 at the tender age of 31 years old. Super excited I got it and got it insured after some long search and little find. The solution is of course the Italian/communicative/face2face approach. As soon as I went into the office of an insurance agent, explained my situation, I found a very willing and motivated lady on the other side of the counter that found out I could register my green beauty as a historic vehicle and could get it insured for E170 per year. This is a big deal as others (like Mumu) have to pay almost 10X that as we don't have yet shown our driving record inside Italy.  Soon Mumu had her Panda too. A much younger version, only 4 years old. Equipped with that we found a translator for our documents and 1 months after our start in the office of the Stia commune, we have a valid application for Residency in Italy. We should receive our ID cards next week. Phffffff Another milestone, one more off the shoulders.

Oh, not to forget and underappreciated. We had our first visitors. The lovely couple from Italy, living in Zurich which we met during the Yoga Teacher Training class in Santa Cruz this year in January. This truly seems like 3 years ago. So much happened. Anyway, Sabrina and her boyfriend Leonardo came to visit us after we linked up at the class and I shoved some sourdough starter into their baggage. They were successful to make some bread, but then could not find the right flour in time during the COVID crisis. It will be replaced. Anyway. They came and we only had a few days together, but it was a really super time together. We hope this friendship keeps on and keeps on growing. Only one Yoga session was not enough, so we will meet again soon to spend more time and do more Yoga together. THANK YOU FOR COMING.

\

Now we are off to our little driving adventure to pick up stuff from France and Germany, to bring it back to Macia. My new friend Roberto was so super kind to loan us his truck for this long trip. He is on summer vacation now and will not need it for the time. I was shocked and not aware of how much driving costs in the EU right now. we Drove for 11 hours and spent E200 just on road fees. Getting through the Mt Blanc tunnel, E62. Wow.

What a surreal time we are all going through these last few weeks and some already do it What a surreal time we are all going through these last few weeks, and some already do it for months. CORVID-19 is showing us how fragile our lifestyle is, how dependent we are on others, on systems, and the neighbor. It is also showing us how fast we can make dramatic changes in our lives and still live pretty well. Many of us transitioned from our regular daily life into confinement and lockdown, from busy everyday life and complaining about “small” disturbances to our routine into a highly confined and constrained life, all within a week or two. I did not yet hear anyone complain about it either. I listen to statements of how surreal and how uprooting it all is. I understand how hard it is for so many businesses, how hard it is on your own business. What we do to cope with it, what adjustments we make to stay motivated and able to interact with one another. How do we go through this phase of becoming an introvert? How do we work on ourselves on our mind to try to understand what just happened and how we are planning to move forward through the next days and weeks. —- I have not heard a real big fat complaint yet. —- And it is the same with me. I feel super lucky to have “landed” in my sister’s property in Germany, in her yard, in her RV during this time. Just a few days later, Mumu was able to make it here as well. Travel restrictions and the pure speed of booking a ticket and flying the next day made it impossible to bring our dog Brioche as well. We took the great offer from friend of ours. She offered to take care of her, and now she is again on a different continent than we are. Not ideal, far from perfect! But still, it was a solution, and we think the best solution for us at the time. We also did not complain. Strange to me how all that goes. This Virus seems to really put our emotions and rational brain at attention and work well. Many of us now do what is best for us, what is best for all of us. We can make decisions that impact our lives dramatically and impact it for an extended time period. They also affect our wallet pretty significantly, and we still do it.

We are **HOMELESS** right now. I am in my hometown Nuernberg, but literally between homes. Muriel is not even @ home but still does not have a home. We will have to see when we can travel down south to Italy into the Casentino Valley to receive our container with Furniture and start the process of planning work on the house, then finally owning it and getting to work on it. This seems all to be far far out at the moment. Just planing the next day, the next week is nearly impossible. We don’t know what will come down on us, what others do to help contain this Virus, what others do to enable it to spread more and more rapidly. It is something I am having a hard time with. My little brain is not very good at dealing with this many unknowns. My intellect tells me to stop trying to plan, there is no point as it is too variable, but I catch myself doing it several times a day.

With all this important stuff that I can’t analyze and make real actionable sense off, I am moving into focussing on the **NOW**. How ZEN of me. But it is the **ONLY** thing that matters at this point, and really, it is the only thing that matters at any point in our life. Tweaking my small life to what is available to me today, what I can do, and influence. I can make excellent dinner for Mumu and Doris and Andy. Taking care of my Mom best I can, visiting her, talking to her, buying groceries for her….. Baking some bread for her. It’s all I can do, and I know it. It’s still hard to deal with it and be ok with it. It seems so little, and yet all there is.

Berlin - Wannsee - Friends - The Wall - and some serious heat

Google Pictures [LINK](https://photos.app.goo.gl/8RPh7VeLoMvWYHKKA)

So this is our 2nd time in Berlin. Last time we were there in the dark of winter solstice. Dark from 4.30pm to 9.30am. This time we had some serious heat wave(s) and we had light from 5.00am to 10.00pm. Berlin is really unique. I don't think I have ever been to a city where it seems like everyone speaks at least one foreign language. And in Berlin, I felt this way in almost all the places we have been. It's the capital of Germany and the employees of a supermarket or Coffee shop speak English among each other and then to me. No big deal. I think that is pretty amazing. And comparing it with London, it did not feel crowded at all in Berlin. Anyone home? The public transport system, well, it's great and it is big and stuff works. I love it.

**Wannsee**, a sizable lake in the south-west of the city. I have heard about it since I was small. My aunt talked about it and the Grunewald, I heard this super fun and upbeat [song](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=H63kiYgMUEM) from the little girl that goes there in the summer time... I had to finally go there to check it out. Accessible easily through train and tram you walk for 10 minutes and you are at the beach. A pretty big beach and the structures there for the client's needs are massive. The water warm and I can see how local Kids are completely excited to go there as a summer getaway. And the water was so warm. Then there was the "Currywurst and Beer" on the way out. German - Beer ok, we all know that. But Berlin puts a different spin on this Beer. Berliner Weisse. It's the one drink that spells BERLIN. It's "obergaeriges bier" and syrup is added to it in the glass. And then, here comes the killer. You traditionally drink it with a straw. I added currywurst to it with fries to make it a full meal here in Berlin. I was super happy to have it but will not need to do this again tomorrow. I am from Nuernberg, not Berlin. ![Weisse](/photos/weisse.png)

\

 

Thanks, Mumu for some of these pictures.

Mumu and I managed to meet some friends here. We met Isabel for dinner and yoga twice. It is so nice to see here, every time. It felt good to finally bend and stretch the body a little, but 2 days later I ended up with some pretty serious back pain. Right out of bed. I don't know how I am supposed to put this together!

![IMG\_20190627\_205907-S.jpg](/photos/img_20190627_205907-s.jpg)

Then there was Andreas and Jennifer, now "enhanced" by there little bundle of joy Callian. We invited ourself there and we were very welcome with them. Their house in Schoenefeld is super nice for them and for us on this hot day we had. It was a truly great few hours we could spend with them in their new home away from California. Customary coffee and cake with nice talks were followed up by a garden BBQ and more talking. Before we know it, Callian was still running around and entertaining us all, though it must have been way past his Bedtime. We made our way back to our hotel, not without a little detour. Getting on the right bus in the wrong direction. It allowed for a nice conversation with a train conductor on his way to work. The former East German family man talked a little about the East, how it really was not all bad and some of his history with the area and the times he patrolled the wall until one month before it was broken down. There is a "kultur park" in the area which was the only Theme par in the whole of East Germany. It now is fenced up and seems to be more like a "Jurassic Park". Some interesting pictures of this abandoned park [here (Spree park)](http://timgori.pw).

![Spreepark](/photos/spreepark.jpg)

### THE WALL

It is such an impressive time and event for me. Germany got divided for this Socialist experiment. 3 nation leaders decide how to divide the EU world at the  [Potsdam Konferenz](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potsdamer_Konferenz), August 1945. One of the results is this giant wall, going through the middle of a city. As it was finally implemented in 1961, the scenes of human desperation were pretty shocking to me again. People jump fences as they were built, families jump out of windows to be caught by firefighters with large fabrics to ease their landing, tunnels are dug and even East soldiers are deserting to the West. The impressive thing today is how it is omnipresent in Berlin. It is sure that this is intended to be made unforgettable and undeniable.

\

We got pretty lucky with the weather. I think a little too lucky. 2 days of about 40C in our 6 days in Berlin. Phew. The 1st day we managed to get to the Freibad in Kreuzberg. It was crowded, the line to get in was 30 meters long and seemed to only crawl.

\[caption id="attachment\_1349" align="alignleft" width="207"\]![Pool.png](/photos/pool.png) Not my picture\[/caption\]

Inside I think I only saw 10% Germans. The whole place seemed to be taken over by the Turkish people. I don't mind them at all but was surprised how few Germans were there. Boy, it was hot, there was every reason to escape to a waterhole. I saw fully covered women swimming and splashing next to their husband in just swim trunks. In my view, the women seem to get the short end of that societal stick. All the work and no real fun and freedom of expression. -- Forget about swimming in this pool. No way! It was so full, incredible.

Cycle-semi

Oh, I almost forgot. Did you ever see a semi-truck that is driven by only one guy? In fact ridden by only one guy, on a recumbent bicycle. This was my 1st time. Amazing.

![Cycle-Semi.png](/photos/cycle-semi.png)

 

 

"You want it green, send it Blue" is their slogan. Looks like another great effort to minimize the carbon footprint of shipping. https://www.myhermes.de/

The water warm and I can see how local Kids are completely excited to go there as a summer getaway. And the water was so warm. Then there was the “Currywurst and Beer” on the way out. German - Beer ok, we all know that. But Berlin puts a different spin on this Beer. Berliner Weisse. It’s the one drink that spells BERLIN. It’s “obergaeriges bier” and syrup is added to it in the glass. And then, here comes the killer. You traditionally drink it with a straw. I added currywurst to it with fries to make it a full meal here in Berlin. I was super happy to have it but will not need to do this again tomorrow. I am from Nuernberg, not Berlin. 

\

 

Thanks, Mumu for some of these pictures.

Mumu and I managed to meet some friends here. We met Isabel for dinner and yoga twice. It is so nice to see here, every time. It felt good to finally bend and stretch the body a little, but 2 days later I ended up with some pretty serious back pain. Right out of bed. I don’t know how I am supposed to put this together!

Then there was Andreas and Jennifer, now “enhanced” by there little bundle of joy Callian. We invited ourself there and we were very welcome with them. Their house in Schoenefeld is super nice for them and for us on this hot day we had. It was a truly great few hours we could spend with them in their new home away from California. Customary coffee and cake with nice talks were followed up by a garden BBQ and more talking. Before we know it, Callian was still running around and entertaining us all, though it must have been way past his Bedtime. We made our way back to our hotel, not without a little detour. Getting on the right bus in the wrong direction. It allowed for a nice conversation with a train conductor on his way to work. The former East German family man talked a little about the East, how it really was not all bad and some of his history with the area and the times he patrolled the wall until one month before it was broken down. There is a “kultur park” in the area which was the only Theme par in the whole of East Germany. It now is fenced up and seems to be more like a “Jurassic Park”. Some interesting pictures of this abandoned park here (Spree park).

THE WALL

It is such an impressive time and event for me. Germany got divided for this Socialist experiment. 3 nation leaders decide how to divide the EU world at the  Potsdam Konferenz, August 1945. One of the results is this giant wall, going through the middle of a city. As it was finally implemented in 1961, the scenes of human desperation were pretty shocking to me again. People jump fences as they were built, families jump out of windows to be caught by firefighters with large fabrics to ease their landing, tunnels are dug and even East soldiers are deserting to the West. The impressive thing today is how it is omnipresent in Berlin. It is sure that this is intended to be made unforgettable and undeniable.

\

We got pretty lucky with the weather. I think a little too lucky. 2 days of about 40C in our 6 days in Berlin. Phew. The 1st day we managed to get to the Freibad in Kreuzberg. It was crowded, the line to get in was 30 meters long and seemed to only crawl.

[caption id=“attachment_1349” align=“alignleft” width=“207”] Not my picture[/caption]

Inside I think I only saw 10% Germans. The whole place seemed to be taken over by the Turkish people. I don’t mind them at all but was surprised how few Germans were there. Boy, it was hot, there was every reason to escape to a waterhole. I saw fully covered women swimming and splashing next to their husband in just swim trunks. In my view, the women seem to get the short end of that societal stick. All the work and no real fun and freedom of expression. — Forget about swimming in this pool. No way! It was so full, incredible.

Cycle-semi

Oh, I almost forgot. Did you ever see a semi-truck that is driven by only one guy? In fact ridden by only one guy, on a recumbent bicycle. This was my 1st time. Amazing.

Best CO2 savings for your GREEN $$

I see cities, counties, states and the Feds struggling to make a somewhat rational choice in the field of reduction of greenhouse gasses. A long time ago in my Sustainability class at UC Berkeley, I think we came up with a pretty decent, rational and numbers based decision matrix.

Imagine yourself having to make the decision between two projects. Both cost $300,000

**One** would allow airplanes parked at the gate of San Jose airport to turn off their engines longer as the A/C needs to keep the plane cool during de-boarding, cleaning and onboarding would be run from the Airports electrical power, vs. the gas-guzzling turbines. Sounds like a pretty worthy project to support.

**Another** project would use the $300,000 to insulate and air seal residential homes for the winter, allowing the homeowners to save on their Natural gas bill and release less CO2 in the Atmosphere.

How do you come up with a decision which one is better? Simple solution I think. use a calculator how much tons of CO2 are removed per year for every $1000 spent and you have an intuitive and rational method to decide. In this case I made a calculation based on the numbers advertised by the respective organization and came up with this.

Airplane A/C substitute: 2 A/C units can be installed, 31,000 lb CO2 saved per unit ==> 62,000 lb CO2 saved

House insulation: 150 houses can be insulated, 1,100 lb CO2 saved per house ==> 165,000 lb CO2 saved

The house project wins. Is that too hard for an average Politician to understand?

I am super excited today. I had a day of bread yesterday and I think it paid off. I made 6 loaves of wonderful bread, all with slightly different recipes or methods to try and learn from the differences, what causes what. I started feeding the starters the night before for two, made the Leaven for one. Three bread types were the goal:

1. Rye starter, yeast addition, my usual method
2. Rye starter, yeast addition, dissolving the starter in the warm water, then adding the rest of the ingredients
3. Rye starter - converted to a wheat starter the night before, dissolving the starter in warm water like in 2) then following the exact description from the Book "Tartine" in terms of finishing/forming the loaf before baking (this is not like me usually!!).

I was so so surprised how different the loaves of bread came out.

The absolute surprise was that my original method 1) worked out the WORST, still good, but a royal pain to work with. The dough was super soft and runny, did not hold any shape and the final bread did not have a lot of taste itself. What I learned was that the time I gave the dough in the Bulk rise made a huge difference in how the dough consistency came out. for about 25-35min after mixing the ingredients, the dough needs to sit and rest, I think the starch and Proteins seem to soak up some of the water and help hold the dough in shape after that. I did that pretty well on the 2) version, as well as I, did use the warm water for the final dough to dissolve the Leaven. It seems to spread out the leaven rising power better throughout the dough. ALWAYS do it, it's easier too.....

3) became the winner (second from the left) as I followed the gentle folding techniques from the book Tartine to help the dough in it's ability to "spring rise" in the 1st minutes in the oven. It seems like the folding and increase in surface tension, without adding any more flour to the dough, "spring-loads" the dough, and the entry in the hot oven triggers the release of the spring loading. This is my 1st sourdough only (no industrial yeast, bread that rose to this level of perfection. I am so amazed. Now, there is still one more thing I learned. I added one more loaf directly in the oven, not inside a dutch oven. THe difference was just as amazing. The leftmost loaf is the one I did without the Dutch Oven. It resulted in a much more flat loaf ==> the lack of moisture and lack of intense radiant heat in the first minutes did not allow the loaf to rise like the other. ==> Duch Oven ONLY from now on.![DSC02203](/photos/dsc02203.jpg)

I have skipped posting for a few days, now here are some updates of my cycle trip.

I have made it through the flattest of flat-lands Belgium and rode through the Netherlands in under 30minutes. Now I am in Germany and make my way East, South-South-East. I am now in the world renown town of Buendingen..... (kidding). It is located just a little north of Frankfurt, Noth-East really. No more Flat tires since I exchanged the old tire. Go figure. Komoot is still treating me well with route finding.

I have made it through 50km of riding along a canal, more than I signed up for, more than I want to do again. It's flat and it is full of heavy industries. So far my most scenic day was getting out of Bonn and crossing through the Westerwald (east of the Eifel). Given the type of trails and roads I ride, it was a full day to be sure. 140km and 2000m climbing. I was happy to fall into bed after riding to Aldi to get anti-hunger supplies. It was the most scenic day on the tour so far.

Canals, canals, canals - The water and bike&hike network of London

Google pictures [LINK](https://photos.app.goo.gl/DbqDAmaqDsBLwPeN8)

I have now been in London a few times and learned to really appreciate the comfort the old canals provide to Londoners. In the old days, they were used for hauling heavy loads into town by animal-drawn cargo ships. They are now used for rejuvenation. Boat tours are scenic and biking and hiking along these is a really enjoyable and fast way to get to places in London. A little over an hour ride brings you into town from Heathrow airport. All but the first few km are along canals. That beats the street craziness any time. There are plenty of pubs, coffee shops, and hip pizza shops to squelch your every need.

The last week's I must have ridden more than 100km on these.

\

We celebrated Mumu's birthday and our anniversary here in London. The morning with Sourdough pancakes for all at home, I finally was able to bake Sourdough bread again and it was well received. I gave a little Bread Training Class to Cassandre was able to repair a few bits and pieces in the store. I finally watched the "Birds in the Bush" brewmaster and assistant in action. It is amazing what you can pull off in an apartment. Brew beer. Cassandre and Gabriele spent 4 hours on Sunday to make ~25 liters of "Hopfenbluetentee" as we call it in Germany. The new Brompton brought me so much fun and some time for good exercise again. I call it our relationship mediator. It helps, you should try it. I know I become a little unbearable without sufficient exercise.

\

After spending an enjoyable and calming 2 weeks with Cassandre and Gabriele here in London we are preparing for EXIT. Thank you very very much for hosting us, thank you for the refresher of my Sourdough starter and the good times together. **Family rocks**!!

We are now of to Poppi. Wish us luck to find the place of our dreams there.

We went to Croatia - Cavtat (pronounced Saftat) to celebrate Gilles' 80'th Birthday. He likes to travel to an all-inclusive place. A good way to travel worry-free.

Yugoslavia ==> Croatia??? I never really understood how the "disassembly" of Yugoslavia and the creation of 6 new countries happened, so here is my short version of what I learned. [LINK](https://www.infoplease.com/spot/timeline-former-yugoslavia) After WorldWar 2 the monarchy becomes a communist republic under Tito. His tight rein on Yugoslavia keeps ethnic tensions in check until his death in 1980. Without his influence, ethnic and nationalist differences begin to flare and eventually the 6 nations appear on the map with a nasty war in the middle. Croatia, Serbia, Slovenia, Montenegro (Black Mountain), Bosnia-Herzegovina, Macedonia appear on the map. Lots and lots of violence and death and all that comes with it of course.

![dsc04007](/photos/dsc04007.jpg)

Happy Birthday Gilles

CDMX - Mexico City for a week

GOOGLE [Pictures](https://photos.app.goo.gl/d1VxPTASRZRFCSWp7) **English** Mexico City, my 1st time here and I had no idea what to really expect. Yes, it's big ~21Million people in the Urban city, yes it's dense, yes it has terrible smog, yes it is high (3250m), yes this and yes that. Still, I had a hard time imagining what to expect. We arrived on a Saturday afternoon, the BnB was in a really nice area, as we heard. There was NO traffic to speak of to get there, no noise, almost no-one on the sidewalks, but stores were open. A tiny-skinny spiral staircase brought us onto the entry door of the place we stayed at. Key was in the flower pot, all was good. The place was OK, but the so-called kitchen is a true work in progress. The shower would need some real tile-work to deserve the name, but it will certainly do for the week we are here. ![](/photos/spiral-staircase-s-1.jpg) Muriel and I really thought we were cheated out of the crowded place we expected. It was just about to rain and it was pretty coldish. Good food was easy to find and so we went to bed in this new town. Watching a movie in bed, cuddled together. We started off exploring with Luis [Barragan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luis_Barrag%C3%A1n), the Mexican "Architect" trained civil engineer. confined - quarantined - in a place that is so close to our happy place

We are finally where we want to be, or at least close to it. Casentino finally has us back. We are so so grateful to be here. Times are changing and life seems pretty difficult right now. Not only for us, but I really only see our life right now, with very little exception. Monday we took the SIXT rental car with Italian license plates and were sent on our way by Doris and Andy at 8.45. The car pretty loaded with our two suitcases and two bags, then a lot of food for the upcoming quarantine. A mid-size folder with a lot of documents. We tried to make sure we have all the documents needed to convince the Italian border patrol officer to let us enter the country. Let the occasional police check be happy with our reasoning to enter the country. It is not for fun or Beach. It is to buy our house. So we were prepared and ready, fill in a short paper on the Austrian border to state we are not stopping for any reason and just driving through. OK, 1 1/2 hours later I expected to see something like this but tougher and more stringent to cross into Italy. The country hit the hardest in the EU by CORVID-19. So we are getting to the top of the Brenner pass, signs start reading in the Italian language, and we come to realize there are no border checks. None what so ever. There were a lot of trucks but only the occasional car. We felt like we were the only ones. Weird and not a place I like to be. But nothing happened, no-one looked at us, checked us, checked any of our papers, no-one checked our temperature as we enter Italy. Crazy in my opinion. But we knew what we wanted to do and where to go, so off we went. Italy here we come. We went into one glass station along the whole route of about 900km. With pee breaks and one local shopping trip, we arrived at our destination in 11 1/2 hours.

We could not believe it. We actually made it. Our rented house was just like we remembered. All we had to do was to register ourselves with the local municipality to start out 14 days of quarantine. That was done via email and worked like a charm. Nationality, health insurance, address of your stay, start off your quarantine and we were off to the Quarantine races.

I was exhausted. After a full day of driving and the nerve-wracking border crossing that was an anti-climax as you can have it, I managed to squeeze a beer in and dropped to bed hard after Mumu’s cooked dinner. I slept long and good, some breakfast and looking around, only to go for a nap in the early afternoon. I was still exhausted. We explored the area a little that afternoon, trying to be careful not to meet anyone on our route. The house is literally in the forest and among fields. So we had an easy time avoiding the company. It is so beautiful here. Pasta dinner. and more deep sleep.

We managed to have a local love cat right on our door and it seemed she was in need of some attention. So nice. I am getting up now earlier and try to go for a walk in the early morning. The light is so nice and it opens the day really well for me. So much nice sun today and we went on another hike together in the afternoon. There we finally saw maybe 10 locals sitting on their bench chatting the local chat. All with masks and all happy to see us wearing masks too. There was a lot more than 2m distance between us. It seemed these people are now officially scared. Scared of anything anyone new and unknown. Who can blame them!!?? We will try and make our way to our hopeful future home tomorrow. By foot and through hiking trails only. If we encounter any number of people, we will turn around. It is not our intention to infect anyone. The woods are empty.

In the meantime, the money finally arrived in the German bank account. What a relief!!! I think this was the last hurdle of any size I can see between us and the house. But who knows what comes tomorrow, what comes next.

I did learn to plan for stuff going wrong in all this time. Have a plan, then at least a plan B. If the result is existential, think a plan C through all the way and be ready to go execute this one. I am a pretty positive thinker, this whole process drove me to the limit of what I can do. Simply put, if it is not important and urgent, I would not even think about it for the last 5 months. Not even close. Calling friends, fixing the car, selling the car on time, bringing the right clothes for the 3 months it will take to get other ones, none of this qualified as important. For the last 5 months, existential problems qualified as important to receive my attention. Will we be health insured, will we have the money available in the geography we need it, …… I am tired of it now. I will not do this again. This was too much and I want it too finally stop and I can switch to cruising mode.

These 2 weeks quarantine will serve me well for a recharge and a reset. I can just walk the woods, read something, lie in the sun, ….. and not think of ANYTHING existentially important. What a change what a relief. I want to spend some time with friends, riding, hiking, laughing, drinking, and just having fun.

We are so close, still two weeks away from signing.
