Cycle-express trip through the "Fraenkische Schweiz" after work hours

Google Pics [LINK](https://photos.app.goo.gl/ssZeh7gPqwhXtDuf7)

Reinhold, a University friend of mine managed to get my other University Cycle friend Robert to commit to a ride after their work hours. What a treat. We did a number of rides together many years ago and getting these busy minds onto a bike at the same time, on the same road if a feat. Thank you!! Robert and I met 17.15 at his work and started riding for 45 min to pick up Reinhold alone the way. We went through well-known roads and areas, even for me, at the beginning. The pace picked up at times and I wondered where the promised BeerGarden would be. I brought no water, no food because of it. 1st warning came from me. “STEFAN HUNGRY” ————— no response. 20-30 min later my second warning came across after we passed through Schnaitach and kept heading north, further out. “Stefan’s blood sugar is dropping”. Finally, Reinhold had mercy with my poor body, not my soul. 2 little bars and a bottle of water. The worst was averted and i could continue to ride after two handfuls of fresh cherries from the tree. We went through Hilpoldstein, a little village with a castle which I almost forgot how amazingly beautiful it is from one side. Memories. We went for a quick ice cream stop along the quicker Bundestrasse way back home but back on our bikes and saying goodbye to Reinhold who also had about 30km to ride till back home. Robert was nice enough to offer a cold glass of beer for me along the way home for me. What a treat it was to ride along memory lane and spend quality riding times together. I got home just before dark and we clocked about 80km together. Not bad for an after-work little ride.

All the riding was part of my prep for the tour that is just about to start. Wednesday if the start for myriad to Poppi and then maybe all the way to Apulia Lecce.

I just started this ride yesterday and I might have asked for good weather a little too desperately, a little too hard. The first two days were really hot with up to 40C. Riding early was the key. But I had a very good reason to start at 9.00 only on the 1st day. My good friend Kurt decided to join me on my 1st-day ride, then ride back home the same day, in this heat. We truly had a great ride along the old Donau-Main canal from Nuernberg (the north end) to Beilngries (almost the south end). It almost doubled our trip distance, but talk about a worthy environment and finally a full 8 hours to talk to my friend. I loved it. THANK YOU for coming along for the kickoff of my ride. I loved it. Kurt must have clocked 170-180km that day, in 38-40C heat. That was tough I am sure.

A few lesions of learning came up for me, thanks to Kurt. We passed by the Brueck-kanal which has a bridge that was built to allow the kanal to get over the Schwarzach (river). Built from 1836-1846. [DETAILS.](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwig-Donau-Main-Kanal#Br%C3%BCckkan%C3%A4le)

![Brueckkanal](/photos/brueckkanal.png)

![DSC01197-S](/photos/dsc01197-s.jpg)

I was welcome by my friend Oliver and his wife that night. With all the treats I could not have expected. BBQ and homegrown cucumber salad and much much more for my super hungry belly. Good talks, but I had to keep them kinda brief as I was really tired after the hot and long ride. ~130km

![DSC01204-s](/photos/dsc01204-s.jpg)

Today I am riding alone and trying to reach closer to the Alps, the second part of the ride is along the Lech river, which assured the hot part of the ride to be under trees and mostly flat. Which is Oberbayern, for the locally inclined and the language is easy to recognize, food and styles are different. These are starting to be TRUE Bavarians, not like us people from Nuernberg who really are true Franconians. Much better people we are of course ;-). Never the less, it was another long and hot day and happy I was to get to the hotel. 162km

We started on complete fog, and it was absolutely beautiful. We did our first x county segment and it was successful. Delivery just as we needed it

### English

Mumu and I were in need, deep need for some slow down, comfort, nice people, some exercise and a whole lot of quiet. Thank you Sucre, you delivered as needed.

Takakumba Hostel offered us the chance to cook and prepare it own meals, bake some bread and meet some people. So so good.

So there is really not to much to write about this as not much happened other that both our minds are more grounded than 7 days ago.

The only unpleasant part was the ride midnight Awakening from the immigration police, checking out passports. I checked up with the hostel owner and it happens rarely but it's not totally uncommon. I would like to write to the boss of police or immigration about this and what this does to innocent travelers and their sleep patterns....

We are now on our way to lake Titicaca, the highest navigable lake on our planet. A few days on Isla del Sol with some hikes should do us well. Let's see what the next few days bring to us.

### German

Mumu und ich waren in der Not, ein tiefes Bedürfnis nach Verlangsamung, Komfort, nette Leute, etwas Bewegung und viel Ruhe. Vielen Dank, Sucre, Sie haben nach Bedarf geliefert.

Das Takakumba Hostel bot uns die Möglichkeit, selbst zu kochen und selbst zu kochen, etwas Brot zu backen und Leute zu treffen. So so gut.

Es gibt also wirklich nicht zu viel darüber zu schreiben, da nicht viel passiert ist, weil unsere Gedanken mehr als vor 7 Tagen geerdet sind.

Der einzige unangenehme Teil war die Mitternachtsfahrt von der Einwanderungspolizei, die Pässe auscheckte. Ich habe mit dem Besitzer der Herberge nachgefragt und das passiert selten, ist aber nicht ungewöhnlich. Ich möchte dem Chef der Polizei oder der Einwanderung darüber schreiben und was dies für unschuldige Reisende und ihre Schlafgewohnheiten bedeutet ...

Wir sind jetzt auf dem Weg zum Titicaca-See, dem höchsten schiffbaren See auf unserem Planeten. Ein paar Tage auf der Isla del Sol mit einigen Wanderungen sollten uns gut tun. Mal sehen, was uns die nächsten Tage bringen.

Diving through an ocean of green forest - South West Kyushu

Vous pouvez maintenant traduire ce message dans votre langue , **en haut à droite** ====> Google photos [LINK](https://photos.app.goo.gl/NJar9KF8c2jtwXdJ8) ### The forrest here is simply breath taking. Two Gaigin on Kyushu We rented a van and went on a drive to the South-West side of this green island. It literally felt like diving into an ocean of different greens and different textures, all was in the shape of a forest but felt like an ocean. I will post some pictures, but like sometimes, they don’t do justice at all. The tree-canopy bulges out like mushrooms or big heads of a Broccoli. They bulge out of other shades of green and other heads of Broccoli or spiky pine tree shapes. Then you imagine all this planted on a curvy hillside, shallow and then steep, valleys and ridges and all of it going on for many many kilometers. My mind was thoroughly blown away. - ![](/photos/dsc09129-s.jpg) - ![](/photos/dsc09139-s.jpg) - ![](/photos/dsc09166-s.jpg) ### Chiran Peace museum We managed to get to the Peace Museum (known as 神風 - Kamikaze - Tokko mission). In the city of Chiran a unique airport and training facility was built at the end of WW2. Training young soldiers to fly deadly missions with small planes, loaded with lots of explosives and run them into high-value targets. A total of just over 1000 of these missions were flown, 40% from Chiran, the rest out of Taiwan. I think all were done with the target to prevent the occupation of Okinawa by the US forces (an important strategic point for the US to stage attacks into Tokyo area). It is tough to see how all these lives were sacrificed, for the good of a country, to defend against another country's aggression, … There are so many reasons that are used to justify any of these actions. I am just sad to see the constant need for this type of waste of human life. It makes me terribly sad. - ![](/photos/dsc09155-s.jpg) - ![](/photos/dsc09158-s.jpg) - ![](/photos/dsc09154-s.jpg) Beaches, beaches beaches. On this 3 day excursion, we managed to see and swim at a few nice beaches. This area has a LOT to offer in that department. They are genuinely untouched, remote, beautiful and very swimmable. - ![](/photos/dsc09087-s.jpg) - ![](/photos/dsc09083-s.jpg) - ![](/photos/dsc09091-s.jpg) ### Eating Japan has some delicious food, excellent food in fact. New tastes, textures, and experiences here are really unique and very welcome. But Mumu and I found that the average food presented to us here was just ok. The other challenge with going far south on Kyushi was that we were almost the only non-japanese people here. Very few are prepared for people that don't speak or read their language. Ordering at a simple Ramen shop consisted of merely saying YES, to all questions and then ordering one big and one small bowl of whatever we just ordered. Interesting, but it worked out to be great Ramen and a great rural experience with the ramen delivery man helping to prepare the Ramen across the counter from Grandma who runs the show in the shop. Hmmmm. Then, that same day we went for a sports-health food restaurant with pictures on the menu. What could go wrong here? You see what you order. All parts came out tasting interesting and enjoyable, except one. Fermented Soybeans (Nato?) and I was the lucky one to get them. As I pull the first part of it from the plate, I see long spiderweb-like strings forming. Hmmmm. Then I dared eating it. And I now hope I will never have to swallow anything like this ever again. I know it is a Love it or Hate it type of food. I don't like it at all! ## Sand bath and Onsen At "[Healthy Land](https://goo.gl/maps/chHpm6sytsJXvvkb9)" we went to for another Onsen session and as a treat in this location, we got a warm "Sand Bath" on top of it. Sand that is heated up from the volcanic activity (a little only) is shoveled on top of you while you lie in the sand. You stay for 15minutes and enjoy the ride of warmth and quiet and not being able to scratch any of your itches. The Onsen has excellent sea view and beautiful pools to hang out. Once I learned a little about the process to follow in these Onsen, I like the idea and taking a little bit part in this long bathing tradition here. Life seems to happen here. It is cute. Description (Wiki) "_**Gaijin** is a Japanese word for foreigners and non-Japanese. The word is composed of two kanji: gai and jin. Similarly composed words that refer to foreign things include gaikoku and gaisha. The word can refer to nationality, race or ethnicity, concepts generally conflated in Japan._" ### **Driving** on the road 8 days of driving and not one person has acted erratically of aggressive. That was a fantastic experience for me. It is not my 1st time to drive on the left side of the road, but it is always a little unnerving at the beginning. The speed limits here are anything BUT German. The "Freeways" I have seen the maximum speed limit of 70-80km/h, on the highways ranges from 40-60km/h and in cities, well it is 30-40km/h. Noone seems very much in a rush, and everyone is respectful. People give whenever they can and don't usually take anything, on the road that is. Slow cars pull over as soon as reasonable, no one pulls up to your bumper because he/she thinks you drive 3 km/h too slow. They keep their distance, friendly and safe and wait for you to do the right thing at the right time. Amazing how that can work. Respect!! Respect others, and they will respect you. The forrest here is simply breath taking.

Two Gaigin on Kyushu

We rented a van and went on a drive to the South-West side of this green island. It literally felt like diving into an ocean of different greens and different textures, all was in the shape of a forest but felt like an ocean. I will post some pictures, but like sometimes, they don’t do justice at all. The tree-canopy bulges out like mushrooms or big heads of a Broccoli. They bulge out of other shades of green and other heads of Broccoli or spiky pine tree shapes. Then you imagine all this planted on a curvy hillside, shallow and then steep, valleys and ridges and all of it going on for many many kilometers. My mind was thoroughly blown away.

Chiran Peace museum

We managed to get to the Peace Museum (known as 神風 - Kamikaze - Tokko mission). In the city of Chiran a unique airport and training facility was built at the end of WW2. Training young soldiers to fly deadly missions with small planes, loaded with lots of explosives and run them into high-value targets. A total of just over 1000 of these missions were flown, 40% from Chiran, the rest out of Taiwan. I think all were done with the target to prevent the occupation of Okinawa by the US forces (an important strategic point for the US to stage attacks into Tokyo area). It is tough to see how all these lives were sacrificed, for the good of a country, to defend against another country’s aggression, … There are so many reasons that are used to justify any of these actions. I am just sad to see the constant need for this type of waste of human life. It makes me terribly sad.

Beaches, beaches beaches. On this 3 day excursion, we managed to see and swim at a few nice beaches. This area has a LOT to offer in that department. They are genuinely untouched, remote, beautiful and very swimmable.

Eating

Japan has some delicious food, excellent food in fact. New tastes, textures, and experiences here are really unique and very welcome. But Mumu and I found that the average food presented to us here was just ok. The other challenge with going far south on Kyushi was that we were almost the only non-japanese people here. Very few are prepared for people that don’t speak or read their language. Ordering at a simple Ramen shop consisted of merely saying YES, to all questions and then ordering one big and one small bowl of whatever we just ordered. Interesting, but it worked out to be great Ramen and a great rural experience with the ramen delivery man helping to prepare the Ramen across the counter from Grandma who runs the show in the shop. Hmmmm. Then, that same day we went for a sports-health food restaurant with pictures on the menu. What could go wrong here? You see what you order. All parts came out tasting interesting and enjoyable, except one. Fermented Soybeans (Nato?) and I was the lucky one to get them. As I pull the first part of it from the plate, I see long spiderweb-like strings forming. Hmmmm. Then I dared eating it. And I now hope I will never have to swallow anything like this ever again. I know it is a Love it or Hate it type of food. I don’t like it at all!

Sand bath and Onsen

At “Healthy Land” we went to for another Onsen session and as a treat in this location, we got a warm “Sand Bath” on top of it. Sand that is heated up from the volcanic activity (a little only) is shoveled on top of you while you lie in the sand. You stay for 15minutes and enjoy the ride of warmth and quiet and not being able to scratch any of your itches. The Onsen has excellent sea view and beautiful pools to hang out. Once I learned a little about the process to follow in these Onsen, I like the idea and taking a little bit part in this long bathing tradition here. Life seems to happen here. It is cute.

Description (Wiki)

“Gaijin is a Japanese word for foreigners and non-Japanese. The word is composed of two kanji: gai and jin. Similarly composed words that refer to foreign things include gaikoku and gaisha. The word can refer to nationality, race or ethnicity, concepts generally conflated in Japan.”

Driving on the road

8 days of driving and not one person has acted erratically of aggressive. That was a fantastic experience for me. It is not my 1st time to drive on the left side of the road, but it is always a little unnerving at the beginning. The speed limits here are anything BUT German. The “Freeways” I have seen the maximum speed limit of 70-80km/h, on the highways ranges from 40-60km/h and in cities, well it is 30-40km/h. Noone seems very much in a rush, and everyone is respectful. People give whenever they can and don’t usually take anything, on the road that is. Slow cars pull over as soon as reasonable, no one pulls up to your bumper because he/she thinks you drive 3 km/h too slow. They keep their distance, friendly and safe and wait for you to do the right thing at the right time. Amazing how that can work. Respect!! Respect others, and they will respect you. Give them the benefit of the doubt. Don’t get me wrong. I was not happy to spend 3 hours on the road to get a total of 150km on the odometer. The streets are narrow. There are a lot of tight turns a lot of little villages … The German in me was in rebellion mode. But I do see the benefits of attentive driving, for sure.

Buildings

I am sorry I did not see a lot of ancient buildings in Japan. Not in villages, not in towns, not in cities. It takes away from the character for me. The only reason I can find for this is the fact that Japan exists in really dramatic environmental conditions. It’s part of the RING of FIRE, has a lot of earthquakes, is surrounded by ocean that seems to produce plenty of Typhoons and then there are the sand storms that come from China “ASIAN DUST”. I believe people don’t see a reason to invest in really well-built houses for themselves as the risk of it being taken away is so huge every year.

There is another, more spiritual explanation for this.

“The ritual is believed to refresh spiritual bonds between the people and the gods. Demolishing houses has no such lofty objective. Yet in Japan they have a similarly short life expectancy. According to Nomura, a brokerage, the value of the averageJapanese house depreciates to zero in 22 years.”

## English

All of this and so much more was going on in this unique place that is considered the dryest place on Earth. We slept at 2300m elevation went to the 4100m and I felt dizzy up there. We rented a big 4x4 and drove all over the place there.

We noticed a few areas with someone green fuzz on the ground. It was actually vegetation. How can that be in this barren and hostile place. And what are these tiny ponds with water doing here? Are we being cheated here..... There was rain! Feb 7th.

![](/photos/screenshot_20190309-2043521539274010258208923.png "Rain in Atacama on Feb 7th")

We stayed in a little mud hut in San Pablo de Atacama. In fact, almost the complete town is made up from mud houses. And they are pretty awesome looking. Their Church is made up of the same materials. This 18th century building made from mud and straw is pretty neat when it comes to churches. Super basic inside and non pretentious.

![](/photos/21320191050545465949881058650608.jpg)

![](/photos/21320191051303907015624638591753.jpg)

![](/photos/21320191049208904058149556712624.jpg)

Sadly, the town is solely dependant on tourism. It seemed all the locals are in one way or another depending on the traveler with a loose wallet. We tried to stay away from the crowd and also managed to find a coffee shop and bakery that deserved that name.

![](/photos/21320191055435973586984724380098.jpg)

What goes on outside of town is hard to describe. It is a world of contrasts, nothing goes on and it's fast changing at the same time. It's a local version of dry; one minute is so dry that not even any spec of plant life can be found. Nothing, just dirt, sand and rocks. Then there are some areas with tiny vegetation, then almost bush size, then more of them, closer together, then yes even water flowing in Creek size. Lizzards, tiny and bigger birds like Flamingoes, Donkeys, Alpacas. Then some historic and some still inhabited housing. No luxury suits but they seem to do the job. Then there is the sky and clouds. We were lucky to have blue sky every day. The wavy, high level clouds sometimes looked like waves then like mountains right above the actual mountains. It was a real treat to drive through all this.

![](/photos/2132019110491181380719554759543.jpg)

Oh, I forgot about the lagoons. Super high salt concentration allows you to float really high up in the water. It really feels weird and pretty cool.

Lagoon float

We come back and only notice at the next hotel the missing items.... That is not a nice finale on our stay in Chile. Not cool, not a disaster but what a drag.

All dies und so viel mehr war in diesem einzigartigen Ort, der als der trockenste Ort auf der Erde gilt. Wir haben in 2300m Höhe erschossen, ging es zu dem 4100m und ich fühlte mich dippie dort oben. Ever heard an EPI Baguette talking to you???

Over the last 1 year or so, I went down the path of learning how to make French style Baguette. The fact that I hang out around French people a lot, at work as well as private I think helped motivate me. Living in California with an upcoming trend to put value in what you eat and drink more and more certainly pushed me along.

### "Ba**guette**" – which literally means "**a stick**" in French.

I started with a recipe from the web, one that seemed to make sense. The **1st** version was OK and had a clear resemblance of a Parisian baguette. After changing the flour,  the yeast, the oven setup and temperature, adding water steam at the beginning, changing the duration, then how to put flour on the dough before you put it in the oven, change the time in the oven,  the shaping and scoring ..... I am now where I am. I am really happy with the results. They come out consistently good. What a process, how fun it is to iterate and discover something new.

Here is a short Video recording of a well baked Baguette about 1min after it got out of the oven. [LINK](https://goo.gl/photos/nk27oEsUxe9cvcGH8).

From the NewYorkTimes

By Meagan Day and Bhaskar Sunkara
Since his ouster from the White House a year ago, Steve Bannon has been barnstorming across Europe, meeting with figures like the former leader of the U.K. Independence Party, Nigel Farage; the French Rassemblement National head, Marine Le Pen; and the far-right Hungarian prime minister, Viktor Orban. Last month Mr. Bannon announced plans to establish a foundation to support right-wing populist movements on the continent.
Mr. Bannon isn’t driving Europe’s ever-growing xenophobia. But his ability to plant roots there and the potential that he and others see in tying together country-level anti-immigrant sentiment into a continentwide movement are both alarming and, for those of us in the United States, a reality check.
Despite the rise of Donald Trump, views around immigration in the United States seem to favor the left. The president may want to build a big beautiful wall, but most polls show that around 60 percent of Americans oppose the idea. In a 1994 Pew survey, 63 percent thought that immigrants were a burden, while only 31 percent said they were strengthening the country. When asked the same question in 2016, just 27 percent see immigrants as a burden, while 63 percent think immigration is a good thing. The trend holds in 2018. In June, only 24 percent said the amount of legal immigration into the United States should be decreased. The situation is different in much of Europe. According to the International Organization for Migration, 48 percent of Europeans believe that migration should be reduced. In Finland, Greece, Sweden and Italy, among other countries, it ranks as the top concern of voters.
There are several factors at work here, but one is clearly the continued relevance of the civil rights movement and anti-racist struggles, which won a more diverse and inclusive America. That’s no excuse for complacency or discontent about how far that progress has gone. But it does remind us that as scary as Trumpism is, right-wing ideas on immigration haven’t penetrated as deeply here as in Europe. The Trump administration is in power, already causing a great deal of harm, and it has a strong base of supporters, but it hasn’t won over the majority.
The danger, of course, is that it could. For a generation, liberals have been content to marry neoliberal economic policies with the rhetoric of diversity and inclusion. They’ve declined to push legislation to counteract growing inequality and have even administered austerity. When your policies don’t help the people who’ve been voting for you, it doesn’t take the machinations of Russian hackers to lose elections.
If Democrats don’t build an economic message for the working class, black and brown voters won’t turn out for elections, and enough white ones who do might drift toward the siren call of right-wing populism. And then the Steve Bannons of the world won’t have to look to Europe to fulfill their political dreams.

I finally need to write about this. It has been highly educational, mind-opening, saddening, refreshing, and many many more adjectives could follow here. As a society, we have been going through a long and I think pretty steep learning curve about sexuality, sexual preferences, sexual identity, transitioning processes, identification processes, and migration processes between two of these states or descriptors. I do not claim completeness, I don't claim to be on top of it all. To be sure, I had to read up on and talk to people about many of the different types and processes that people go through, want to go through or have to go through to change their identity. It is highly complex and it is highly confusing to me. Many many emotions came up in me while learning about this process. Like in many learning processes, I went through denial, pushing it away, minimizing it, NIMBY it, and acceptance of it. I think I reached the state where I know enough about it and I started analyzing all this and what we, as a society all do with this complex and confusing data, not to talk about any person in detail yet at all. All this is still fully conceptual, not personal. I am trying to understand what it is I am looking at, who is involved, and what impact it all has and can have.

## The discovery and the choice

1st, I have to say that I am always overcome with the deepest sadness when I hear about people going through any kind of sex change process or going through a process of redefining themself. Why am I sad you ask? I am sad to see any human suffer or be hurt. And however this one person gets to the decision to not be able to identify with their own sex, sexuality or body, it seems like they are in for a long long time of really hard psychological, mental, and sometimes also physical pain. That is why I feel sad at that time. I am also very concerned about the seemingly increasing number of people going through this type of re-definition process. We are exposing people at a really young age to information that is highly complex and it influences them. What I am concerned about is that we expose teenagers to this information, at a time that is probably one of the hardest times in their lives. I know the teenage years were hard for me, and believe me, I had it easy for many reasons. I am a white male, born in Germany, to German parents, in a household that was not rich, but rich in love and care. We are exposing what seems like all of our teenagers to many more questions they need to answer for themself during this period. Don't get me wrong, choices are good. But many choices make it harder. Many more choices make it a lot harder, now and for a long period of their life. Choice is good, don't get me wrong. The damages that people endured and still endure while NOT coming out and making the changes needed are heart-wrenching..... But, please, make no mistake, choice has its cost too. To the person and to the society. ==> The decision process for this individual is much more complex and as a result, it must be more error-prone. The person might make a big decision in their life, only to find out 1-2-13 years later, the decision was rushed, made too early in life, that this solution might not have been the solution that was truly needed and was best at the time. There is a huge cost to making suboptimal decisions of this magnitude. For that person and for all of us as a society.

## Rights and duties of the individual; We all are the same, I respect you and you respect me

Let's say I decide to go through this process of a sex change. Who am I doing this for and why am I doing this? It needs to be done for ME and my personal needs, however intricate they may be. If I feel like I need this, I need to go through this process, with all the pains and gains it delivers. The rest of you people, I expect you to accept my decision and treat me with respect. I DON'T do this for any reason other than MY reasons. I also cannot expect the whole world to change, just because of me and the process I am going through. That would be crazy. I also need to try and make the life of everyone around me the least impacted by this, because it is ME who needs this change, no one else asked me to do this. If I feel very strongly that I need to go to the bathroom that best suits me, I behave like a good human and expect everyone else to behave like good humans too. If I talk to someone, they will address me with the name I tell them I have, with respect and decency. It is a give and a take, it is a process that needs tolerance from BOTH sides. It is a give and a take. I would cause a problem, in my opinion, if I started demanding the whole rest of society to treat me differently than everybody else. I want my own bathroom, I want to be addressed with "THEM" "IT" "THEY" ...... In my view it is an act of arrogance, demanding special treatment because of something I felt like I needed to do. How should everybody else know how to address me, by just looking at me? Even if this situation is playing in a company setting and I am known to my co-workers. I was "HE" and now I am "HER". OK, If I look like a woman, I will make it easy for my co-workers to remember and address me as an "HER". What if the week after I come up with a new rule and want to be addressed with "YOURS TRULY". Or to top it off, I am putting myself in the non-binary category and demanding pronoun changes on a daily basis? ==> I see this as arrogant, intolerant, and problematic. This is why I say, You are You, and I am Me. I will treat you with respect and demand the same from you. I will not try to make myself special and unique by posing these demands. I know or can somewhat imagine life is a truly hard thing to master, adding any sex re-defining process on top of this will only make it so much harder. But I am very sorry to say, if anyone decides to go through this process it is his/her life and his/her choice and he/she needs to deal with most of this, not downloading it to the rest of society. I am willing to help, but it must be a sharing effort, and you must carry your hard and heavy share. I am just a bystander, trying to work through my own issues and own problems.

## Attention is a limited good - we need to focus on existential problems

I think I made clear that the topic is dear to me and my heart, I don't want to hurt anyone or accuse anyone of any wrongdoing in any specific instance. I am trying to look at this topic from a little bit above the ground. I am trying to bring some abstractions into this discussion. I find it the only way to stay on any course. When I listen to the news, I used to hear a lot about topics that touch on sexual orientation (before the Ukraine war that is). When I look at politics, I see a large amount of attention to be given to this very topic as well. I just heard a report about the Berlinale Film Festival and its nominations and winners of certain prizes. All these areas are occupied with working through this topic, they are in my view clogged with this topic. It seems like the only way to be nominated for a prize at the Berlinale, the only way to get news coverage is to report about a sexual orientation-related topic. And I can tell you, I am tired of it. These cases are hard and important for us as a society, but they are not all topics we need to work on. They cannot be all we report on or legislate on all we see movies about. In my opinion, we do have a number of global problems that involve the very existence of our planet with us humans. One more reason for adjusting how we treat this topic is fairness. We are not treating ~50% of our world population equal to the other 50% today (male <--> female). That is a problem that needs a solution for many years and we are only inching toward equality (woman's rights). I don't know how many people belong to the LGBTQ+ group (I read a number of about 1% of our population). What I do know it is less than 50% of society. It seems like the news coverage, and political engagement is strongly tilted toward the LGBTQ+ topic, weighted toward the number of people on this planet. Let's work on topics that are the mosrt urgent and the most relevant, not on the ones that people vocalize the best about.

I feel like we need to address the problems and issues around LGBTQ+ topics. But I also think we HAVE to save the planet we are living on, if we lose this, we have nothing to live on anymore and no LGBTQ+ topic matters.

## Learning

This is what I think about this topic right now. It is incomplete and based on what I read, heard, and experienced in my life so far. I will learn more and just my opinion along with that. If you feel differently, have input, or want to speak out, please tell me. I want to learn more.

**_After discussions with some nice and smart people... I want to add something._**

I think what I am really all hung up about is not the people that go through this process, but I am fed up with the Movement of LGBTQ+. It seems to me to be not very well defined (look at the [WiKi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LGBT) page). It seems to me to be unstructured to the core, inclusive to almost everyone, trying to do everything and really IMO getting nothing really done. The main thing IMO is time. This type of change needs time in society. And it seems to me, this is not what is really given. This is what is bugging me so much.

I am a white male, born in Germany, to German parents, in a household that was not rich, but rich in love and care. We are exposing what seems like all of our teenagers to many more questions they need to answer for themself during this period. Don’t get me wrong, choices are good. But many choices make it harder. Many more choices make it a lot harder, now and for a long period of their life. Choice is good, don’t get me wrong. The damages that people endured and still endure while NOT coming out and making the changes needed are heart-wrenching… But, please, make no mistake, choice has its cost too. To the person and to the society. ==> The decision process for this individual is much more complex and as a result, it must be more error-prone. The person might make a big decision in their life, only to find out 1-2-13 years later, the decision was rushed, made too early in life, that this solution might not have been the solution that was truly needed and was best at the time. There is a huge cost to making suboptimal decisions of this magnitude. For that person and for all of us as a society.

Rights and duties of the individual; We all are the same, I respect you and you respect me

Let’s say I decide to go through this process of a sex change. Who am I doing this for and why am I doing this? It needs to be done for ME and my personal needs, however intricate they may be. If I feel like I need this, I need to go through this process, with all the pains and gains it delivers. The rest of you people, I expect you to accept my decision and treat me with respect. I DON’T do this for any reason other than MY reasons. I also cannot expect the whole world to change, just because of me and the process I am going through. That would be crazy. I also need to try and make the life of everyone around me the least impacted by this, because it is ME who needs this change, no one else asked me to do this. If I feel very strongly that I need to go to the bathroom that best suits me, I behave like a good human and expect everyone else to behave like good humans too. If I talk to someone, they will address me with the name I tell them I have, with respect and decency. It is a give and a take, it is a process that needs tolerance from BOTH sides. It is a give and a take. I would cause a problem, in my opinion, if I started demanding the whole rest of society to treat me differently than everybody else. I want my own bathroom, I want to be addressed with “THEM” “IT” “THEY” … In my view it is an act of arrogance, demanding special treatment because of something I felt like I needed to do. How should everybody else know how to address me, by just looking at me? Even if this situation is playing in a company setting and I am known to my co-workers. I was “HE” and now I am “HER”. OK, If I look like a woman, I will make it easy for my co-workers to remember and address me as an “HER”. What if the week after I come up with a new rule and want to be addressed with “YOURS TRULY”. Or to top it off, I am putting myself in the non-binary category and demanding pronoun changes on a daily basis? ==> I see this as arrogant, intolerant, and problematic. This is why I say, You are You, and I am Me. I will treat you with respect and demand the same from you. I will not try to make myself special and unique by posing these demands. I know or can somewhat imagine life is a truly hard thing to master, adding any sex re-defining process on top of this will only make it so much harder. But I am very sorry to say, if anyone decides to go through this process it is his/her life and his/her choice and he/she needs to deal with most of this, not downloading it to the rest of society. I am willing to help, but it must be a sharing effort, and you must carry your hard and heavy share. I am just a bystander, trying to work through my own issues and own problems.

Attention is a limited good - we need to focus on existential problems

I think I made clear that the topic is dear to me and my heart, I don’t want to hurt anyone or accuse anyone of any wrongdoing in any specific instance. I am trying to look at this topic from a little bit above the ground. I am trying to bring some abstractions into this discussion. I find it the only way to stay on any course. When I listen to the news, I used to hear a lot about topics that touch on sexual orientation (before the Ukraine war that is). When I look at politics, I see a large amount of attention to be given to this very topic as well. I just heard a report about the Berlinale Film Festival and its nominations and winners of certain prizes. All these areas are occupied with working through this topic, they are in my view clogged with this topic. It seems like the only way to be nominated for a prize at the Berlinale, the only way to get news coverage is to report about a sexual orientation-related topic. And I can tell you, I am tired of it. These cases are hard and important for us as a society, but they are not all topics we need to work on. They cannot be all we report on or legislate on all we see movies about. In my opinion, we do have a number of global problems that involve the very existence of our planet with us humans. One more reason for adjusting how we treat this topic is fairness. We are not treating ~50% of our world population equal to the other 50% today (male <—> female). That is a problem that needs a solution for many years and we are only inching toward equality (woman’s rights). I don’t know how many people belong to the LGBTQ+ group (I read a number of about 1% of our population). What I do know it is less than 50% of society. It seems like the news coverage, and political engagement is strongly tilted toward the LGBTQ+ topic, weighted toward the number of people on this planet. Let’s work on topics that are the mosrt urgent and the most relevant, not on the ones that people vocalize the best about.

I feel like we need to address the problems and issues around LGBTQ+ topics. But I also think we HAVE to save the planet we are living on, if we lose this, we have nothing to live on anymore and no LGBTQ+ topic matters.

Learning

This is what I think about this topic right now. It is incomplete and based on what I read, heard, and experienced in my life so far. I will learn more and just my opinion along with that. If you feel differently, have input, or want to speak out, please tell me. I want to learn more.

After discussions with some nice and smart people… I want to add something.

I think what I am really all hung up about is not the people that go through this process, but I am fed up with the Movement of LGBTQ+. It seems to me to be not very well defined (look at the WiKi page). It seems to me to be unstructured to the core, inclusive to almost everyone, trying to do everything and really IMO getting nothing really done. The main thing IMO is time. This type of change needs time in society. And it seems to me, this is not what is really given. This is what is bugging me so much.

### Flamkuche vs. Tarte Flambe - Don't mix it up

What is that anyway? Flames? cake? Tarte? What is all this about. It’s just a Pizza you say, a little thinner. No no, you are stepping into dangerous waters, my friend. You enter the Area of Alsace and you don’t mess around with that.

For the un-inclined, I am talking about a long tradition of making something delicious out of dough, onions, olive oil and some yogurt mixture. You can call it related to a pizza but of course, it is not a Pizza.

1. it is of rectangular shape
    
2. It is big
    
3. It is paper thin (I am not kidding)
    
4. There is (almost) nothing on it
    
5. You can eat 2 or 3 of them and will live to talk about it
    
6. Today you can get them savory (usual) and sweet as a dessert style
    
7. Then need to be made in a wood-fired oven
    
8. 2 minutes and they are done
    

I had the opportunity to try some of these beauties during our stay with Frederique and Jean-Loup in Barr, just south of Strasbourg. They have built themselves an amazing home 15 years ago, made exclusively from concrete. Steel and concrete, no wallpaper and very little else that would disrupt your impression of this well planned and amazingly beautiful home. Jean-Loup managed to place a few decorative plants in the forms before the concrete was poured. The result is the Relief of the plant on the face of the concrete, sometimes the stem or part of the leaves remain in place. Then some leaves are lightly painted to accentuate the form. Awesome. Even the light fixtures are concrete and they are pretty, provide great lighting and look super modern.

HOUSE PICTURES

Back to the Tarte Flambe!! Frederique and Jean-Loup brought us to a party where the local Tarte Flambe master showed off his skill. Christian, he comes from the area and comes from a bakers family. If I understood right, he thinks his Dad brought the Tarte Flambe from an area a few km south to Barr. He worked there for a while, learned the skill of Tarte Flambe and then moved, brought along the art and skillset. Christian makes Tarte Flambe for the last 40 years in different settings. whether it is from home or in a commercial kitchen or like now our to his mobile, wood-fired oven. He set it up on a trailer and brings all her needs to serve 20 or 100 people with what they want. **Tarte Flambe.**

[https://www.vegetaria.at/flammkuchen-ein-experiment-tarte-flambee-an-experiment/](https://www.vegetaria.at/flammkuchen-ein-experiment-tarte-flambee-an-experiment/)

GUESS WHAT? I ended up talking to Christian a bunch over the course of the night and he is a great great guy. He works hard for sure, and he is funny and knows a lot about local history and Tarte Flambe.

After listening to him I started reading a bunch of Blogs and websites and I think the difference is more regional than actual. Not to play it down, maybe I am wrong but that is what I read so far. Needless to say, I will have to try to make some of these beauties. Stay tuned.  Go to http://www.tartes-flambees.fr/ for the real deal.

\

### How accidents are handled in France

We were picked up by our friends Natalie and Francois and went into Strasbourg proper now. Amazing and fun to see them again, after they visited us 6 years ago in California. We dropped the bags, had a little Apero (appetizers) and went into town by bike after Emmanuel came off the TGV from Paris to join us all in the fun. Family and friends, awesome. Natalie showed us around and the weather was super warm and sunny. Strasbourg is a small and really pretty town, with a great old town center that is an island embraced on all sides by the river Ile. It is the capital of Europe. I found it a great mixture between German and French there. Exquisite French food, German structure. We rode into town, took pictures and Oooops, Emmanuel managed to turn his bike a little fast and a lady on her electric scooter came shooting along the bike path. The result was a scraped up knee, a hard fall on the back on the head on the ground. She did not move much at first, but it was soon clear that she was ok in the grand scheme. Having lived in the US for 23 years, I was amazed about the ease this case was handled. Natalie called the Ambulance, I managed the bike and pedestrian traffic and when the helpers arrived (a little slow I must say), there was very little fuzz given to who did what and no police was present anyway. 10 minutes in the van for a quick checkup and an exchange of email addresses is all it took to get her on the way to X-Rays and us back on our way into town. No insurance and no anxiety about the dramatic expense this all will cause. Amazing what a healthcare system can do to a population. Take one more worry out of your hair and you can actually live. Why dod the US citizen prefer to struggle so much with the concept of a population that is cared for when it comes to health. I am in awe and will never understand.

\

### Breakfast in Strasbourg, plates ????

It's just a little thing, but I liked it. We were so perfectly hosted at Natalie’s and Francois’ apartment, I was amazed and still, I am in debt. Thank you. There always is a laugh, a little something to eat and a little something to talk about. There is no rush to get anywhere and harmony seems to be on top of the list. For breakfast, there were pastries, of course, coffee and tea, fruit and juices. But there were no plates. Just a napkin and the table. That is all I needed, but just so unusual for me not to have a plate. Cute.

**And now we are off to Berlin**. Two train rides and close to 800 km distance. Less than 7 hours and we will be there, and no driving needed. I love it. Berlin, here we come.

Thanks, Chris for giving us so many handy tips on what to do and where to go there. We are looking forward to seeing Isabel again. She will be there too and we will tag along the former native “_Berliner_”.

# Floodgate: How the Water District and City’s Comedy of Errors Became a Local Tragedy

##### By Jennifer Wadsworth and Josh Koehn/ March 1, 2017

On the first day of the flood, Jose Villalobos had to get his 5-year-old sister to school. It was a few minutes after 8am, and [Coyote Creek had already jumped its bank](http://www.sanjoseinside.com/tag/san-jose-flood/)—the riverine surge creeping into the playground across the street and down the block.

Though alarmed by the encroaching waters, Villalobos, 20, persisted to stay on schedule. After dropping his sister off at Shirakawa Elementary School, he returned home to the apartment he shared with his mom, girlfriend and year-old daughter to change for his 10am shift at Off the Wall, an indoor soccer complex. When he opened the front door for a second time that morning, the mud-thickened water looked deep enough to swim.

At a quarter-to-10, Villalobos slammed the door, clambered upstairs, stuffed whatever belongings he could find into a bag and raced back outside. Before loading up his car, he tried to warn a neighbor—an elderly man in the next unit—about the sudden deluge. Trying to outpace the panic and bring his girlfriend and toddler to dry land, Villalobos waded to his silver Volkswagen Passat, a car he scraped up $5,000 to buy after high school, and threw it into reverse. The water crept up past the hubcaps and seeped into the cab as he backed out. Villalobos made it no more than a few feet before the water hit the chassis and killed the engine. A neighbor offered to drive them out in a pickup, but the family would have to leave everything behind.

As the neighbor drove them toward Phelan Avenue, Villalobos saw firefighters and sheriff’s deputies arrive on boats to rescue more than 300 people left stranded. Had he remained just minutes longer, Villalobos and his family would have needed rescuing, too.

“I’m angry because the city didn’t say nothing,” he said. “We got no heads-up. Nothing.”

![16 (5)](/photos/16-5-771x515.jpg)

**Submerged**

Nearly 40,000 people in the heart of the 10th largest city in the nation were caught off guard by flooding Feb. 21 and 22 along Coyote Creek. All told, 14,000 people were given mandatory orders to evacuate their homes in areas as economically diverse as Spartan Keyes, Rock Springs, Olinder Park, Roosevelt Park and Naglee Park as well as three mobile home communities along Old Oakland Road. Another 22,000 were strongly advised to relocate until authorities deemed the creek’s flood zone safe. San Jose’s immense homeless population—one of the nation’s largest, with at least 4,000 people, including 1,500 or so who live along local waterways—was especially vulnerable. Some were forced to cling to trees to avoid being swept away in the rushing water. Remarkably, there have been no reported fatalities.

The material toll, however, is staggering. Though inspectors red-tagged only three homes, nearly 500 others remain effectively uninhabitable, and countless more need serious repair. Financially speaking, the damage amounts to upward of $50 million for private property and $23 million for public, according to estimates submitted by the city in a petition for state and federal disaster aid. The outlay in unincorporated Santa Clara County comes to something on the order of $22 million.

The city and the Santa Clara Valley Water District, which supplies drinking water and flood control for 1.8 million people, have offered a variety of reasons for the flood: heavier storms than expected, spillover from Anderson Dam, potential obstructions that should have been cleared from Coyote Creek.

But the answer many residents are wondering: Why didn’t the public know sooner?

San Jose Mayor Sam Liccardo has gone from suggesting Anderson Dam was poorly maintained to saying the city accepts full responsibility. In the immediate aftermath, however, he candidly blamed the district for giving bad information, leading to the city’s failure to notify the public.

“Those issues are very much linked,” Liccardo said. “I have been as clear as possible: there was a fundamental failure in relying on communication methods we had, everything from social media to the (county) alert system. I do not shy from the criticism that there should have been direct notification to those residents in all languages that they can understand. The question is, though: what would we have informed them about? That’s why these issues are so connected, because obviously we don't knock on doors citywide any time there is a big storm.”

It appears even more is at play than the district giving vague warnings or the city lapsing in its legal duty to alert the public. In the past week, San Jose Inside has interviewed more than a dozen high-level district and city sources in addition to reviewing emails that trace from years back through the days and hours preceding the floods.

Over the past two decades, district officials have made key decisions that let Coyote Creek flood protection to languish in favor of [pet projects](http://www.sanjoseinside.com/2015/09/23/water-district-chair-calls-for-da-to-investigate-conflicts-of-interest-alleged-improper-billing/)—one of which may have personally benefited the district’s interim chief operating officer, [Melanie Richardson](http://www.sanjoseinside.com/tag/melanie-richardson/), who oversees Silicon Valley watersheds and flood control. Coincidentally, Richardson likely would have been one of the key people in charge of the district’s Emergency Operations Center during last week’s floods, except for one problem—she was on a ski retreat.

![Many vehicles were ravaged by flood water as residents received little or no warning. (Photo by Greg Ramar)](/photos/42-3-771x515.jpg)

**‘What a Mess’**

Jose Villalobos waited a day for the waters to recede before heading back to Rock Springs, a largely working-class Vietnamese and Latino neighborhood in San Jose’s East Side. Some streets were still submerged in a foul lagoon of gasoline and raw sewage, others were covered in slippery muck, strewn with detritus—shredded plastic bags, a deflated Mylar Valentine’s Day balloon, a plastic doll, makeup bottles, sandals and sneakers and a waterlogged skunk carcass.

“See where that car is?” he asked, pointing toward a white SUV in the middle of the road. “They were trying to drive out, but the car died. They had to leave it right there.”

A block away from his apartment, Villalobos pulled two trash bags over each foot to protect his sneakers from the filth. He needed to retrieve some clothes, diapers and other necessities to bring back to his aunt’s house, where his family will stay for the time being.

The bright sun and blue skies seemed incongruent with the still-flooded streets, where several people were venturing back to recover whatever they could from their homes. First responders marked neon orange and hot pink X’s on the buildings and cars to indicate they were clear of evacuees. Dumpsters sat in the middle of the pitted street, having been swept out of place by the rush of water.

“What a mess,” Villalobos said, gingerly stepping his way through the slime.

When he opened the door to his unit, he reeled from the stench and pulled his shirt over his mouth and nose. He walked to the kitchen, leaving behind a trail of footprints on the muddy tile. Pretty much everything on the first floor would have to go, he said—the couches, the tables, the drum set he cherished, his daughter’s toys.

“This is just sad” he said, glancing around the living room, where the watermark rose about a half-foot off the floor. “It’s not normal. I don’t even know what to take right now.”

At least the top floor was spared, he remarked. In his room—the one he shared with his daughter and girlfriend—he unfurled a plastic Target store tote and began filling it up with baby clothes. He stuffed a few more trash bags full of belongings and made sure to grab his girlfriend’s plastic makeup bin.

“Maybe it’s not the most important thing right now,” he said, with a laugh. “But it’ll make her happy. That’s what matters, right?”

Outside the apartment, his landlord, Luis Rascon, crossed his arms and shook his head while surveying the damage. He wanted to start cleaning up, he said, but had to wait on the insurance company.

“It’s hard to sit here and do nothing,” said Rascon, clad in dark denim jeans and black rubber boots. “I live here, too. My dad lives here. My daughter lives here. I want to get to work, but I can’t yet.”

This wasn’t his first flood since moving to San Jose as a young father 27 years ago, he said, but it was definitely the worst. During the Coyote Creek flood of 1997, Rascon lived in the same slate-gray building as a tenant. Back then, the city told them days ahead of time about the impending flood, which gave his family enough time to move their valuables to the second floor.

“This time we didn’t know,” he said. “It came too fast. I didn’t know about it until I got a call at work.”

By then, his building was submerged beneath four feet of water. His elderly father, who was on the second floor, didn’t even notice until Rascon told him to look out the window.

“Nobody told us it was coming,” he said. “We had to tell each other.”

![San Jose Mayor Sam Liccardo visited with residents in Naglee Park the day of the flood but had little info to share. (Photo by Dan Pulcrano)](/photos/IMG_8035-771x578.jpg)

**Good Project?**

In 2000, with the 1997 floods still fresh in their memories, Santa Clara County voters passed the Clean, Safe Creeks Initiative, called Measure B on the ballot. The 15-year parcel tax included what was known as the Coyote Creek Flood Protection Project, which would earmark $32 million for flood mitigation along Coyote Creek. The project just stopped.

District officials say efforts were made to secure federal funding, but these overtures were denied and the district had no choice but to look for “better projects.” Another water parcel tax dubbed Measure B passed in 2012, and other projects became the priority.

One of these projects is Upper Llagas in South County.

According to internal district emails, Melanie Richardson, then a deputy operating officer in charge of watersheds, was told that $8 million to 10 million in Coyote Creek funds got redirected to the Upper Llagas project near Morgan Hill. What makes this decision concerning is that RMC, a contractor overseeing the Upper Llagas project, was part-owned by Richardson’s husband, Tom Richardson. While $20 million sat untouched in the Coyote Creek fund, RMC—and by extension the Richardsons—stood to personally benefit from any rerouting of funds to Upper Llagas.

Starting in 2015, San Jose Inside began publishing a series of stories looking into conflicts of interest at the water district involving RMC, which has since been acquired by Woodard & Curran. Those reports found that Melanie Richardson, who was once the district’s former head of procurement, routinely came into contact with RMC business, despite claims from district executives that a “firewall” had been put in place. These reports prodded the water district’s elected board to successfully push for the resignation of district CEO Beau Goldie last year.

In a phone interview Tuesday, Melanie Richardson defended the firewall and denied being aware of any money moving away from Coyote Creek flood protection to other projects. “I am not aware of that,” she said. “I would have to look at those emails.” She promised to provide answers later in the day but failed to call back before presstime.

In the course of reporting on RMC and the district, San Jose obtained emails that show Melanie Richardson was alerted to the Coyote Creek funding shifts by a subordinate from December 2014 to January 2015. RMC was initially selected to do the Coyote work, emails show, but the contract was canceled after the proposed Anderson Dam retrofit would have changed the scope of work. RMC also attempted to stick the district with project insurance costs, which is against the law.

Acting district CEO Norma Camacho defended Melanie Richardson, now the interim COO of watersheds, in a phone interview Tuesday, noting that her chief deputy may have known about money moving between RMC projects but didn’t have any control to transfer the funds herself.

“She wasn’t actually transferring the funds or the money,” Camacho said. “These were discussions that we had in trying to prioritize the budget.”

Afshin Rouhani, a district unit manager for mid-Coyote Creek, says the flood mitigation efforts voters have asked for and funded going on two decades will simply need to wait until more important projects are completed.

“It’s waiting for a good project to build,” Rouhani said.

However, unless residents have been attending water district board meetings the last few years, they might not have realized they were sliding down the priority totem pole while still paying into the fund.

“We haven't really had the community meeting,” Rouhani admitted.

![Property damage in San Jose has been estimated at $73 million, according to a city request for disaster relief. (Photo by Greg Ramar)](/photos/44-1-771x515.jpg)

**‘Too Late’**

When Sheila McGann-Tiedt heard about the flood coursing downstream last week, she had two hours to prepare. But precious time was lost driving to the water district’s sandbag sites off Phelan Avenue. When the flood closed in around that site, she headed north off Mabury Road. Before the flood of ’97, McGann-Tiedt said, the water district dropped off a bunch of sandbags at William Street Park, a block from her house. This time was different.

“We had no message from the city, no message from the water district about what was coming,” she said, standing on her driveway as a neighbor hosed mud off the sidewalk. “If it weren’t for all those posts on social media, we wouldn’t have known how bad it got.”

Their only official warning came from Councilman Raul Peralez, who went door to door in Naglee Park to tell people to flee their homes. As the waters spilled across the nearby park, volunteers—including Peralez and county Supervisor Cindy Chavez—began filling up sandbags.

“But honestly, it was too late by then,” McGann-Tiedt said.

Luckily, the water pinched off right before her house and flowed into her backyard, sparing the living quarters. Damage to the basement, however, will cost a fortune to fix.

“I feel bad for my neighbors,” McGann-Tiedt said, gesturing toward nearby houses, where volunteers were scrambling to tear up flooring and drywall in a race against the moisture-induced black mold. “They got the worst of it.”

One door down, Judy Georges fought back tears while assessing the damage. She and her husband bought their home off 16th and William streets a few years after the 1997 flood.

“We had no frame of reference for this,” she said. “We didn’t really know what to do—not that we had time to do much anyway.”

She barely had a moment to think.

“We just went through the motions,” Georges said. “We didn’t have time to feel a lot. First, there was the scramble to save whatever we could, then numbness, and then shakiness. I didn’t have the luxury of freaking out.”

Two days after the flood tore through her yard and drenched all her belongings on the first floor, Georges stood on the sidewalk chatting with neighbors.

“People have been wonderful,” said Georges, a humanities professor at San Jose State University. “I can’t tell you how many times people—some of them absolute strangers—have stopped by and said, ‘I am so heartsick for you.’”

Because of the topography of the upscale Naglee Park neighborhood, some homes were unaffected—looking over the toxic loch from high ground. Midday, after the flood flushed Georges out of house and home, she joined a group of fellow evacuees for lunch at a neighbor’s house on high ground, where they shared stories about their loss.

“Lunch was for freaking out,” Georges said. “By dinnertime, we were all cracking jokes and laughing. I guess we needed some sense of normalcy. Maybe we were too exhausted to panic.”

But the anxiety crept back as she stood outside her torn-up home.

“I’m shaking again,” Georges said. “I think the reality of this is really hitting now, the reality of how much we’ve lost.” At least no one died, she added. “That’s the perspective I need to keep. We survived. We all survived.”

![Anderson Reservoir reached the emergency spillway for the first time since 2006, creating a waterfall into Coyote Creek. This photo was taken Feb. 19. (Photo by Robert Eliason, via Morgan Hill Times)](/photos/Anderson-Spillway.jpg)

**Silent Alarm**

District officials claim they sounded the alarm bells loud and clear to the city’s Emergency Operations Center just before 3am Tuesday. This should have left plenty of time for alerts and evacuations. At 2:47am, Jim McCann, a public information rep for the district, emailed Cheryl Wessling, a spokeswoman for the city’s Department of Planning, Building and Code Enforcement, to tell her that water levels along Coyote Creek had reached 6,000 cubic feet per second (CFS) hours ahead of district projections. The magic number for flooding was pegged around 7,000, so one might assume this change presented a clear and present danger.

Wessling asked, “Is this a minor or major change in what we were expecting?”

“\[R\]elatively minor,” McCann wrote back, “in that it’s a few hours earlier than previously forecasted.”

To the layman, this type of language would hardly indicate an impending crisis. But this appears to be one of many instances of insouciance on both the city and district’s part.

Rachael Gibson, a district spokeswoman who worked closely with the mayor’s office days ahead of the flood, routinely offered overly optimistic assumptions. She noted there was “no major update” as of 6:40pm Monday and the district expected peak flows by Tuesday afternoon. Two emails sent by the water district's public affairs team at 8:31am and 8:39am hinted at “incidental flooding along parks and access roads.” As late as 9:41am Tuesday, Gibson told Alex Wilson, a deputy spokesman in the mayor’s office, that nothing had changed from the night before.

By then, Rock Springs was already underwater.

Rick Callender, the district’s communications director, dismissed McCann’s lack of urgency as a failure to read between the lines on the city’s part. He added that Gibson’s erroneous information was irrelevant because she was not in the water agency’s EOC and the mayor’s office had no formal role in evacuations or rescue operations. “If you're not in the EOC, then you really don’t know what was going on,” Callender said.

Vincent Gin, a deputy operating officer in charge of the district’s EOC from Monday evening until about 6:30am Tuesday, said the district was well aware of the “earlier shift” in water levels but didn’t expect flows to exceed 6,000 CFS. By the time Gin clocked off and left Jim Fiedler, COO of water utility, in charge of the district’s emergency command hub, he deemed the situation still manageable.

“We thought that it would be close because some of the channels could handle it,” Gin said. “I did not think it would be this widespread. That’s just my personal opinion.”

A report compiled by a former district employee recommended triggering an alarm system when the water flow in Coyote Creek reached 4,000 CFS, which would have occurred early evening Monday, Feb. 20. The plan shows a flowchart on how to deliver sandbags to Rock Springs within two hours of the alarm. It appears, however, that the district never bothered to finalize the plan, for reasons unknown.

![Screen Shot 2017-03-01 at 12.55.37 AM](/photos/Screen-Shot-2017-03-01-at-12.55.37-AM.png)

For some reason, the city asked the county to help to send those alerts.

County Executive Jeff Smith [said in a county memo](https://www.sccgov.org/sites/scc/Documents/EOC-activation-winter-storms-memo.pdf) to the Board of Supervisors that “each city is responsible for emergency management within its boundaries, and the county is responsible for this role in unincorporated areas.” According to Smith, agencies have to follow that protocol to qualify for state and federal disaster aid. So these so-called official communications don’t really get the word out to these communities. What happened here is the very definition of socio-economic injustice.”

The Franklin-McKinley school district has a better emergency plan than the city’s, Rodriguez added. Once administrators heard about the deluge, they activated a calling tree, began knocking on doors, sent out emails in Spanish and Vietnamese and started fundraising online for the hundreds of students whose families were displaced. Over the weekend, the school held a donation drive that drew about 150 flood victims and a dozen volunteers.

“Listen, a lot of people don’t know where to turn for help,” said Rodriguez, seated amid donated cans of food, diapers, first-aid kits and second-hand clothing in a room at Shirakawa Elementary on Saturday. “Some of our families are undocumented, and there’s this fear that prevents them from turning to other agencies. But they trust their school. This is where they find help.”

Ana, an undocumented woman who declined to share her full name, said the school has become a lifeline. All together, her family lost four cars, she said. Their corporate property management company has offered nothing in the way of reassurance that they could move back, she added, and it’s unclear at this point what she’ll do for transportation or whether she’ll be able to keep her job as a nanny.

“It’s horrible, asking for help,” she said in Spanish, through a translator. “I feel stressed. I feel desperate. I’m not sure what comes next.”

Her sister chimed in: “I need a car. I need a house. I may need a new job.”

“Tell them they can count on the school,” Rodriguez said in English, instructing the translator to relay the message. Looking at Ana directly, he added: “We’re here for you.”

**Crisis Control**

The #Spillgate blame game is just getting started. Mayor Liccardo has shifted for the high road, saying the city accepts total responsibility, although a fair number of surrogates are operating on background. The water district, for its part, has taken an aggressive stance that its responsibility extends only so far as the information it provides—even if that information turned out to be inaccurate or incomplete.

In advance of a protracted legal battle, the district has not only placed a hold on the destruction of all documents, but also paid a $25,000 retainer to bring on PR crisis manager Sam Singer. His previous clients include former Congressman Mike Honda, who was was embroiled in an ethics scandal; the San Francisco Zoo, after a tiger escaped and mauled three teens; and the Oakland Children’s Hospital in the Jahi McMath case, when the young girl was declared brain dead.

None of this solves the greater question of how to properly notify residents in the event of another Coyote Creek flood, which will inevitably happen in the coming years—and all the more frequently because of climate change.

Richard McMurtry, a civil engineer and board member for Friends of Coyote Creek, questioned the district’s contention that it released as much water as it could from Anderson Reservoir in the weeks leading up to last week’s floods. But perhaps even more important, he said, is the need to change the public’s expectations. Watershed protections are designed to withstand a 100-year flood, which has a 1 percent chance of occurring in a given year. Last week’s storm didn’t even meet that threshold.

“What happens when we get a 200-year storm?” said McMurtry. “The whole flood control mentality—you keep building flood mitigation projects and all the people downstream get flooded.”

The public is unlikely to relinquish their homes and make way for levees along Coyote Creek, similar to the concrete floodwalls that line the Los Angeles River. The alternative, McMurty said, is to have all new structures built on stilts, like the ones in Alviso or any number of boroughs that lie in clearly mapped, federally designated floodways.

Until then, it might be wise to stop calling these events once-in-a-generation floods and refer to what they truly represent: the new normal.
