However, unless residents have been attending water district board meetings the last few years, they might not have realized they were sliding down the priority totem pole while still paying into the fund.

“We haven’t really had the community meeting,” Rouhani admitted.

‘Too Late’

When Sheila McGann-Tiedt heard about the flood coursing downstream last week, she had two hours to prepare. But precious time was lost driving to the water district’s sandbag sites off Phelan Avenue. When the flood closed in around that site, she headed north off Mabury Road. Before the flood of ’97, McGann-Tiedt said, the water district dropped off a bunch of sandbags at William Street Park, a block from her house. This time was different.

“We had no message from the city, no message from the water district about what was coming,” she said, standing on her driveway as a neighbor hosed mud off the sidewalk. “If it weren’t for all those posts on social media, we wouldn’t have known how bad it got.”

Their only official warning came from Councilman Raul Peralez, who went door to door in Naglee Park to tell people to flee their homes. As the waters spilled across the nearby park, volunteers—including Peralez and county Supervisor Cindy Chavez—began filling up sandbags.

“But honestly, it was too late by then,” McGann-Tiedt said.

Luckily, the water pinched off right before her house and flowed into her backyard, sparing the living quarters. Damage to the basement, however, will cost a fortune to fix.

“I feel bad for my neighbors,” McGann-Tiedt said, gesturing toward nearby houses, where volunteers were scrambling to tear up flooring and drywall in a race against the moisture-induced black mold. “They got the worst of it.”

One door down, Judy Georges fought back tears while assessing the damage. She and her husband bought their home off 16th and William streets a few years after the 1997 flood.

“We had no frame of reference for this,” she said. “We didn’t really know what to do—not that we had time to do much anyway.”

She barely had a moment to think.

“We just went through the motions,” Georges said. “We didn’t have time to feel a lot. First, there was the scramble to save whatever we could, then numbness, and then shakiness. I didn’t have the luxury of freaking out.”

Two days after the flood tore through her yard and drenched all her belongings on the first floor, Georges stood on the sidewalk chatting with neighbors.

“People have been wonderful,” said Georges, a humanities professor at San Jose State University. “I can’t tell you how many times people—some of them absolute strangers—have stopped by and said, ‘I am so heartsick for you.’”

Because of the topography of the upscale Naglee Park neighborhood, some homes were unaffected—looking over the toxic loch from high ground. Midday, after the flood flushed Georges out of house and home, she joined a group of fellow evacuees for lunch at a neighbor’s house on high ground, where they shared stories about their loss.

“Lunch was for freaking out,” Georges said. “By dinnertime, we were all cracking jokes and laughing. I guess we needed some sense of normalcy. Maybe we were too exhausted to panic.”

But the anxiety crept back as she stood outside her torn-up home.

“I’m shaking again,” Georges said. “I think the reality of this is really hitting now, the reality of how much we’ve lost.” At least no one died, she added. “That’s the perspective I need to keep. We survived. We all survived.”

Silent Alarm

District officials claim they sounded the alarm bells loud and clear to the city’s Emergency Operations Center just before 3am Tuesday. This should have left plenty of time for alerts and evacuations. At 2:47am, Jim McCann, a public information rep for the district, emailed Cheryl Wessling, a spokeswoman for the city’s Department of Planning, Building and Code Enforcement, to tell her that water levels along Coyote Creek had reached 6,000 cubic feet per second (CFS) hours ahead of district projections. The magic number for flooding was pegged around 7,000, so one might assume this change presented a clear and present danger.

Wessling asked, “Is this a minor or major change in what we were expecting?”

“[R]elatively minor,” McCann wrote back, “in that it’s a few hours earlier than previously forecasted.”

To the layman, this type of language would hardly indicate an impending crisis. But this appears to be one of many instances of insouciance on both the city and district’s part.

Rachael Gibson, a district spokeswoman who worked closely with the mayor’s office days ahead of the flood, routinely offered overly optimistic assumptions. She noted there was “no major update” as of 6:40pm Monday and the district expected peak flows by Tuesday afternoon. Two emails sent by the water district’s public affairs team at 8:31am and 8:39am hinted at “incidental flooding along parks and access roads.” As late as 9:41am Tuesday, Gibson told Alex Wilson, a deputy spokesman in the mayor’s office, that nothing had changed from the night before.

By then, Rock Springs was already underwater.

Rick Callender, the district’s communications director, dismissed McCann’s lack of urgency as a failure to read between the lines on the city’s part. He added that Gibson’s erroneous information was irrelevant because she was not in the water agency’s EOC and the mayor’s office had no formal role in evacuations or rescue operations. “If you’re not in the EOC, then you really don’t know what was going on,” Callender said.

Vincent Gin, a deputy operating officer in charge of the district’s EOC from Monday evening until about 6:30am Tuesday, said the district was well aware of the “earlier shift” in water levels but didn’t expect flows to exceed 6,000 CFS. By the time Gin clocked off and left Jim Fiedler, COO of water utility, in charge of the district’s emergency command hub, he deemed the situation still manageable.

“We thought that it would be close because some of the channels could handle it,” Gin said. “I did not think it would be this widespread. That’s just my personal opinion.”

Perhaps even more distressing is that the district drafted an emergency plan in December 2002 that could have prevented much of the damage in Rock Springs. A report compiled by a former district employee recommended triggering an alarm system when the water flow in Coyote Creek reached 4,000 CFS, which would have occurred early evening Monday, Feb. 20. The plan shows a flowchart on how to deliver sandbags to Rock Springs within two hours of the alarm. It appears, however, that the district never bothered to finalize the plan, for reasons unknown.

Just Us

Rudy Rodriguez, a Franklin-McKinley School District trustee, fought back emotion when he spoke at a La Raza Roundtable meeting Friday night, where he went to tell people about the devastation at Rock Springs. Families that already struggle to scrape by will have to start over.

“That was one of the hardest speeches I’ve ever made,” Rodriguez said. “I feel so much for the victims, for all our students.”

One of the emotions he felt was anger—anger toward the city for failing to tell families about the imminent danger. Councilman Tam Nguyen, whose district was hit the hardest, slammed the city for neglecting to disseminate information to Vietnamese residents. Rodriguez said he feels the same about the city’s outreach to Spanish-speaking households: that official outreach was vastly inadequate.

Despite joining more than a dozen conference calls with the county, water district, National Weather Service, Caltrans and PG&E before the first day of flooding, the city didn’t tell anyone to evacuate Rock Springs or Naglee Park. A full day before the Coyote Creek spilled its banks, the National Weather Service sent an urgent “flood watch” alert to phones throughout the South Bay. That same day, the county issued a flood warning to the cellphones of 282 residents of an unincorporated swath by highways 85 and 87 and one about a mudslide to 527 people west of Cupertino and Saratoga.

Days before the flood, virtually every agency in the South Bay knew that Anderson Dam was on the brink of spilling over. The legal onus was on San Jose to notify people within its well-documented floodways about the impending overflow. On the first day of the flood, around 7am, rescuers saved five homeless people stranded in the trees along Los Lagos Golf Course. Yet residents of Rock Springs and Naglee Park received no warning at all. At 9:40am—nearly three hours after the Los Lagos rescue, time that could have been spent sounding the alarm—Rock Springs was under four feet of water. By afternoon, so was Naglee Park. By the second day of the flood, the city finally asked the county to use its cellphone alert system as the dam-spilled torrent barreled northward.

In a memo from the county that summarizes the actions taken by each agency to notify the public, it appears the city relied heavily on the emergency response plans of other entities. Though the county bought and operates the phone warning system, called AlertSCC, each municipality within the region has been trained to use the system independently. For some reason, the city asked the county to help to send those alerts.

County Executive Jeff Smith said in a county memo to the Board of Supervisors that “each city is responsible for emergency management within its boundaries, and the county is responsible for this role in unincorporated areas.” According to Smith, agencies have to follow that protocol to qualify for state and federal disaster aid. The city apparently dropped the ball to such a degree that it may not even be eligible for relief funds.

“The city failed,” Rodriguez said. “They screwed up. They didn’t warn anybody. What they should have done, even within a few hours of the flooding, was start knocking on doors. They had time to do that. They had time to do it right.”

Had that happened, Rodriguez said, Villalobos would have had his car and some of his family’s prized belongings, like his drum set and his daughter’s toys. It’s unacceptable, Rodriguez noted, that some neighborhoods got multiple phone alerts to evacuate while others got none at all.

“The people in charge need to harness the way people communicate on the grass-roots level,” said Teresa Hernandez, a schoolteacher at George Mayne Elementary School in Alviso and activist who lobbed online criticism against the city under the hashtag #Spillgate. “A lot of the people impacted by the flood don’t have smartphones, cellphones, internet, many don’t speak English and use public transit. So these so-called official communications don’t really get the word out to these communities. What happened here is the very definition of socio-economic injustice.”

The Franklin-McKinley school district has a better emergency plan than the city’s, Rodriguez added. Once administrators heard about the deluge, they activated a calling tree, began knocking on doors, sent out emails in Spanish and Vietnamese and started fundraising online for the hundreds of students whose families were displaced. Over the weekend, the school held a donation drive that drew about 150 flood victims and a dozen volunteers.

“Listen, a lot of people don’t know where to turn for help,” said Rodriguez, seated amid donated cans of food, diapers, first-aid kits and second-hand clothing in a room at Shirakawa Elementary on Saturday. “Some of our families are undocumented, and there’s this fear that prevents them from turning to other agencies. But they trust their school. This is where they find help.”

Ana, an undocumented woman who declined to share her full name, said the school has become a lifeline. All together, her family lost four cars, she said. Their corporate property management company has offered nothing in the way of reassurance that they could move back, she added, and it’s unclear at this point what she’ll do for transportation or whether she’ll be able to keep her job as a nanny.

“It’s horrible, asking for help,” she said in Spanish, through a translator. “I feel stressed. I feel desperate. I’m not sure what comes next.”

Her sister chimed in: “I need a car. I need a house. I may need a new job.”

“Tell them they can count on the school,” Rodriguez said in English, instructing the translator to relay the message. Looking at Ana directly, he added: “We’re here for you.”

Crisis Control

The #Spillgate blame game is just getting started. Mayor Liccardo has shifted for the high road, saying the city accepts total responsibility, although a fair number of surrogates are operating on background. The water district, for its part, has taken an aggressive stance that its responsibility extends only so far as the information it provides—even if that information turned out to be inaccurate or incomplete.

In advance of a protracted legal battle, the district has not only placed a hold on the destruction of all documents, but also paid a $25,000 retainer to bring on PR crisis manager Sam Singer. His previous clients include former Congressman Mike Honda, who was was embroiled in an ethics scandal; the San Francisco Zoo, after a tiger escaped and mauled three teens; and the Oakland Children’s Hospital in the Jahi McMath case, when the young girl was declared brain dead.

None of this solves the greater question of how to properly notify residents in the event of another Coyote Creek flood, which will inevitably happen in the coming years—and all the more frequently because of climate change.

Richard McMurtry, a civil engineer and board member for Friends of Coyote Creek, questioned the district’s contention that it released as much water as it could from Anderson Reservoir in the weeks leading up to last week’s floods. But perhaps even more important, he said, is the need to change the public’s expectations. Watershed protections are designed to withstand a 100-year flood, which has a 1 percent chance of occurring in a given year. Last week’s storm didn’t even meet that threshold.

“What happens when we get a 200-year storm?” said McMurtry. “The whole flood control mentality—you keep building flood mitigation projects and all the people downstream get flooded.”

The public is unlikely to relinquish their homes and make way for levees along Coyote Creek, similar to the concrete floodwalls that line the Los Angeles River. The alternative, McMurty said, is to have all new structures built on stilts, like the ones in Alviso or any number of boroughs that lie in clearly mapped, federally designated floodways.

Until then, it might be wise to stop calling these events once-in-a-generation floods and refer to what they truly represent: the new normal.

By Jennifer Wadsworth and Josh Koehn/ March 1, 2017
From Nürnberg-Germany to Stia-Tuscany with a stopover in Silicon Valley

**SILICON VALLEY** is in the news almost every day, discussing stories around the technology giants that truly shape our day. Software and its products are what shapes our lives in so many ways, **not much** of this software is architected in the **VALLEY**. The hardware is what we touch, is what makes it all possible. The heart of the hardware is silicon chips. No one talks about them much in public view.

**As a Silicon Semiconductor Engineer,** I came to Silicon Valley in 1996. I was imported from Germany, almost straight from University. I was fresh, able and hungry for challenges. As a well-trained engineer with an innovative mindset, I did not really fit well into the German workforce. I wanted to stir things up, change things, make a difference. After 2 years of working in Germany, I managed to find a way out, a way up. I landed straight in the **VALLEY**. I made it, I did it, it was a big deal for me to be hired by LSI Logic Milpitas. As proud as you can be, I packed my bags, married my 13 year-long girlfriend and we immigrated to the **VALLEY**. My supervisor was German as well, my US manager is now my good friend.

I was not even fully landed and I already synthesized hardware-based multipliers for the latest technology test chip, did what I was trained to do. The technology just transitioned from _micrometer_ to _nanometer_ technologies. Gates now were no longer wired up "by hand" but "synthesized". All that is GEEK talk. Things went really well for me, I wrote up patents,  my way of thinking and working fit really well into the valley of the time. My manager titled me a "cheap copy of a German" and meant it as a compliment. With a good strategy, to be sure I solved the right problem and being detailed enough to solve the problem right. The **VALLEY** was humming as I saw it. People worked hard and things were moving along at a rapid pace.

After 23+ years in the **VALLEY**, I am hearing a lot of VC talks in coffee shops, employment interviews over the phone or over WhatsApp on the street. People are working from any and all places imaginable and it seems like the earlier cohesion between people**,** is not nearly as strong now. Corporations grew more influential over people's lives and day to day actions. The Valley changed. People needed to do more in less time, people move from one company to the next faster than even 10 years ago. The **VALLEY** seemed too small and more companies expanded their office locations up the peninsula, up to Sunnyvale, Menlo Park, San Francisco and even further North. What I heard way too many times was; It is so crowded here, it takes me 1.5h for a 30mi drive, it takes me 2 h for a 40mi drive, I don't drive there anymore it's just too much time. The accessibility of fun things to do, the quality of life outside of work is what brings so many people here. You work hard, then you play hard. Now the playing hard is much harder to reach. Getting to skiing can be a 5-hour standing expedition, a visit to Yosemite Valley can set you back 6 hours before you know it. Try to visit Napa Valley and you are on the road for 3-4hours. Of course, you do it. It’s your time off.

**Any day of the week can look like this.** Your boss calls you at 10.30PM to discuss the results of the last release. This call just ends before you need to jump on the call with India, to discuss the feature list of the new version, due to go to QA in 23 days. Then, yes you write up the report of the call because no one else can capture it quite the same way you can and no one was in all the relevant meetings and can bring it down to the point just the way you can. You allow yourself to drop to bed well past 1am. Sleep comes later, much later. The next morning, on the way to the office, you take it easy. You take a "Four Barrel Coffee" in a real cup. It is so relaxing to just sit there and slurp your $3.20 espresso, hand made for you, by your favorite Barrista. You feel good about yourself. Life is so good. Only 2.5 minutes after you got your coffee you are back in the car to finish the rest of your 2hour commute. No, you are not bored as you attend 3 conference calls in sequence and then arrange for your oversee travel next weekend for the PVT release meeting in Taipei. The product your CTO relies on for the next company breakthrough. Then your regular 8-hour job starts in the office at 9.30am. ------- I am not exaggerating. 

In a more generic term, I see people creating their own little bubble, the bubble of work-work-work, only this matters, everybody else needs to be excluded from this bubble. It seems like a sate of deep psychological something. I don’t have a name for it. But the power of this bubble destroys friendships, relationships, wealth and more. In the bubble many people don’t work because they need more money, they work because they are so driven by something, something that drives many so many, manages to destroy their life. The out-of-box thinking that draws people into the **VALLEY** now ruins the life they were trying to build. It makes me sad. I am also trying to make a point. Any and all your energy is demanded and expected as a bare minimum effort. Just to have the right to work in your position for this company. All your peers work the same or more than you do, so it seems ok to do that, required to do that. It is no wonder I am seeing more people clearly under the influence of drugs, as an escape and also as the only way to stay in the game and keep up with it all, keep up with peer expectations. Some show the signs of drug use more visibly than others. Still many take it regularly. 

In private conversations I hear more people talking to each other and in a clear tone, talking about their **EXIT STRATEGY**. The way they plan to make it out of this mad circle, out of this **VALLEY**. Making it out alive. Making it out rich. Making it out sane. Making it out at all.

A responsible way out was what I looked for next. I had a lot of choices but really had no choice if I wanted to stay true to myself. Staying was not an option. The **VALLEY** was in the process to change my personality, the very core of who I am. My wife and I decided during our last 2 years that we will not let the **VALLEY** change us and we will exit. We took one year off. We quit the jobs and started our trip around the world. The year was to serve as a tool. A tool to slow down our minds and get us grounded again. From this grounded state of mind, we wanted to make a decision about what to do next. A decision of this magnitude deserves time. It needed to be a process, not an event. In the process of traveling South America, we meet several **VALLEY** people. All, really all of them used the phrase of **EXIT STRATEGY** within the first 10 minutes of conversation. It is on so many people's minds. I was amazed.

**Fast forward**. We are now exiting. We bought a house in Tuscany, we are on our way back to the **VALLEY** and we will sell the house of ours in the capital of Silicon Valley. Just to keep our sanity. Just to stay true to ourselves and stay alive.

Take-away: What I am really trying to say or do with this text is, there is still a huge draw to the **VALLEY.** But there also is a strong outward movement in progress for some time. It is driving the People out of the very jobs that got them here. The very areas they are working in and used to love are turning on them. Some jobs lose the heart and soul, the reason one used to love working there, some are just incredibly demanding, some areas are just too expensive, even for the salaries in the **VALLEY**. The golden handcuffs of money, company equity, status seem to still work, but the tides are certainly turning, the way I see it.

**English**

**San Cristobal de las Casas in Chiapas**

Back up in 2200m elevation, we are hitting our new home for a few days. Chiapas state is really only marginally still Mexico. It is also a lot like I imagine Guatemala to be. The people look different to me here, they eat differently, live in lower and pretty well-built houses. It seems that much fewer non-Mexican tourism is coming here than to other places. Our severe lack of decent Spanish showed "_results_" the last few days. But they do have coffee shops here. I found 3 best in town level ones, one even had a Slayer machine and a Compact grinder. There is some money being invested in good coffee here. The town is pretty small and feels even smaller. 180,000 people and I still found a way to get myself hurt while running. LOOK WHERE YOU RUN, idiot. The old Grandma smiled and talked to me a little concerned, but mostly sounding dismissive, the 2 boys on the street started laughing full out after I must have seemed "_far enough away_" to them. I still managed to get a good run in, steep and steeper, just the way I like it.

![](/photos/img-s.jpg)

We stayed in a Museum, not kidding. [Na Bolom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casa_Na_Bolom). Or House of the Jaguar. A pretty small establishment with big big impact on the area. Positive impact to the natives in the local Jungle and to the nature in the area. Read up on it! A really interesting story that continues today.

![](/photos/nabolom-s.jpg)

Please remind me next time I try and sign up for a 19hour tourist tour, 12 hours of driving, 5 hours of looking, the rest sitting around. Please remind me to say **NO WAY**. While the sites were all really nice and worth it, it was simply torture to do this. I can only imagine what the driver went through. This was a challenging road.

BUT, I will be back here to hike and experience the Jungle there. And with a little luck I might get the chance to meet some locals there too.

Who is up to join me next time??? Really, I am serious. Let's plan something like this. 1-2 weeks in that area would be a great trip.

![](/photos/map-s.jpg)

The town itself was really nothing out of the ordinary to me, it had enough vibes but not all that livable to me. I would go on a bike-through-town "underground" tour next time. [Pura Bicci I](https://www.facebook.com/noimportanpipol/) also found the local UNI scene here.

Back up in 2200m elevation, we are hitting our new home for a few days. Chiapas state is really only marginally still Mexico. It is also a lot like I imagine Guatemala to be. LOOK WHERE YOU RUN, idiot. The old Grandma smiled and talked to me a little concerned, but mostly sounding dismissive, the 2 boys on the street started laughing full out after I must have seemed “far enough away” to them. I still managed to get a good run in, steep and steeper, just the way I like it.

We stayed in a Museum, not kidding. Na Bolom. Or House of the Jaguar. A pretty small establishment with big big impact on the area. Positive impact to the natives in the local Jungle and to the nature in the area. Read up on it! A really interesting story that continues today.

Please remind me next time I try and sign up for a 19hour tourist tour, 12 hours of driving, 5 hours of looking, the rest sitting around. Please remind me to say NO WAY. While the sites were all really nice and worth it, it was simply torture to do this. I can only imagine what the driver went through. This was a challenging road.

BUT, I will be back here to hike and experience the Jungle there. And with a little luck I might get the chance to meet some locals there too.

Who is up to join me next time??? Really, I am serious. Let’s plan something like this. 1-2 weeks in that area would be a great trip.

The town itself was really nothing out of the ordinary to me, it had enough vibes but not all that livable to me. I would go on a bike-through-town “underground” tour next time. Pura Bicci I also found the local UNI scene here.

The Posh or Pox drink from the Mayans is to be treated with CARE. It is super delicious and locally made from a mixture of GOOD stuff, but it gave Mumu and me a really upset stomach for 3 days. Not kidding.

A Trump Insider Embeds Climate Denial in Scientific Research

I should not be surprised, but I am baffled to read about this still going on.

From the NY Times: By Hiroko Tabuchi

- March 2, 2020Updated 8:15 a.m. ET

An official at the Interior Department embarked on a campaign that has inserted misleading language about climate change — including debunked claims that increased carbon dioxide in the atmosphere is beneficial — into the agency’s scientific reports, according to documents reviewed by The New York Times.

The misleading language appears in at least nine reports, including environmental studies and impact statements on major watersheds in the American West that could be used to justify allocating increasingly scarce water to farmers at the expense of wildlife conservation and fisheries.

The effort was led by Indur M. Goklany, a longtime Interior Department employee who, in 2017 near the start of the Trump administration, was promoted to the office of the deputy secretary with responsibility for reviewing the agency’s climate policies. The Interior Department’s scientific work is the basis for critical decisions about water and mineral rights affecting millions of Americans and hundreds of millions of acres of land.

Die Geschichte (Krieg und Atombombe) ist allen Lebenden bekannt. Aufgrund der Goldenen Woche hier hatten wir sehr wenig Auswahl bei der Unterkunft. Wir landeten in einer tollen zentralen Gegend, in einem Ort, der sauber war und alles hatte, was wir brauchten. ABER direkt neben den Bahngleisen und der großen Straße schien das Badezimmer für ein Wohnmobil gedacht zu sein, so klein. Ich konnte mich nicht setzen oder vom Toilettensitz aufstehen und nicht irgendwo auf einen meiner Körperteile treffen. Unglaublich. Der Duschschlauch ist undicht. Das alles zum Preis von 188 US-Dollar pro Nacht. Ansonsten war es ein guter Besuch. Die A-Bomb-Kuppel war aufschlussreich, das Peace Museum hatte eine Wartezeit von mindestens 1 1/2 Stunden, so dass wir nicht gingen. In der Nacht, als wir ankamen, strömte es mit Regen und wir gelangten mit Bier zu einem Ramen-Platz.

Was ist mit dieser Bombe und der verbleibenden Strahlung? Ich weiß, dass die Japaner sehr gründlich sind, aber es ist ein langes Gefühl, eine Site zu besuchen, deren Geschichte so viel mit Strahlung verbunden ist. Dauert die Strahlung nicht fast immer? Wie können all diese Menschen hier leben, sicher mit all dieser Kontamination, fragte ich mich. Was fehlt mir? Der große Unterschied besteht in Art und Herkunft der Strahlung. Wenn eine Atombombe explodiert ODER ein Atomreaktor irgendwie leckt, sind das zwei sehr unterschiedliche Arten von Problemen. Anscheinend ist die auslaufende Reaktorstrahlung die Art, die buchstäblich “für immer” bleiben wird. Die Art einer Bombe scheint so schnell abzuschwächen, dass Menschen in dieser Gegend nach wenigen Jahren sicher leben können. Wie etwa 5 Jahre. LINK - HiroshimaLINK

Das winzige Badezimmer wurde gerade für mich neu definiert.

Inselhüpfen

Es gelang mir, einen Fahrradladen zu finden, der ein für mich angemessenes Fahrrad vermietete. Und es war wie erwartet in einwandfreiem Zustand. Der Laden heißt Poo Grumpy und ich kann ihn nicht höher empfehlen. Er ist jung und alles andere als mürrisch. Ein Laden, der sehr gut zusammengestellt ist, sogar Kaffee. Ich meine guten kaffee Wir haben eine Tasse gratis bekommen, nachdem ich das Fahrrad gemietet hatte und einen Fahrradreifengürtel gekauft hatte. Er hat mir an den Tagen gemietet, an denen er tatsächlich geschlossen ist. Er schloss das Fahrrad vor dem Laden ab, ich nahm es am Morgen mit dem Schlüssel auf, den er mir gab. Nachdem ich fertig war, sperrte ich es einfach wieder ein und steckte den Schlüssel in die Mailbox. VERTRAUEN funktioniert so, ich liebe diese Erfahrungen wirklich. Am nächsten Morgen stieg ich mit der Fähre nach Etajima, einer Insel in der Bucht von Hiroshima. Auf einer ziemlich beliebten Tour führte sie mich den ganzen Weg um die Insel herum, hoffte auf die nächste Insel, radelte um diese herum, hoffte auf die nächste Insel und radelte um diese herum, dann entlang der Küste zurück nach Hiroshima. Es ging so für 110km und 1km Höhenunterschied. Das meiste davon war wirklich Ackerland und Oyster-Ackerland. Einfache Leute machen ihr nicht so einfaches Handwerk. Der Seeblick kam herein und es wurde feucht und salzig, die Aussicht war dadurch etwas gedämpft. Die einzige Versorgung mit Lebensmitteln waren Bauernhöfe in dieser Gegend. Es waren keine Geschäfte geöffnet und keine Restaurants in Sicht. Bis wir den kleinen Laden mit 7 bis 11 erreichten, schienen sich alle Biker für den letzten Energieschub für die letzten 30 bis 40 km nach Hause zu treffen. Die Brücke, die uns auf das Festland zurückbringt, war für die Auffahrt interessant. Ein ziemlich steiler Spiralstil auf der Rampe durchlief 3 vollständige Kreise, bis wir die Brücke erreichten. Ich liebte es.

Spiralbrücke auf der Rampe
Der Rest des Rückweges war weniger landschaftlich, aber nur der letzte Teil, nach Hiroshima zu kommen, machte wegen der vielen Autos und des Verkehrs nicht so viel Spaß. Ich habe eine Menge Autos im Stau passiert. Guten Tag, müder Tag. Mumu hatte einen guten Tag in der Stadt, kaufte Tickets und tat dann, was sie liebte. ==> Win - Win. Hier gab es noch ein weiteres “Muss”, das Tory-Tor im Wasser auf Miyajima. Ein wahrhaft touristischer Ort, TONNEN Menschen kommen mit der Fähre dorthin. Nicht lustig, stressig. Das Gate ist am besten zu sehen, wenn der Tidenstand über 260 mm liegt, was knapp unter dem üblichen Hochwasserpegel liegt. Mumu und ich gingen zum Mt. Misen ist ein 500 m langer Anstieg durch wunderschöne Wälder und bietet Zugang zu einigen Tempeln. Die Aussicht ist von oben großartig. Als wir wieder runter kamen, wurden wir mit den richtigen Pegelständen und einer großartigen Aussicht mit Sonnenuntergang über dem Tor belohnt. Das war wunderbar.

Hmmmm

Das nächste Ziel war Miyazaki auf der Insel Kyushu und das Treffen mit Rebecca.

French

Kyoto est sorti, Hiroshima est dedans.

Donc, il va ici sur ce voyage. On m’a dit qu’Hiroshima est la plus grande ville possible. La configuration a fière allure de la ville, située dans une baie, avec de nombreuses îles autour. L’histoire (la guerre et la bombe atomique) est connue de tous. En raison de la semaine d’or ici, nous avions très très peu de choix en matière d’hébergement. Nous nous sommes retrouvés dans un super quartier central, dans un endroit propre et doté de tout ce dont nous avions besoin. MAIS, juste à côté des voies de train et de la grande rue, la salle de bain semblait avoir été conçue pour un camping-car, si petite. Je ne pouvais pas m’asseoir ou me lever du siège des toilettes et ne pas toucher au moins une partie de mon corps quelque part. Incroyable. Le tuyau de douche fuyait. Tout cela pour le simple prix de 188 $ par nuit. En tout cas, à part ça, c’était une bonne visite. Le dôme de la bombe A était perspicace, le Musée de la Paix avait une file d’attente d’au moins une heure et demie, donc nous n’y sommes pas allés. La nuit de notre arrivée, il pleuvait abondamment et nous avons réussi à nous rendre dans un restaurant Ramen avec de la bière.

Qu’en est-il de cette bombe et du rayonnement restant? Je sais que les Japonais sont très consciencieux, mais il existe un sentiment persistant lorsqu’on visite un site qui a tellement d’histoire liée aux radiations. Le rayonnement ne dure-t-il pas presque toujours? Comment tous ces gens peuvent vivre ici, en toute sécurité avec toute cette contamination je me suis demandé. Qu’est-ce qui me manque? La grande différence réside dans le type et l’origine du rayonnement. Si une bombe A explose ou si un réacteur nucléaire fuit, il s’agit de deux types de problèmes très différents. Apparemment, le rayonnement du réacteur qui fuit est le type qui restera littéralement «pour toujours». Le type d’une bombe semble s’affaiblir à un tel rythme que les humains peuvent y vivre en toute sécurité après seulement quelques années. Comme 5 ans ou plus. LIEN - hiroshimaLINK

La petite salle de bain a été redéfinie pour moi.

île en île

J’ai réussi à trouver un magasin de vélos qui louait des vélos de taille raisonnable (pour moi). Et comme vous vous en doutez, il était en parfait état. Le magasin s’appelle Poo Grumpy et je ne peux pas le recommander plus haut. Il est jeune et est tout sauf grincheux. Un magasin très bien préparé, même du café. Je veux dire bon café. Nous avons eu une tasse gratuitement après que j’ai loué le vélo et acheté une ceinture-pneu-vélo. Il m’a loué le vélo les jours où il est effectivement fermé. Il a verrouillé le vélo à l’extérieur du magasin, je l’ai ensuite récupéré le matin avec la clé qu’il m’a remise. Après avoir terminé, je l’ai simplement remise en place et ai mis la clé dans la boîte aux lettres. TRUST fonctionne très bien comme ça, j’aime vraiment ces expériences. Le lendemain matin, je suis monté sur le ferry pour Etajima, une île située dans la baie d’Hiroshima. Lors d’une randonnée assez populaire, il m’a guidée tout au long de l’île, j’ai espéré me rendre sur l’île voisine, puis j’ai fait du vélo autour de celle-ci, j’ai espéré me rendre à côté de cette île, puis de retour à Hiroshima, le long de la côte. Cela a été le cas pour 110 km et 1 km d’élévation. La plupart de ces terres étaient de véritables terres d’agriculture et d’ostréiculture. Les gens simples font leur métier pas si simple. La brume marine est entrée et elle est devenue humide et salée, la vue a été un peu atténuée à cause de cela. La seule source de nourriture était les fermes de cette région. Aucun magasin n’était ouvert et aucun restaurant en vue. Jusqu’à ce que nous ayons atteint le petit magasin 7-11, où tous les motards semblent se réunir pour profiter de l’énergie du casse-croûte des derniers 30 à 40 km à la maison. Le pont qui nous ramenait sur le continent était intéressant car il se trouvait sur la rampe. Un style en spirale sur la rampe, assez raide, a parcouru 3 cercles complets jusqu’à ce que nous atteignions le niveau du pont. Je l’ai aimé.

Pont en spirale sur la rampe
Le reste du chemin était moins pittoresque, mais seule la dernière partie, entrer à Hiroshima n’était pas aussi amusant, à cause du trafic de voitures et de véhicules. J’ai croisé beaucoup de voitures dans les embouteillages. Bonne journée, journée fatiguée. Mumu a passé une bonne journée en ville, achetant des billets puis faisant ce qu’elle aime. ==> Win - Win. Il y avait un autre site à ne pas manquer ici, la porte Tory dans l’eau sur Miyajima. Un lieu vraiment touristique, des tonnes de gens y arrivent par ferry. Pas amusant, stressant. La porte est mieux visible lorsque le niveau de la marée est supérieur à 260 mm, juste en dessous du niveau de la marée haute habituel. Mumu et moi sommes allés au mont. Misen, qui est une montée de 500m à travers une belle forêt et avec l’accès à quelques temples. La vue est superbe du haut. En redescendant, nous avons été récompensés par les bons niveaux de marée et une superbe vue au coucher de soleil sur la porte. C’était génial.

How US prosecuters seem to be above the law

The way I read this in brief;

- A man is held accountable for a murder he did not commit
- He is held in prison for 18 years,
- Is on Death row for 14 years of this
- The prosecutor of this case knowingly and intentionally withholds evidence of the case that shows him not being guilty (DNA), violating the "Brady Rule"
- The man is set free.
- The man who lost 18 years of his life in prison proves that the US prosecutor did all this just to get a conviction, not to find out the truth and hold him accountable for this act.
- The case goes to the US Supreme court and gets turned down, leaving the prosecutor in office and free to do the same life destructive thing today and tomorrow again.

HRP 2024 is coming - My biggest Party hike yet.

We have now 3 people doing the full distance of the HRP (Haute Route Pyrenees). It is a hike of about 840km distance with about 50km of climbing over this distance. It traverses the complete length of the Pyrenees, trying to stay on the ridge for most of the distance. It traverses between the better known GR10 (France) and GR11 (Spain). These are long established Grande Routes, with trail markers and fully maintained trails. The HRP is not fully defined and multiple versions exist and are advertised. Some segments of the route will go over "use-trails" and are not really marked, which makes finding the right path to a summit or pass a challenge, as I read. But if it was too easy to do, it would not be quiet so interesting.

![](/photos/screenshot-2024-06-20-at-10.53.38.png)

Rosa, Ryan and me will try to walk this trail from beginning to the end. Then we have this incredible group of people that will join us for parts of the way. 2 will start the trail with us (Christian, Alec) , Christian will leave us after 9 days and Kim will join us. Alec will leave on day 11, then Kim will leave us on day 18. On day 38 we plan to leave L'Hospitalet with 8 of our friends from California, now in Oregon and Canada. 2 Families, with 2 Kids each. After 5 days and nights together they will head back and we will go on for another 9 days to finish the trek at the Mediterranean Sea. I read a lot of trip reports about this HRP, but I never read about so many people doing it together to make this hike into such a party. I am super excited and a little nervous about it of course. But I really think we have a good team together and we are setup well for giving this our best shot and make it not only through this trail, but have a lot of fun in the process, see a lot of amazing things during this time.

I plan to send updates to this blog from the trail. Let's see how the internet coverage will be along the way to make this happen as well.

## Some statistics of the team / trip.

- Youngest team member 11, oldest I think 61.

- Nationalities: USA, Germany, Japan, South Korea, Canada

- Base weight of packs: Between 6kg and 11kg

- Planned departure 8th July 2024 from Saint Jean de Luz (not Hendaye)

- Planned finish date in Banyuls-sur-Mer 25 August 2024.

Today was the day off changing of the guards. Christian left us and he left big shoes to fill.... For Kim. He joins us for the next 8 days of the hike. The proper initiation procedure was applied. THE SLIDE. Kim passed and was accepted in the group, of course. We walked 5km on tiny roads, but but up hill steep. The scenery changed distinctly to higher mountains and rocky. Very out open and incredibly beautiful..... again. We climbed 1500m almost in one climb and it took a little bit of a tool on our legs. Even the traverse through this hugely open area was not only with simple footwork. I felt good today but was really tired in the end. A more basic Refugio waited for us, with sink washing but great people and a lake. Good was great and enough and we played two rounds of Mikado with a lot of fun. Tomorrow we want to move away from the main HEP trail and summit a mountain..... or not. Let's see. Stefan

After a good meal and am exciting game of Mikado, we went to bed. Some outside, some inside. After 4h sleeping inside, I woke up and it was so hot, so bad air in our tiny room, I had to escape and went outside with my sleeping bag. Super. We went through our morning wakeup and stretching routine and opted for an alternate route, including a summit. It worked out that the climb we choose was much more technical than anticipated, but we made it up safely, not so comfortable. It took about 2h out of our day and we got into the late afternoon heat. I suffered a lot with it and with the help of salted peanuts and special magnesium I recovered and we made it to the ski town of Candancu'. Incredible scenery and sorry colored mountain sides I will not forget. Again, to much food for dinner and it tastes very good. We are being tested like queen and king here food wise. Tomorrow we will be off to Pombie hut. It should be super scenic. Stefan

We left Gavarine really late, but with one more team member. Gilad, an Israeli young man we meet briefly and had great discussions with over dinner decided to join us for this segment 3. After I strongly encouraged him to lighten his pack by a few kilograms, he switched over with us to the HRP route. Great from the military, he is for enough to do all we can do and then some. Climbing of it of the Gavarine valley, it was still cold, but great for climbing. I got a new set of hiking poles, aluminium ones and they are much much heavier than my previous ones. My shoulders complained about it the whole day. Nowadays, 1500m climbs on the morning don't seem to be a big deal anymore. Days are a bit mixing together. I don't remember details about this day. Day 20 We start the day with a step and long climb again. This time through the clouds. A part of the climb was in shingle type rocks, step and exposed. The way up was a little tricky, the way down in party's plain scary. It might also have been the steepest packed dirt descent i have ever done. It took some time. Two more climbs over adjacent passes and we finally saw the Baroude lakes. That day they presented themselves on cloud cover and with strong wind. It did not prevent us from a dip in the lake, drying off was fast. After dinner the wind died down almost completely and I could sleep under the stars, behind a big big rock. As the wind gusts kicked back into gears, I was a little more protected, at 2400m I was comfortable all night in my little sleeping bag. Meeting two dutch people and chatting with them over dinner was really supper interesting. Max and Natalie where hiking companions on our next day trip to Parzan. Day 21 We took an alternate route over a summit and into a scenic valley and hoped for a hitch hike down to Parzan for food supplies. Only 20 min later we were in a camper van on our way. Lunch in the heat of the e valley together was great. Then phone and battery charging, did shopping and we hiked in the baking sun along the road, only for 1.2km, but it was still no fun. The long long climb up the gravel road was much easier to handle with conversations with our new friends. Almost 4h later we arrived at a little reservoir, does and fetched a close camp site. Late dinner together and in the sleeping bag we go. Day 20 We got a good start, early and in a group. We picked up the two Germans along the trail, also just getting started. Super nice day in the morning but warm afternoon. The decent was through trees and not hard at all. We reached the small Refugio Viados at 12.30, before they lunch kitchen opened. After lunch we needed to face the heat on our way up 850m. First hot, then these last 550m up we're super super steep. I felt strong and good. We are spending the night practically at the pass, near a little lake. We need to get out of the Rutt where we climb in the afternoon, somehow. Tomorrow is another day. Day 22 The night was windy and pretty cold, Ryan almost setup a tent, Rosa helped herself to a Bivi sack to get warmer,Gilad seemed to have a cold child night. I only had trouble with the for opening of my sleeping bag and had cold feet as a result. A we are on a GR10 trail, footwork is much easier and we make faster progress. We decendet to the next hour for about 2h and had bad coffee and expensive sandwich before we moved on, re - united with it new German hiking friends, Kilian and Katie from Munich. 7 people in total we matched down towards the bottom of the valley and a restaurant, with great talks and good company. Time flew by and we had lunch pizza and FRESH salad. Amazing. Matt, Kilian and Katie stayed there and got food supplies while we marched in the heat, up to three unmanned Refugio for tonight 800m climb on the road. Mountains are huge again here and colors and patterns simply amazing. We could briefly talk to the Guardia Civil people that just returned from their hiking/climbing training. Impressive people. We meet another Spanish hike at the hut after eating out clothes and ourself. Spanish people are amazing and super friendly and humble. His dogs name is Massai and super cute.... Really. Today we had a cold dinner with our far traveled salame and cheese. Looks like tomorrow might finally be an easier day. Let's see.

I only had trouble with the for opening of my sleeping bag and had cold feet as a result. A we are on a GR10 trail, footwork is much easier and we make faster progress. We decendet to the next hour for about 2h and had bad coffee and expensive sandwich before we moved on, re - united with it new German hiking friends, Kilian and Katie from Munich. 7 people in total we matched down towards the bottom of the valley and a restaurant, with great talks and good company. Time flew by and we had lunch pizza and FRESH salad. Amazing. Matt, Kilian and Katie stayed there and got food supplies while we marched in the heat, up to three unmanned Refugio for tonight 800m climb on the road. Mountains are huge again here and colors and patterns simply amazing. We could briefly talk to the Guardia Civil people that just returned from their hiking/climbing training. Impressive people. We meet another Spanish hike at the hut after eating out clothes and ourself. Spanish people are amazing and super friendly and humble. His dogs name is Massai and super cute… Really. Today we had a cold dinner with our far traveled salame and cheese. Looks like tomorrow might finally be an easier day. Let’s see.

\

Day 23

We started from our charming and unmanned Refugio reasonably early, paying from our newly found fried Jaime from Spain, blueberry farmer with an amazing body and smile. Rocky path made walking slow and draining. The sick that I lost in the dying line only minutes before I wanted to pick them up will be missed. The climbs up the pass was pestered with big and lose rocks, same procedure on the way down to Lauset Refugio, a very modern hit. Spaghetti carbonara and a beer made us ready for the rest of the decent..... Almost. It got really step and very very tiring as we descended die hours over big rocks with huge steps. Amazingly beautiful, but so hot and so draining. Getting to the road we hoped to get to the Refugio for some dinner and sleep. We got none of these and only received a sandwich. The only really unfriendly Spanish people so far made it a point to be sure we will remember him in a bad light. Sleeping in the first near bye was fine and dark, but we could hear the reasonably busy highway. Day 24 We did not get started too early but made good progress as we finally climbed in the morning again. Phuuuu. A cute mix of first trail and steep rocky climbs brought us up to the coll. We decided on the shorter route based on our tiredness. Another 2 hours of draining descent through great landscapers followed, in 32C hear. Frequent stops die water on the body and into the body kept is in a same state. The last ascent was probably 100% in parts. The Refugio Restanca is on a beautiful lake, but you are not allowed to swim in it. But warm hearted people and warm shower was well received. We enjoyed the first long afternoon without hiking in many many days. Welcome by the body and mind. Incredibly, or friend Max joined us in the hut after 19.00 . He is one tough guy making 1.5 of our least tough days in only one day.... Maybe more.

Day 25 We left Restanca around 8.00, 5.5h of step up and down passes to get to the next refugio for lunch. In the shade we chatted and had deliciousness. The scenery there was fantastic, relatively similar to the sierra Nevada in California. A pretty popular path brought us down valley in a lot of hiker company. Large meadows and small forests in the middle of a big valley. That all ended at a parking lot and we ended up in a street. Waiting for a car to hitchhike or one of the frequent tacos to bring is the 8km to Salardu. With a good stop at a swimming hole we were in a good mindset and started walking. Several cars stopped, but only later two cats took all of us, saving us a long boring walk. It seems like Salardu is a significant ski town in the winter. The resort looks big and interesting, having plenty of randomee ski options as well. Well well well, maybe one day. The hotel was easily found and or did supply packages have arrived there. Good good!! Clean sleep in a bed. Small things can make a difference.

Day 42I had a horrible night with snoring companions and a beating heart because of the 14.30 espresso I drank. Moved out to the Picknick Bench to finally get some sleep, only to be awaken by rain. Inside I slept in the entry room on the floor, with motion controlled bright lights. Not optional. I need another good night again. We had to say a sad good bye to the 8 friends of this last 4 days of hiking. It was amazing to have you part of the trip, incredible that all the details happened as we all wanted, super that none of the possible bad travel events happened and we could see you again. Some of you after 4+ years. Incredible. With our new team member Erica, friend of Rosa, we got started and managed to see a bunch of beautiful lakes in the way down to Bolquere ski resort town. We caught a good store open still and got some food for the night and the next day. We managed to get a hitch to Enye with the first or second car we put the thumb out. That is a record. A gentle climb through beautiful forrest on an easy path. This way we will shave off distance and climbing of the day tomorrow. Found a great camping spot right next to the river. Awesome. Day 43 It was a cold night but nothing serious. Early start and lots lots of wind with cold temperatures almost the whole day. But the day was one of my favorite days of the trip so far. The climbs were plentiful but easy, the views amazing and breathtaking. We probably summited 6-7 peaks in the process, one close to 3000m. Arriving at a Spanish Refugio is always a treat. So was today. Yes, of course, how can I help you and a smile is a great standard to have.

We finally had our first rain day. We could have done without, but it fits with our first day of camping out ...... Maybe. Train at night, so we stretched the breakfast or longer. It paid off as we had about one hour of walking without much rain. But the rest of the day was almost solidly rain, but some times it ended up dry. Great views came out of it, and really wet feet. The landscapers are simply beautiful and amazing every day. The paths we walked through were so scenic, I am simply impressed. Our camp spot left much to wish for, but we did not have great other options. Two additional down sides where, 1) i found one sardine can opened up in my pack, leaving pull in many places it should not be. 2) I broke my Spork on first use. Cheers Stefan and team

The horses fashion seems to shift towards blonde with brown for in this area, and they are beautiful. Had amazingly good lunch along the way at Chalet Pedro, incredible. We had a great night in this Gite' etape in Iraty. We could cook there and eat outside, meet some new people. A great time. Alec and Ryan cooked is some pasta we had a bottle of beer and wine, we could stay outside till late. Very good evening. The hike liked of with a super step party, right at the beginning, I felt strong and the views were far and fabulous again. But the wind was super strong. Because of this, we had to alter out route and decided not to climb the first 2000+m peak of our trip today. Lentil clouds on top convinced is. Right at the start of this traverse, I started feeling weaker, not bad, but maybe 75% of me. The stretch around these two peaks was harder work but again amazingly beautiful. After our lunch, strength came back a bit. Going down to our night camp Ardane. So so many sheep today, incredible. We seem to be all setup for a calm night today. Dog rolls in and out, it's warm and have our couscous coconut curry with veggies for dinner. Dates and other bars for dessert, tea to finish it all up. Another fabulous day.. It's now one week that we walk. 19km 700m climbing.

I missed to mention yesterday that we managed to buy some amazing cheese from a sheep farmer along the way. A bit without electricity and I think 2 Rooms, 2 dogs. A gentile reminder of all the luxuries we take for granted.

Today we had to say good bye to Alec. What a joy to have him with us for 11 days. Really sad to see you go. We had another really really late start 9.30. or was already really warm again and we had to walk up a street for quiet some time. Which convinced us to take a chair lift up the first 400m climb. 1st time in my life taking the lift in the summer. We have very rocky and steep terrain here with lots of little lakes. There number if people became much much more. We are in the national park now and it shows. I did not go up the extra credit summit but used the time to sleep a little after my snoring infested night. We went along a few more beautiful lakes, then prepped for our big and hot ascent to a pass with filling water bottles and soaking all our clothing in water, just to cool us down there and before we go up. It was so worth it. Rosa in the lead we all cruised up the 700+m pass. Water bottles at the ready, legs moving strong. It took quiet a while till we finally reached the Pombie hut. We set up tent and jumped in the lake and meet or now"long" term friend Jasper from Belgium again. And interesting and nice guy who wants to bag some peaks for his license of a French mid mountain guide. We made dinner together sharing stories and cooking ingredients and meals. Only till the British man was called over to join us. Very interesting guy who seems to take his time with this Pyrenees crossing. Every day we hike, takes him roughly 3 days. Between yoga and meditation in the morning and the seemingly strickt time Limit of, 3h of hiking a day, his progress is slow. Super conversations that night and I'm the morning.

Day 13 I could convince the team to get up early to avoid most of the heat and get to our destination at a reasonable time. Breakfast at 6:30 and leaning around 8.00. The day started with a split team. Rosa and me, Ryan and Kim. Based on my experience 2 days ago, getting overheated, i wanted to minimize the chances of this, almost any way I can, knowing we will have a1350m ascent that day, in one stretch. It ended up to be out toughest day. The climbs was hard, but that was not the problem. Both groups managed to miss judge an intersection and avoid double checking the route, leading to us all clinking the wrong pass. We all fixed this in very similar ways, which lead is the the actual crux of the day. Climbing "Port du Lavedan" a series of hard to find crossings in Boulders, then Slate rock crossings followed by the challenge to find the right position to actually cross this pass, then crossing it in near vertical orientation, then not killing your team mate by intimidating any rockfall towards them. Not an easy task, for the mind and the body. It was followed up by a number of snow field crossings, in soft snow that where risky but not overly difficult. Seemingly endless lose rock descents taxes the already will utilized body and mind. I managed to slip on a flat section and rescued myself with a nice roll in the grass. No damage to me, but one of my hiking poles got crushed in the process. Even the mental break with some snacks could not avoid that fall and loss. We managed to do the 17km and 1350m climbing in about 9.5h. ~1.8,km/h. And we were moving almost all the time. Ryan and Kim managed to get here just as dinner was served. We had some very productive and honest discussions about group communication and how to refine it after dinner. The team of the Pombie Refugio was simply amazing. All women, only one young guy as the staff. One comes from the Pyrenees an cannot live anywhere else but I'm the mountains or on the Sea ⛵. She has lots and lots of energy, is funny friendly and really unique. Others where very personable and accommodating, nice..... Super team. Ryan decided that his shin split did not recover after our one ZERO day and decided to take a 3 day break from walking. We will meet him up in Garverin in 3 days. Day 14 (+1) We managed to get the team to breakfast at 6.30 with tent packed and backpack ready(almost). But it was still impossible to get started walking before 8.00 . The walk down from the hut was like in a fairy tale. Two mountains on both sides, the sun on the top, shade in the valley floor, a creek flowing through the few trees. 2h down hill and we dropped Ryan of with a friendly Spanish father and son to bring him or of the mountains. We started out 1350m climb on reasonably Smith trails, the Meadows sprinkles with rocks looked amazing in the rising sun. Several hours later we made it to the top and it was beauty again to be seen. We also met a Spanish family, shared good with them and good stories. We went down together, only to find out that the Mama is kind of obsessed with swimming in mountain lakes. So we joined in one doing session and the water was chilled down by the ice patches. Also small salmon was there. What a beautiful family. Activity, curiosity, honesty, togetherness; I loved to see all that. We ended up having dinner together in the Walton Refugio. Great times to be part off their group. Before I understood what was going on, they changed their hiking plan for the next day, just to be with us some more. We sleep outside again today after a cold shower. Day 15 (+1) Super sleep last night for me, Rosa has trouble as she forgot her pillow in the last Refugio. We had breakfast with our new friends and then headed out at a record time for us 7.45. It was plain out a little chilly and the morning light proved again to be amazing. It is so nice to walk when it is still cold. Pleasant conversations helped all of us to get over the continuous climbing, then, just below the first pass Marine was drawn to swim in another lake. Rosa followed the call while the rest of us tested, are and chatted away. The colored stripes on this one mountain gave it an amazing lol and structure. Beautiful! We made it to "Aulettes de Gaube" in unserer 5h with all the fun. Lunch there and beer for the group, great Spanish ham and a lot of love to go around. We exchanged phone numbers with a clear promise to see each other again very soon. Madrid is not so far and they have snow there at least once a year...... Good bye had to come and we headed for our destination of the day, Refugio de Bayssellance. In the afternoon sun we apply A/C water to all exposed parts and head up the 600m climb without much trouble. Meeting an Israeli gut who just started drawing this week, a Belgian guy and later after dinner at the hut meet his two German friends too. Living in the northern most corner of Germany, 5min from the Danish border. The views of the cirque de Gavarine were fantastic and we discovered a most displaced pyramid, right next to it. Another night in the tent this time higher and dryer. Good night. Going for internet tomorrow.... Finally after 5 days without.

Stefan

HRP - LANDING in society and back home

I am so happy and overwhelmed by all the things and all the people that happened to me during the 7 weeks of walking in July and August, it is hard for me to process, even harder to spell it out in words. But it seems like writing things down / writing about it is a good way to process things. So here we go, take it or leave it. This Blog is mostly for my own processing of events that touched me, and this one did touch me in a lot of different ways.

1st I have to say, that I expected this trip to be physically hard and long, I prepared for it for at least 9 months and felt pretty good about my conditioning. Maybe even to the point that I felt a little over-prepared. How wrong was I??!! I also considered this 7 weeks trip to be another level of mental challenge. And that part was 100% spot on. The HRP was not only longer, but longer in every day **km** walked and meters of elevation **climbed** and **descended**, but most significantly, it proved challenging when looking at the **type of trail surface** we needed to move over. This is an effect I knew about of course, but found hard to assess before starting the day's route. Some days we only walked 7km, but it took us 6 hours to get this done and we were really tired mentally and physically. Other days, with similar gradients up and down, could have 25km and we would manage this day with relative ease in 6-7 hours. Hiking 7-11 hours a day, day after day played tricks with my mind. We had the whole day, tried to be efficient with our use of time, and still ended up falling short of some of the things we needed to do in our time AFTER hiking. My mind was focused more and more on only the things that are essentially needed for the next task at hand. Things like washing sox, walking shirt, shorts; seeing the rest of the gear in working order through sewing, patching, gluing, ..... keeping your body limber and ready for the next day, massaging parts that needed help, cooling parts that might cause trouble the next few days through inflammation or other symptoms of overuse, massaging feet, legs shoulders, .... all that between arriving at camp from a long day of hiking and before dinner had to be cooked or we could get it from the Refugio. Sounds like a lot? YES. That was only to take care of the body. What do I do to this mind of mine? Isolate myself? Listen to music? Meditate? Talk to others some? Sleep? Do you even have time for this or should I better use the 10 min before dinner to take some amazing Pictures of this area we are in? It seems to me now, that life was reduced to a minimum of absolute necessities. This is fine with me, I am a simple-minded guy, I don't need a lot of the fluff of daily life that is offered on many city street corners, shops, malls, and online. 

I want to share one event of one night about 8 days before the finish. I usually sleep like a rock, fall asleep fast and only wake up to get up and start the day. This one day, I could not fall asleep. I was not calm at all and I felt a lot of emotions coming from my heart area. I never felt that way before, I did not understand what was going on and did not know if I needed to be worried about it or not. But I was not worried about this, just super interested and curious. After I sat up straight in our tent for several minutes, not knowing what to do, Ryan woke up next to me. Good, I thought, someone I can talk to about this and he will listen and try to understand. So we talked, and finally, I told him that most likely Ineeded a hug. A good one, let's see if this does something. Oh boy. Did it do something!! I started crying for a few minutes and I could feel how much it helped. So we hugged some more. If anyone here knows Ryan, he is a World-Class hugger. When I stopped crying we talked some more about what all that could be about and finally, I decided that it should be ok to try and sleep now. Hand in hand, we fell asleep and I slept like a rock. What an experience!! Analysis with a number of different people made it pretty clear to me that it must have been the tension of organizing it all, thepressure of every day to do what we did, and now the relief that we only had another 7-8 days to walk and we would be done. No more major obstacles to overcome. We had a pretty good shot at completing this mission. All this mixed up in my chest and mind made it necessary to cry those tears of relief and let all this come out of me.

## Re-entry

After our last day of hiking, in the heat, in the strong wind, downhill for what seemed forever, the last 2 hours of what seemed to be walking into the stream of a hot hairdryer; the effect did not show yet for me. Emotions took the driver seat and relief, happiness was the dominating emotion. Even when we ate our leftover food near the beach, with no issues, finding a hotel room ... dinner, and sleeping breakfast all failed to show a big impact on me. But arriving in Barcelona changed everything. I felt completely lost. I was at a loss of meaningful thoughts for the situation and without any idea of what to do, or what to do about it. After a small beer Ryan and I sat on a rental bike to see some sites. We did not seem to find what we were after. We decided to lock the bikes and eat some overpriced tourist foods and a BIG beer. I remember looking at the people passing by on this Sunday afternoon and many thoughts and questions came to mind. These people seemed so "conditioned" so much living a "shell life" Some seemed truly empty, without purpose or reason. I think insome ways, coming from where I came from, this was very much life without purpose. Why are you walking around with this pretty dress / fancy shirt, make-up, handbag, ..... Why aren't you doing something productive to your goal of today?How can you NOT have a goal today?

These are just the thoughts I remember. I am sure there was much more going on in my head at the time. I also don't want to create the impression I judged any of these people in any way. These were just thoughts of this time, of this state of mind of mine, coming from the 7 weeks of hiking I did. Just a little snapshot I wanted to recall because I think this might not come much more often in my life. It reminds me a little of what I believe the movie "[Poor Things](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poor_Things_\(film\))" wanted to highlight, among many other things. Society conditions us all.

## [HRP 2024 is coming – My biggest Party hike yet.](https://gorunamountain.wordpress.com/2024/06/24/hrp-2024-is-coming-my-biggest-party-hike-yet/)

Posted on [June 24, 2024](https://gorunamountain.wordpress.com/2024/06/24/hrp-2024-is-coming-my-biggest-party-hike-yet/)

We have now 3 people doing the full distance of the HRP (Haute Route Pyrenees). It is a hike of about 840km distance with about 50km of climbing over this distance. It traverses the complete length of the Pyrenees, trying to stay on the ridge for most of the distance. It traverses between the better known GR10 (France) and GR11 (Spain). These are long established Grande Routes, with trail markers and fully maintained trails. The HRP is not fully defined and multiple versions exist and are advertised. Some segments of the route will go over “use-trails” and are not really marked, which makes finding the right path to a summit or pass a challenge, as I read. But if it was too easy to do, it would not be quiet so interesting.

![](/photos/AD_4nXfXBHx1en2rdMcu-FdSX2o5tBA9K_EpT0Jas18QlLDhqHyv7HzGMHx83WzmCQlzbF2_qfvICbuOpAAvCc0eSDBYp3ScZUbmzd0b97IfUvzqp4MeYztC0W6TJJU99khaoIVIgzYN)

Rosa, Ryan and me will try to walk this trail from beginning to the end. Then we have this incredible group of people that will join us for parts of the way. 2 will start the trail with us (Christian, Alec) , Christian will leave us after 9 days and Kim will join us. Alec will leave on day 11, then Kim will leave us on day 18. On day 38 we plan to leave L’Hospitalet with 8 of our friends from California, now in Oregon and Canada. 2 Families, with 2 Kids each. After 5 days and nights together they will head back and we will go on for another 9 days to finish the trek at the Mediterranean Sea. I read a lot of trip reports about this HRP, but I never read about so many people doing it together to make this hike into such a party. I am super excited and a little nervous about it of course. But I really think we have a good team together and we are setup well for giving this our best shot and make it not only through this trail, but have a lot of fun in the process, see a lot of amazing things during this time.

I plan to send updates to this blog from the trail. Let’s see how the internet coverage will be along the way to make this happen as well.

### Some statistics of the team / trip.

- Youngest team member 11, oldest I think 63.

- Nationalities: USA, Germany, Japan, South Korea, Canada, France

- Base weight of packs: Between 6kg and 11kg

- Planned/actual departure 8th July 2024 from Saint Jean de Luz (not Hendaye)

- Planned finish date in Banyuls-sur-Mer 25 August 2024.  Actual finish day August 24.

- Actual rest days:
    - Larbet Refugio after 13 days of hiking.
    
    - Salardu on day 27
    
    - L'Hospitalet (Ax de Terme) on day 35 for 2 days

- Trail we followed was a mix, but mainly the Cycerone HRP guide. There are a few shortcomings to the way the guide is written in my view, but it is a very good guide through this concept of a hike, rather than a trail.

Rain at night, so we stretched the breakfast a little longer. It paid off as we had about one hour of walking without much rain. But the rest of the day was almost solidly rain, but sometimes it ended up dry. Great views came out of it, and really wet feet. The landscapes are simply beautiful and amazing every day.  
The paths we walked through were so scenic, I am simply impressed.  
Our camp spot left much to wish for, but we did not have great other options.  
Two additional down sides where,

- I broke my Spork on first use.  
    

Cheers  
Stefan and team

## [HRP Day 7](https://gorunamountain.wordpress.com/2024/07/16/hrp-day-7/)

Posted on [July 16, 2024](https://gorunamountain.wordpress.com/2024/07/16/hrp-day-7/)

We had a great night in this Gite’ etape in Iraty. We could cook there and eat outside, meet some new people. A great time. Alec and Ryan cooked some pasta and we had a bottle of beer and wine, we could stay outside till late. Very good evening.  
The hike started off with a super steep climb, right at the beginning, I felt strong and the views were far and fabulous again. But the wind was super strong. Because of this, we had to alter our route and decided not to climb the first 2000+m peak of our trip today. Lentil clouds on top convinced us to make this change. Right at the start of this traverse, I started feeling weaker, not bad, but maybe 75% of my usual. The stretch around these two peaks was harder work but again amazingly beautiful. After our lunch, strength came back a bit. Going down to our night camp Ardane. Sooooo many sheep today, incredible. We seem to be all set for a calm night today. Clouds roll in and out, it’s warm and we had our couscous coconut curry with veggies for dinner. Dates and other bars for dessert, tea to finish it all up. Another fabulous day.. It’s now one week since we started walking.  
19km 700m climbing.

Let’s see.
