# Quantum Politics: Part I

by [Amit Goswami](http://www.amitgoswami.org/author/feadmin/ "Posts by Amit Goswami") | Mar 31, 2015 | [Articles](http://www.amitgoswami.org/category/articles/ "View all posts in Articles")|

## Quantum Politics: Part I

By Dr. Amit Goswami

The concepts of state, citizens, and politics—the relation of state and its citizens, the relation between various sovereign states, etc.—are all quite old. Also what is old is the idea of elitism and hierarchy in politics.  It has been argued for millennia that the governing body of an organization—that’s what a state is—must have expertize that ordinary people do not have; they must belong to an elite.  And since the elite in this way consists of superior people, the governors and the governed must form a simple hierarchy in which the upper level (governors) dominates the lower level—the governed. For millennia, states and their politics have been organized by elites of various kinds in the form of kings, aristocrats, oligarchy, and all that.

Things were expected to change when, with the advent of modern science, a new economic system calledcapitalismwas discovered that tended to remove the economic elite by promising a redistribution of wealth to form a vast middle class.  And indeed capitalism initially delivered.  Along with the idea of liberal education based on a liberal philosophy that all people are created equal and capable of acquiring expertise and making money, the idea of democracy—government of the people, by the people, and for the people—also took hold.  All this happened as recently as the eighteenth century.

What does it mean to say government of the people and by the people?  It was recognized, again millennia ago, that our best chance at equality in democracy lies in electing representatives of the people from amongst ourselves. What does it mean that these representative elected will work for the people?  Democracy works only if these representatives use their political power to empower the people who elected them.  So empowered, other people, even ordinary people, will seek and find election.  In this way, power will rotate among the electorate, and elitism will be eliminated.

What is amazing is that at least in the United States and much of Europe, this “dream” of eliminating elitism in democracy and society in general was taking fruition in the twentieth century.  In the 1970s, fully eighty percent of Americans belonged to the economic middle class with a large number of them college educated.  Even women and racial minorities were getting opportunities to fulfill the American dream—if you worked hard enough, you could move up anywhere in society including being elected president of the country. But subsequently, this movement toward equality stopped.  Why?

I have already mentioned the role of modern science in initiating all these movements toward equality.  Before the advent of science, the worldview everywhere was based on what religions told us.  Religions had a very old concept of hierarchy from the beginning, that of an almighty God who is the ruler of the universe.  To make God acceptable along with the religious oligarchy of the leaders of religion (the Church) to the governing elite, early on, religions made a compromise of power sharing with the tacit agreement that the king or aristocrats are specially chosen by God (who else?) to rule the rest of the people in worldly matters.  The king or aristocrats, in their turn, agreed to the hierarchy of the Church in religious matters.

Science challenged the authority of the Church to such an extent that a new compromise, a new worldview, came about. It was a truce calledmodernism: worldly matters were to be settled by science; but religious matters still belonged to the Church’s authority. Science was dominated by laws; laws knowing no elite, thereby equally applied to all material things. So naturally the idea grew that societies for dealing with worldly matters should also be governed by laws, not arbitrarily by the whim of elite kings and aristocrats who were beyond the laws. Capitalism and liberal education that “liberated people” from religious dogmas helped this transition to democracy and the rule of law.

However the religious influence on society did not entirely go away.  Since the mind or psyche of people was God’s territory, here God’s rules–be good, be truthful, love everyone, otherwise known as ethics—ruled the roost.  Of course, these rules were still interpreted by the Church and you could find discrepancies in how they were applied.  For example, you never loved everyone equally, certainly not people who belonged to other religions, etc.

And this was good.  Human civilization made giant strides under the worldview of modernism.  Witness the three pillars of modern civilization: capitalism, democracy, and liberal education.

As science progressed, scientists became curious about the affairs of the psyche as well and soon discovered enough regularities (laws?) to bring to question God’s authority and, thus, also the Church’s authority.

The idea of matter-mind duality seemed to violate a sacrosanct scientific law that was discovered in the nineteenth century, the law of conservation of energy—energy of the physical universe alone always remains a constant, in all transactions. The thinking went like this: if the nonmaterial psyche interacted with matter, such interactions must involve signals that carry energy, and so energy would escape and enter the physical universe contrary to the energy conservation law.

So the psyche must not be a separate dual object; instead it must be a material phenomenon; our feelings, thoughts, even intuitions are nothing but the play of the material brain.  Dualism is out. Let’s face it, religions are assuming dualism—God is separate and dual from the world.  God and religions must give way to thinking that matter is the only reality, matter and its interactions causing material movement in space and time.  This thinking is called thephilosophy of scientific materialism.

With God and the underlying hierarchy of God reigning over us gone, democracy and the advancement of equality should get a boost, right?  Wrong.

First of all, religionists did not surrender. To them it is equally appalling that we should be depicted as material machines only subjected to material laws.  How about God’s laws, ethics?  Without ethics, how can our social organizations function?

But religions notwithstanding, with the advent of scientific materialism, ethics lost its luster.  Even religionists’ belief in ethics was shaken.  Everybody became a little confused, cynical, wishy-washy about following ethics. After all, ethical laws don’t seem to be binding, do they?  If you try to violate gravity, you will take a fall, an immediate punishment.  But if you violate an ethical necessity to sustain democracy such as using your power to empower people, not you, there is no discernible punishment, is there?

So the immediate consequence of the advent of scientific materialism was that ethics went away from politics; politicians unabashedly began to use their power to dominate others and perpetuate hierarchy.  This is a movement that began in America as a conservative movement in the 1980s (and it is still continuing), and this movement has all but stopped the liberal movement towards equality.

And in truth, the liberals, the believers in equality, also took a step backward as they continued to slide down the slippery slope of science and scientific materialism.  They, too, became subscribers to a new kind of hierarchy—a hierarchy of meritocracy, of people who have the capacity of processing knowledge and information, especially the latter (more and more of it), to their advantage.

This requires some background analysis.  The ideal of equality, as philosophers such as John Locke and Thomas Jefferson adapted, originally came from mystical thinking, the precursors of the world’s religions.  Mystical thinking everywhere, millennia ago, was the same, in India, in the Middle East, in Greece:  we should follow ethics, because underneath our separateness we are all one and therefore have a responsibility to one another’s well being.  There is no God hierarchically telling you what to do.  It is you, your “inner self,” your conscience which is telling you to help your neighbor.  But religionists who started with the noble intention of selling this truth to the populace found it a hard sell.  So they simplified their pitch for ethics in terms of reward and punishment from a hierarchical God, a stern father figure, a personification of our mystical unity.

There is more.  In the eighties, just as the conservative movement of politics lost its faith in ethics and God because of scientific materialism, philosophers called deconstructionists began to shake the faith of liberals by deconstructing the idea of oneness of mystical philosophy shaking the liberal faith in ethics.

The net result is: today, politicians, liberal and conservative, do not follow ethics themselves; albeit they pay lip service to ethics for fear of political repercussions if they don’t.  They use their power to dominate others, not to empower people to participate in the democratic process.  Without such participation from the grass roots, the same group of people—the elite—stays in power perpetually.  For these reasons—hierarchy and elitism—we don’t see democracy working in America (and other nation-states, too) today.

And it has become even worse, if you can imagine a worse scenario than this. The two elite factions support different competing worldviews: the conservatives gravitate toward the old dualist worldview of religions: the liberals toward the new worldview of scientific materialism.  Both worldviews are dogmas, exclusive views of how the world works.  With ethics gone, the followers of the two opposing dogmas develop intolerance toward one another.  When the intolerance becomes pathological, they cannot even compromise enough to govern smoothly.  The democratic ideal “government for the good of the people” is forgotten.  The ideal upon which the very concept of nation-state is based, namely, the state is for us and we are for the state (all for one and one for all) is also forgotten.

Is there a remedy for this situation?  This situation is against the evolutionary movement of consciousness toward more justice, more love, more goodness, and more abundance that was going on under modernism; that much is clear.  So what is consciousness doing to correct this aberration?  Well, the same movement of consciousness that created scientific materialism has given us quantum physics, a physics of extraordinary power to integrate.  Quantum physics is based on the idea that objects are possibilities for consciousness to choose from.

Can this one idea unify the two poles of the dogmatic worldview of politics in America and other nation-states?  Can this one idea rescue us from elitism in politics?  Can this one idea bring back ethics? Can this one idea get rid of political intolerance?  The succinct answer to all of these questions is:yes.

And that is the subject of the next article in this series.  Be patient.  I have to create some background for you, a context for new thinking.  How consciousness enters physics is one of them.  How consciousness becomes embodied in the physical world is another.  When we find the answer to these questions, we also find an answer to “how to get rid of hierarchies in politics?”

Intolerance becomes pathological for religions when they, following the practice of science, interpret religious scriptures literally, as logos.  But the story told there is not logo; it is myth, stories that are guidelines, not step-by-step rules, of how the more subtle aspects of us—our feelings, thinking, and intuitions—are designed to progress.  Can a science based on quantum physics restore our faith in mythology?  Yes, it can.  It does.

Ride Big Sur - go do it

### English

I am finally riding through Big Sur. After 22 years in California I am actually doing it. And as usual, not in the season I would like, not with the bike I would like and a little more rushed than I like it.

That said, this type of December weather is pretty awesome. Blue sky, sun all day and every day so far. Temperatures ranging from 5C (40F) to 17C (65F) and all tail wind. After a pretty tough day getting to Monterey we only had a 1/2 day ride to Big Sur for our first camp. The beauty of this area can hardly be over stated. The coastline is simply stunning and the slower you go the more you see. We had time that day and could take all the time we wanted. Yes, there are areas with a lot of hills, so what? It gives you more time to look around as you go even slower. But I recommend to bring a bike with gears. A fixie like the ones we ride, don't add to the joy.

![](/photos/112820182041152304595067821023061.jpg)

The second day was a different animal. We had to do close to 100mi in a day and it was hilly. Yes very hilly for the first 1/2. As soon as you pass Rugged Point the street seems to magically straighten out completely and the wind is constantly on your back. Once you get over riding your bike on the freeway it's all great and miles fly by really fast.

![](/photos/dsc00115_resized335284772556665771.jpg)

![](/photos/112820182046188296081777668095266.jpg)

The second day scenery is not as dramatic as the first but very rewarding because of the long and far views you get there. And there are vastly fewer cars in the roads further south. We got lucky to be able to spend the night in the airstream of Chris's dad.

It took us 4 weeks to prepare the house for sale. What a trip, so much work. But on true silicon valley style, we had a buyer, 6 days before we put it on the market. The Mexican connection somehow worked is magic and a couple of the neighborhood walked by and we had an offer on the table the next day. Right where we wanted to have it $$ wise. Accepted it 4 weeks later and some smaller troubled later we had it sold and the money in the bank. What a trip. Timing could not have been better as the US seems to go into a CORVID-19 panic a few days after. Good to sell, good to have cash, good to be out.

CORVID-19 caused many of the retail shelfs to be cleaned out in only two days. Mumu and I decided to pull in the schedule of our departure by 2 weeks and booked tickets. One day later we receive an email the flight is cancelled. So we decide to split up and have me head out today, Mumu trying to get the right vaccinations for Brioche, sell the car and come right after me, if still possible. We just have to be able to receive the container with our stuff in Italy, middle of April somehow. My exit feels rushed and now a little lonely. Without Mumu and without Brioche. SFO has a dystopian look to it today. So so empty.

## I think sharing is scary.

I am NOT talking about sharing your last drop of water with your friend of course. I am referring to our omnipresent SocialMedia platforms and how we all use them. Sharing an interesting article with my friend, cool. Getting the almost identical messages flashed back on my screens, 100 times….. Not COOL.

[![](/photos/sharing-is-scary.png)](nonprofitcenters.org)

We share things we like things on SocialMedia. Repetitive messages and articles are offered over and over again. What we share, what we like, what we search for gives these algorithms an idea of what excites us. Our excitement is good for these corporations.

As a result, we read and hear less dissenting information ==> But we also become less tolerant of other views, other opinions. We react faster and faster to small bits of information, and don't check the validity of this information. 

SocialMedia providers make more money the more we share, also the more time we spend with them.

I know I am changing because of all this. I am assuming others are too. 

I know the way I interact with each other is changing. It's changing fast and it's changing not in a direction of _listening_, _inclusiveness_ and _trying to understand_ each other, not in a direction of _togetherness_, but towards "_island-building_", _isolation,_ and _pushing_ each other away. I quickly disregard someone as a person, just because of ONE bit of information I heard/saw about them. It is exactly the opposite of what we as a world society need to solve the existential problems we need to fix. We want to be able to survive in the long term on this planet.

* * *

**Here is my question then**: 

- We know we are going in a direction that is hurting us 

- We know some of the main players that dictate the way we receive information

- We know the main players make Billions and Billions of $$$ in the process

- Why are we not doing anything about the actual cause of this problem?

- Why do we seem to fiddle around the edges?

- Why do we not really change the situation we are in, the direction we are heading? 

* * *

We have options to FORCE these algorithms to change. I see this as one way to start addressing this. But we would be forcing big players to agree to make a whole lot less money or invite them to make their money differently, doing less damage to the people and societies using their services.

No call to action here. No Newsletter to sign up for. No group to join. 

## BUT

Do what is in your reach, what is in your power to make changes in your reach, what is in your power to make changes to.

**SHOCK EVENT: Be Aware of what is happening in our country.** From Heather Richardson, professor of History at Boston College: "I don't like to talk about politics on Facebook-- political history is my job, after all, and you are my friends-- but there is an important non-partisan point to make today. What Bannon is doing, most dramatically with last night's ban on immigration from seven predominantly Muslim countries-- is creating what is known as a "shock event." Such an event is unexpected and confusing and throws a society into chaos. People scramble to react to the event, usually along some fault line that those responsible for the event can widen by claiming that they alone know how to restore order. When opponents speak out, the authors of the shock event call them enemies. As society reels and tempers run high, those responsible for the shock event perform a sleight of hand to achieve their real goal, a goal they know to be hugely unpopular, but from which everyone has been distracted as they fight over the initial event. There is no longer concerted opposition to the real goal; opposition divides along the partisan lines established by the shock event. Last night's Executive Order has all the hallmarks of a shock event. It was not reviewed by any governmental agencies or lawyers before it was released, and counterterrorism experts insist they did not ask for it. People charged with enforcing it got no instructions about how to do so. Courts immediately have declared parts of it unconstitutional, but border police in some airports are refusing to stop enforcing it. Predictably, chaos has followed and tempers are hot. My point today is this: unless you are the person setting it up, it is in no one's interest to play the shock event game. It is designed explicitly to divide people who might otherwise come together so they cannot stand against something its authors think they won't like. I don't know what Bannon is up to-- although I have some guesses-- but because I know Bannon's ideas well, I am positive that there is not a single person whom I consider a friend on either side of the aisle-- and my friends range pretty widely-- who will benefit from whatever it is. If the shock event strategy works, though, many of you will blame each other, rather than Bannon, for the fallout. And the country will have been tricked into accepting their real goal. But because shock events destabilize a society, they can also be used positively. We do not have to respond along old fault lines. We could just as easily reorganize into a different pattern that threatens the people who sparked the event. A successful shock event depends on speed and chaos because it requires knee-jerk reactions so that people divide along established lines. This, for example, is how Confederate leaders railroaded the initial southern states out of the Union. If people realize they are being played, though, they can reach across old lines and reorganize to challenge the leaders who are pulling the strings. This was Lincoln's strategy when he joined together Whigs, Democrats, Free-Soilers, anti-Nebraska voters, and nativists into the new Republican Party to stand against the Slave Power. Five years before, such a coalition would have been unimaginable. Members of those groups agreed on very little other than that they wanted all Americans to have equal economic opportunity. Once they began to work together to promote a fair economic system, though, they found much common ground. They ended up rededicating the nation to a "government of the people, by the people, and for the people." Confederate leaders and Lincoln both knew about the political potential of a shock event. Sicily -- it is or is it not

Gooogle Pictures [LINK](https://photos.app.goo.gl/WvPe8eGSxGKQ9UzT9)

I mean, **is it or is it not** part of Italy? I personally did not know what to expect and went on to think I will see just another, a different part of Italy. Well, I did. So different to me that I have to scratch my head a few times. Parts of Sicily are much closer to Tunis that they are to Rome, just speaking geographically. We saw signs on houses, in Arabic ![DSC02227-S](/photos/dsc02227-s.jpg)writing. I saw people whos facial features much closer resemble ones I expect to see in the African continent that here. I think it is another clear evidence races, looks and ways of life don't follow borders but follow geographies and connections between people. I find that fascinating to see and discover.

On our way from the West to the East side of Sicily, we made our way through some serious agricultural areas. Not at all scenic, the driving was hectic, pushy and really tiring. The valley of the temples right outside of Agrigento was truly worth a visit.

\[caption id="attachment\_1491" align="alignright" width="361"\]![DSC02301-S](/photos/dsc02301-s.jpg) Greek temple with a Church resembling modification inside.\[/caption\]

Here history does not seem to stop at Year 0, Jesus birth. Here you see the temples and clear evidence of what Greek people did here to expand their territories. Even though some temples were built way before Year 0, it had to change the temple look to something resembling the qualities of a church or be destroyed.

 

 

We stayed in Comiso for the night and had a nice interaction with an Italian man, well into retirement age. He worked at VW plant in Wolfsburg for 30 years and praised the hell out of

![IMG\_20190913\_190836-S](/photos/img_20190913_190836-s.jpg)

Germany. He now gets his retirement payments from Germany and has a good life as it seems. Still, he is worried a lot about his two sons, they try to make it work here in Sicily and he has little confidence it will work out well for them. He and his old friend were a cute Duo.

 

A trip to the winery Occhipinti was on our list of things to check out. an organic winemaker that is up an coming. I found most interesting that the same grape type in an almost identical area (200-500m apart), following the identical winemaking processes,  can deliver such a different taste in wine. I did not like even one of their wines, but that was "almost" besides the point.

We spent 4 days in Syracuse, a pretty wealthy city on the east coast of Sicily. Noone less than Archimedes was born here. I mean, is it or is it not part of Italy? I personally did not know what to expect and went on to think I will see just another, a different part of Italy. Well, I did. So different to me that I have to scratch my head a few times. Parts of Sicily are much closer to Tunis that they are to Rome, just speaking geographically. We saw signs on houses, in Arabic writing. I saw people whos facial features much closer resemble ones I expect to see in the African continent that here. I think it is another clear evidence races, looks and ways of life don’t follow borders but follow geographies and connections between people. I find that fascinating to see and discover.

On our way from the West to the East side of Sicily, we made our way through some serious agricultural areas. Not at all scenic, the driving was hectic, pushy and really tiring. The valley of the temples right outside of Agrigento was truly worth a visit.

[caption id=“attachment_1491” align=“alignright” width=“361”] Greek temple with a Church resembling modification inside.[/caption]

Here history does not seem to stop at Year 0, Jesus birth. Here you see the temples and clear evidence of what Greek people did here to expand their territories. Even though some temples were built way before Year 0, it had to change the temple look to something resembling the qualities of a church or be destroyed.

 

 

We stayed in Comiso for the night and had a nice interaction with an Italian man, well into retirement age. He worked at VW plant in Wolfsburg for 30 years and praised the hell out of

Germany. He now gets his retirement payments from Germany and has a good life as it seems. Still, he is worried a lot about his two sons, they try to make it work here in Sicily and he has little confidence it will work out well for them. He and his old friend were a cute Duo.

 

A trip to the winery Occhipinti was on our list of things to check out. an organic winemaker that is up an coming. I found most interesting that the same grape type in an almost identical area (200-500m apart), following the identical winemaking processes,  can deliver such a different taste in wine. I did not like even one of their wines, but that was “almost” besides the point.

Sicily we are getting started -Trapani - Favignana - Erice

Google Pictures [LINK](https://photos.app.goo.gl/JbWyPoPGFttU74Ro9)

While the house purchase is not complete, we are starting our trip through Sicily the day after my birthday. The French are back home, we are back on the road.

What we heard, it will not really matter that we don't speak Italian here, almost no one in Sicily does either. Siculo (sìculu) seems to be a really different language, it even sounds different to the casual listener (not understanding a word). "_It the oldest of the Romance **languages derived** from Latin, and it's spoken in Sicily and in parts of southern Italy such as Reggio di Calabria and southern Puglia."_ Sicily seems to have received influence from Africa just as well as from Europe. We visit little cities here that certainly have an Arab feel to it. This will be interesting, in much more than just a beauty kind of way.

The landscape here is really really dry. Water seems to be a premium here and it shows. We see much more cactus and succulents here, but many areas are just barren and sometimes plain dirt. The coastline is truly stunning in so many places, the water is turquoise and blue and ...... amazing colors and shapes unite. We had lunch at a really well designed and placed [Agritourismo](https://goo.gl/maps/PpYdAUupUriZMU447) in Scopello. The Swiming hole close by gave us the first view of what is to come here.

\

The drive to Trapani, our next stop was nothing special, Trapani is an industrial town with a niceish Centro Storico. The next day we slept in big time and got out of bed at about 10.30. Coffee and we had a look at the port for our trip to Favignana, an island just off the coast here. As it goes when traveling, we found ourself on the next boat 15 minutes later with no bag, no toothbrush or anything to prepare for the next two days on the island. Well, here we come. We used the 10 min wait to book a room on the island and the rest was history. It was a good decision to go and it was truly beautiful there. I was amazed by the fact that most of the roads in and out of town seemed "elevated". What are all these holes for, why are they so structured and straight? We eventually learned it is the TUFF mines on the island. It is a type of stone that was apparently mined already at the times of the Romans.

![DSC01981-S](/photos/dsc01981-s.jpg)

The afternoon we dedicated to the southern part of the island and its beautiful coastline. On bikes and ready to stop any minute we were off. I think we dipped 3 times and saw so many beautiful spots. Dramatic, interesting, smooth, beautiful. As you wish, as we liked it.

The town was still busy with tourists, not crazy, but busy. I wonder what it looks like in August, the Italian tourist month. People are personable and nice, the town is cute and the food needs to be seafood. So good, so different. the 2nd day we rented a little scooter and took off to the northern part of the island. The coastline is not as dramatic as the island does not have the same cliff style drop off like the south. Still super nice and it seemed even fewer people. Our chosen lunch spot was a disappointment as they refused to serve us afer guiding us to a table. Very strange! At the backup place we received a similar, not so warm welcome, but actually got food and a great view. We took the last boat back to Sicily and found ourself touching our arms as they were sensitive from all the sun exposure the last two days. And a toothbrush was next on our agenda. NICE.

We went to a concert in the old Tuna factory in Favignana. A really great experience. We learned a lot about the island there and listened to young people making good music. The factory was part of several movies, mainly Italian language. One of them, "[The Italians](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt2875018/plotsummary?ref_=tt_ov_pl)",  is in English and draws a passionate and sensitive picture of Italy and the people. The fashion segment of it is on [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WQ3VsAKYU-A).

\

A family used to own the complete island, together with 2 others. The [Florio](https://www.mareandmoretour.it/eng/highlights/florio-family-tonnara-9) family who was very successful in business at the time used to own all three of them, completely.

**Erice** was on our agenda next. It's a little town 750m above Trapani on the hill. A charming town with so much history and ancient buildings. This mixed with a few clouds coming in and out made for really great views. Italy is truly oozing with history, where ever you look, where ever you go. I know so many people say this, but experiencing it is a different story. We treated ourself to local pizza from the place 50m down the street from our stay. **SO** crowded, so crazy, so good. Not a thin crust, but still a good pizza.

\

 

**Pizza Siciliana**

Good morning.
(Want to get California Today by email? Here’s the sign-up.)
J. Grant Brittain is the dean of skateboard photography. Over a 40-year career that began when he started photographing locals at the Del Mar Skate Ranch, Mr. Brittain has documented skateboarding’s rise from a niche Southern California activity into a lifestyle and international sport that will debut at the 2020 Olympics in Tokyo.
Mr. Brittain spent most of his career working for Transworld Skateboarding and The Skateboard Mag, but over the past few months he has been going through a lifetime of photos for a book project he’s planning. Now 62, he continues to shoot skateboarding, but says his favorite period remains the 1980s.
“It was before video, YouTube, Instagram, before the internet,” he said. “These guys were making up all these tricks, and they did it with their friends and pushed each other. It was so private and I think that’s what I liked about it.”
He shared some of his favorite old photos and talked about the history behind them. His comments are in the captions, and a gallery of his work can be found here.
Kyle Jensen, Del Mar**, 1979**
“I started working at Del Mar the second day after it opened. About six or seven months after I started there I borrowed a camera from my roommate and started shooting. I didn’t know anything. He had to load the film for me and said ‘Just have the sun behind you.’ I got a couple good photos on the first roll and was hooked.” J. Grant Brittain
Tony Hawk, Del Mar, 1982
“Tony was just skating and I told him, ‘Next time you go up, just look at me.’” J. Grant Brittain
Jim Thiebaud, San Francisco, 1986
“In San Diego you would drive to a spot, skate the spot, drive to another spot. The San Francisco style is just skating all over town and going to your favorite spots with your friends until you get kicked out. This was just a neighborhood people skated a lot. It was out in the avenues someplace.” J. Grant Brittain
Christian Hosoi, Westminster, 1986
“When skateboarding started dying in the late ’70s, the parks started closing. Everybody started building ramps. This was Skilly’s ramp up in Orange County. I forget what his real name was. There weren’t many photographers back then. It was me or one of the Thrasher guys. Right place, right time, right era.” J. Grant Brittain

Google Photos [LINK](https://photos.app.goo.gl/dj5hyTYhbi3ZQh42A) **English** We are in Sucre right now. It's in Bolivia for the ones that are geographically as challenged as I am. It's considered a low elevation city in this country of smiles and friendliness. 2810m low. Well, that is almost the elevation of Tioga Pass for reference. On our way through the dessert coming from Calama Chile we crossed some mountain passes on Gravel roads that where well over 4000m high. I stepped out of the bus for a quick pee, I was out of breath, not kidding. After managing though little immigration trouble for my lovely USA travel partner and lover and partner in crime, not to forget Main Squeeze, we managed not to have to go back to Chile and just get a Visa for her in Uyuni during our 4 hour lay over till the next bus. Close, but we made it in. The trip to Uyuni was pretty rough, as busses go. Mostly gravel road, some if it more in shape of a washboard, then there were detours because of road construction from the February surprise rain event. These little detours were a little more humpty bumty than the rest of the ride. The bus did not have any working A/C and only two tiny windows for 40+ people ==> it was a little hot in that sardine can. Our 1st uncomfortable Bus ride in all of South America. Sucre found us at 5.30AM in the morning, after a rushed Taxi ride to our Hostel we were able to get into our room early and get a little more sleep. Awesome welcome. Sniffing around the city was good, it seems to be a clean and calm city. Lots of white older buildings and really short people here. I mean really short. On 1st contact we felt there is so much more warmth and friendliness in Bolivia than we felt in Chile. People smiled genuinely, interacted with respect with each other and it all felt just great here. Mumu and I decided this will be a week of calm and doing not much at all. Just to get a little routine going and calm all of our systems down a little. And so it went. I could bake a couple different Baguette here in the 1st days, all without scale as I left mine at the last accommodation. BUMMER. But it will bring me to a new level of being a good baker. On our 3rd day here, we had a short but memorable visit by the Bolivian Immigration Police @ 1.30am. What a weird moment that was. They did not only check our Passports and Visa, no. Almost the whole hostel was checked. It took quiet a while till we finally got back to sleep. What a rude awakening, unnecessary act and really upsetting. It makes you wonder how people in other countries feel when they are harassed by the local law enforcement. Let's see. Sunday we decided to go to a BIG festivity in Tarabuco. a small town about 75km away. Something like a Thanksgiving (Erntedankfest) of the area. Lot's of locals, most in traditional clothing, then dances and festivities all around. What a treat that was. You will see lots of pictures of these amazing people in the LINK. Our host brought us there and explained as much as possible which was awesome. Then, to round it all up, they managed to get us into a place that offered food for lunch and it was good food, great people in a realy inviting environment. The cook seems to have received some award, and it was our best meal in Bolivia so far (but we had pretty mid level food this far....). People were really community oriented and it was clear to see and feel how much fun they had doing this, how much pride they had to do it well. It seems to be an event that is handed over from one location to another every year. And no-one can let down the community with bad food, bad service ...... you know it. What a day, what an event, we were so so lucky to be able to be part of this. Thank you Jorge (Horhey) and your staff for a really great day and experience. - - **German** Wir sind gerade in Sucre. Es ist in Bolivien für diejenigen, die geografisch genauso gefordert sind wie ich. In diesem Land des Lächelns und der Freundlichkeit gilt es als eine niedrige Stadt. 2810m niedrig. Nun, das ist fast die Höhe des Tioga Pass als Referenz. Auf dem Weg durch den Nachtisch aus Calama Chile überquerten wir einige Passstraßen auf Schotterstraßen, die weit über 4000 m hoch waren. Ich stieg aus dem Bus, um schnell zu pinkeln, ich war außer Atem, kein Scherz. Nachdem wir für meinen lieben USA-Reisepartner und Liebhaber und Partner in der Kriminalität nur geringe Einwanderungsprobleme bewältigt hatten, um Main Squeeze nicht zu vergessen, schafften wir es nicht, nach Chile zurückzukehren und in Uyuni während unseres 4-stündigen Aufenthaltes ein Visum zu bekommen bis zum nächsten Bus. Nah dran, aber wir haben es geschafft. Die Fahrt nach Uyuni war ziemlich rau, wie Busse fahren. Meist Schotterstraße, manche mehr in Form eines Waschbretts, dann gab es wegen der Straßenkonstruktion Umwege vom Überraschungsereignis im Februar. Diese kleinen Umwege waren ein bisschen mehr Humpty als der Rest der Fahrt. Der Bus hatte keine funktionierende Klimaanlage und nur zwei winzige Fenster für 40+ Leute ==> es war etwas heiß in dieser Sardinenbüchse. Unsere erste unbequeme Busfahrt in ganz Südamerika. Sucre fand uns um 5:30 Uhr morgens, nachdem wir mit dem Taxi schnell zu unserem Hostel gefahren waren, konnten wir früh in unser Zimmer gehen und ein wenig mehr schlafen. Super willkommen. Das Schnuppern in der Stadt war gut, es scheint eine saubere und ruhige Stadt zu sein. Viele weiße ältere Gebäude und wirklich kurze Leute hier. Ich meine wirklich kurz. Beim ersten Kontakt hatten wir das Gefühl, dass in Bolivien so viel mehr Wärme und Freundlichkeit herrscht als in Chile. Die Leute lächelten ehrlich, tauschten Respekt aus und es fühlte sich alles großartig an. Mumu und ich beschlossen, dass dies eine Woche der Ruhe sein wird und nicht viel tun wird. Nur um ein bisschen Routine in Gang zu bringen und alle Systeme ein wenig zu beruhigen. Und so ging es weiter. Ich konnte in den ersten Tagen hier ein paar verschiedene Baguette backen, alles ohne Maßstab, als ich meine letzte Unterkunft verlassen hatte. BUMMER Aber es wird mich auf ein neues Niveau bringen, ein guter Bäcker zu sein. An unserem dritten Tag hier hatten wir einen kurzen, aber unvergesslichen Besuch der bolivianischen Einwanderungspolizei um 1.30 Uhr. Was für ein komischer Moment das war. Sie haben nicht nur unsere Reisepässe und Visa überprüft, nein. Fast die gesamte Herberge wurde überprüft. Es dauerte eine Weile, bis wir endlich wieder einschliefen. Was für ein unhöfliches Erwachen, eine unnötige Tat und wirklich ärgerlich. Sie fragen sich, wie sich Menschen in anderen Ländern fühlen, wenn sie von der örtlichen Strafverfolgung belästigt werden. Mal schauen. Sonntag entschieden wir uns für ein großes Fest in Tarabuco. eine kleine Stadt ca. 75km entfernt. So etwas wie ein Erntedankfest der Gegend. Viele Einheimische, meistens in traditioneller Kleidung, dann Tänze und Feste. Was für ein Vergnügen das war. Im LINK sehen Sie viele Bilder dieser erstaunlichen Menschen. Unser Gastgeber brachte uns dort hin und erklärte so viel wie möglich, was großartig war. Zum Abschluss hatten sie es geschafft, uns an einen Ort zu bringen, an dem Essen zum Mittagessen angeboten wurde. Es war gutes Essen, großartige Menschen in einer wirklich einladenden Umgebung. Die Köchin scheint eine Auszeichnung erhalten zu haben, und es war bisher unsere beste Mahlzeit in Bolivien (aber wir hatten bis jetzt ziemlich gutes Essen …). Die Leute waren wirklich gemeinschaftsorientiert und es war klar zu sehen und zu spüren, wie viel Spaß sie dabei hatten und wie viel Stolz sie dafür tun mussten. Es scheint eine Veranstaltung zu sein, die jedes Jahr von einem Ort zum anderen übertragen wird. Und niemand kann die Gemeinschaft mit schlechtem Essen und schlechtem Service im Stich lassen … Sie wissen es. Was für ein Tag, was für ein Event, wir hatten so viel Glück, Teil davon sein zu können. English

We are in Sucre right now. It’s in Bolivia for the ones that are geographically as challenged as I am. It’s considered a low elevation city in this country of smiles and friendliness. 2810m low. Well, that is almost the elevation of Tioga Pass for reference. On our way through the dessert coming from Calama Chile we crossed some mountain passes on Gravel roads that where well over 4000m high. I stepped out of the bus for a quick pee, I was out of breath, not kidding. After managing though little immigration trouble for my lovely USA travel partner and lover and partner in crime, not to forget Main Squeeze, we managed not to have to go back to Chile and just get a Visa for her in Uyuni during our 4 hour lay over till the next bus. Close, but we made it in.

The trip to Uyuni was pretty rough, as busses go. Mostly gravel road, some if it more in shape of a washboard, then there were detours because of road construction from the February surprise rain event. These little detours were a little more humpty bumty than the rest of the ride. The bus did not have any working A/C and only two tiny windows for 40+ people ==> it was a little hot in that sardine can. Our 1st uncomfortable Bus ride in all of South America.

Sucre found us at 5.30AM in the morning, after a rushed Taxi ride to our Hostel we were able to get into our room early and get a little more sleep. Awesome welcome. Sniffing around the city was good, it seems to be a clean and calm city. Lots of white older buildings and really short people here. I mean really short. On 1st contact we felt there is so much more warmth and friendliness in Bolivia than we felt in Chile. People smiled genuinely, interacted with respect with each other and it all felt just great here. Mumu and I decided this will be a week of calm and doing not much at all. Just to get a little routine going and calm all of our systems down a little. And so it went. I could bake a couple different Baguette here in the 1st days, all without scale as I left mine at the last accommodation. BUMMER. But it will bring me to a new level of being a good baker.

On our 3rd day here, we had a short but memorable visit by the Bolivian Immigration Police @ 1.30am. What a weird moment that was. They did not only check our Passports and Visa, no. Almost the whole hostel was checked. It took quiet a while till we finally got back to sleep. What a rude awakening, unnecessary act and really upsetting. It makes you wonder how people in other countries feel when they are harassed by the local law enforcement.

Let’s see. Sunday we decided to go to a BIG festivity in Tarabuco. a small town about 75km away. Something like a Thanksgiving (Erntedankfest) of the area. Lot’s of locals, most in traditional clothing, then dances and festivities all around. What a treat that was. You will see lots of pictures of these amazing people in the LINK. Our host brought us there and explained as much as possible which was awesome. Then, to round it all up, they managed to get us into a place that offered food for lunch and it was good food, great people in a realy inviting environment. The cook seems to have received some award, and it was our best meal in Bolivia so far (but we had pretty mid level food this far…). People were really community oriented and it was clear to see and feel how much fun they had doing this, how much pride they had to do it well. It seems to be an event that is handed over from one location to another every year. And no-one can let down the community with bad food, bad service … you know it. What a day, what an event, we were so so lucky to be able to be part of this. Thank you Jorge (Horhey) and your staff for a really great day and experience.

German

Wir sind gerade in Sucre. Es ist in Bolivien für diejenigen, die geografisch genauso gefordert sind wie ich. In diesem Land des Lächelns und der Freundlichkeit gilt es als eine niedrige Stadt. 2810m niedrig. Nun, das ist fast die Höhe des Tioga Pass als Referenz. Auf dem Weg durch den Nachtisch aus Calama Chile überquerten wir einige Passstraßen auf Schotterstraßen, die weit über 4000 m hoch waren. Ich stieg aus dem Bus, um schnell zu pinkeln, ich war außer Atem, kein Scherz. Nachdem wir für meinen lieben USA-Reisepartner und Liebhaber und Partner in der Kriminalität nur geringe Einwanderungsprobleme bewältigt hatten, um Main Squeeze nicht zu vergessen, schafften wir es nicht, nach Chile zurückzukehren und in Uyuni während unseres 4-stündigen Aufenthaltes ein Visum zu bekommen bis zum nächsten Bus. Nah dran, aber wir haben es geschafft.

Die Fahrt nach Uyuni war ziemlich rau, wie Busse fahren. Meist Schotterstraße, manche mehr in Form eines Waschbretts, dann gab es wegen der Straßenkonstruktion Umwege vom Überraschungsereignis im Februar. Diese kleinen Umwege waren ein bisschen mehr Humpty als der Rest der Fahrt. Der Bus hatte keine funktionierende Klimaanlage und nur zwei winzige Fenster für 40+ Leute ==> es war etwas heiß in dieser Sardinenbüchse. Unsere erste unbequeme Busfahrt in ganz Südamerika.
Sucre fand uns um 5:30 Uhr morgens, nachdem wir mit dem Taxi schnell zu unserem Hostel gefahren waren, konnten wir früh in unser Zimmer gehen und ein wenig mehr schlafen. Super willkommen. Das Schnuppern in der Stadt war gut, es scheint eine saubere und ruhige Stadt zu sein. Viele weiße ältere Gebäude und wirklich kurze Leute hier. Ich meine wirklich kurz. Beim ersten Kontakt hatten wir das Gefühl, dass in Bolivien so viel mehr Wärme und Freundlichkeit herrscht als in Chile. Die Leute lächelten ehrlich, tauschten Respekt aus und es fühlte sich alles großartig an. Mumu und ich beschlossen, dass dies eine Woche der Ruhe sein wird und nicht viel tun wird. Nur um ein bisschen Routine in Gang zu bringen und alle Systeme ein wenig zu beruhigen. Und so ging es weiter. Ich konnte in den ersten Tagen hier ein paar verschiedene Baguette backen, alles ohne Maßstab, als ich meine letzte Unterkunft verlassen hatte. BUMMER Aber es wird mich auf ein neues Niveau bringen, ein guter Bäcker zu sein.

An unserem dritten Tag hier hatten wir einen kurzen, aber unvergesslichen Besuch der bolivianischen Einwanderungspolizei um 1.30 Uhr. Was für ein komischer Moment das war. Sie haben nicht nur unsere Reisepässe und Visa überprüft, nein. Fast die gesamte Herberge wurde überprüft. Es dauerte eine Weile, bis wir endlich wieder einschliefen. Was für ein unhöfliches Erwachen, eine unnötige Tat und wirklich ärgerlich. Sie fragen sich, wie sich Menschen in anderen Ländern fühlen, wenn sie von der örtlichen Strafverfolgung belästigt werden.

Mal schauen. Sonntag entschieden wir uns für ein großes Fest in Tarabuco. eine kleine Stadt ca. 75km entfernt. So etwas wie ein Erntedankfest der Gegend. Viele Einheimische, meistens in traditioneller Kleidung, dann Tänze und Feste. Was für ein Vergnügen das war. Im LINK sehen Sie viele Bilder dieser erstaunlichen Menschen. Unser Gastgeber brachte uns dort hin und erklärte so viel wie möglich, was großartig war. Zum Abschluss hatten sie es geschafft, uns an einen Ort zu bringen, an dem Essen zum Mittagessen angeboten wurde. Es war gutes Essen, großartige Menschen in einer wirklich einladenden Umgebung. Die Köchin scheint eine Auszeichnung erhalten zu haben, und es war bisher unsere beste Mahlzeit in Bolivien (aber wir hatten bis jetzt ziemlich gutes Essen …). Die Leute waren wirklich gemeinschaftsorientiert und es war klar zu sehen und zu spüren, wie viel Spaß sie dabei hatten und wie viel Stolz sie dafür tun mussten. Es scheint eine Veranstaltung zu sein, die jedes Jahr von einem Ort zum anderen übertragen wird. Und niemand kann die Gemeinschaft mit schlechtem Essen und schlechtem Service im Stich lassen … Sie wissen es. Was für ein Tag, was für ein Event, wir hatten so viel Glück, Teil davon sein zu können. Vielen Dank, Jorge (Horhey) und Ihre Mitarbeiter für einen wirklich großartigen Tag und eine tolle Erfahrung.

It is a real tradition by many standards now. Spring hike # 18 was underway last Saturday. Always the same route, always changing hikers, Flowers, and weather. The scenery is usually really amazing in the springtime with many changing Wildflowers along the way. This year we ha8 9 people to start with, one had to turn around at the Murietta falls intersection. It is always no fun to send back one of the team. But he was in good hiker company on the way back as he found a new Indian friend on the trail and they walked back together.

The Rest, 8 of us, went on and pulled it all through. Just over 9 hours from start to finish, Temperatures were truly ideal, almost a little warm on Rose Peak, but who would complain about that after such a long cold CA end of winter and Spring so far.

Ludger, Christian, Kim, Yan, Oscar, Ronja, Rosa and me.

The highlight of the hike where the 2 male Rattlesnakes battling it out on the side of the trail. Totally unimpressed by our presence.

Strides in Europe - Paris - London - Nuernberg

Google Pictures [LINK](https://photos.app.goo.gl/BbvmCwfie5Ssuknv8)

We are heading for a real Winter here, now. It's our 1st real fall and now heading for a real winter time. It rained and poured in Poppi, we collected amazing mushrooms and Mumu and I headed for some change in scenery.

Paris, we had the great benefit to be able to stay with Veronique and Sandrine, good friends of Mumu for the 1st 5 days in Paris area. A super warm welcome and lots of care for the two of us still coughing and sneezing ones. We held some bread baking sessions and I learned how to make a Kings Cake, we made Lebkuchen together and ate them as well. Mumu and I managed to squeeze a little walk in between rain, but we staid indoors almost all the time. Oh yes, we did rake their leaves, from the property of ~4000m2.

\

Manu was nice enough to let us stay at his apartment in the center of Paris. It was a little nicer weather these days, but Winter is simply what it is in these areas. Cold and wet, not much sunshine. We had a nice good bye dinner with Manu and Marine, then off to Cassandre and London. My 1st time using the tunnel to get to England. I think it is 50km long and it goes bye in a flash. London was just as dark and cold in weather, but we had Cassandre and Gabrielle to warm our hearts on.

![IMG-20191121-WA0000-S](/photos/img-20191121-wa0000-s.jpg)

\

With the plane to Nuernberg and a warm welcome from Doris and my Mom. Arriving in Moms meticulously clean and organized place is always a happy place for Muriel, and I go my Mom to hug. What can go wrong with that??? Nuernberg showed a pretty nice side so far with cold temperatures but a pretty regular occurrence of SUN. Yepeee.

I always try to go climbing with my friend Kurt here, indoor of course now. So I bought new shoes for it, finally and we already had two sessions. The E4 Climbing Gym is such a great and big place. Rock climbing is a real culture in this area. Sunday I arrived at 14.00 and I am sure there were at least 150 people in the Gym, all ages, all shapes and all skill levels. We even have comic books, just about Rock Climbing.

\

I also got to pick up my new drivers license and can now buy a car in Italy. YEPEEE. A serious word of praise for German bureaucracy. I am looking for guidelines how to design and build a kitchen were I can hold legally baking classes. I asked at least 10 different people in Italy and I could not get one clear pointer where to find this or really anything intelligent for that matter. Frustrated, I went to go to the Town of Nuernberg and went to the "**Ordnungs Amt**" (office of order). GOT IT. order Order oRder orDer ordEr ordeR----- Things need to be in order here. I spoke to one lady and she quickly and competently directed me to one floor lower into a room and to a specific man. I asked him if there would be a guideline on how I would have to build a kitchen like this in Germany. Well sure he says. It is EU Verordnung 852/04 Anhang 2 Kap. 1,2,4-12 Read this and you know what you need, he says. But let me give you the gist of it. really easy ...... 2 minutes of precise and competent explanation made me smile all the way around. I must have said thank you 10 times into his face, I shook his hand with both of mine and really wanted to hug him. A total of 5 minutes in a German government office gave me exactly what I needed.

![ILG](/photos/ilg.png)

## **I LOVE GERMANY**

London was just as dark and cold in weather, but we had Cassandre and Gabrielle to warm our hearts on.

\

With the plane to Nuernberg and a warm welcome from Doris and my Mom. Arriving in Moms meticulously clean and organized place is always a happy place for Muriel, and I go my Mom to hug. What can go wrong with that??? Nuernberg showed a pretty nice side so far with cold temperatures but a pretty regular occurrence of SUN. Yepeee.

I always try to go climbing with my friend Kurt here, indoor of course now. So I bought new shoes for it, finally and we already had two sessions. The E4 Climbing Gym is such a great and big place. Rock climbing is a real culture in this area. Sunday I arrived at 14.00 and I am sure there were at least 150 people in the Gym, all ages, all shapes and all skill levels. We even have comic books, just about Rock Climbing.

\

I also got to pick up my new drivers license and can now buy a car in Italy. YEPEEE. A serious word of praise for German bureaucracy. I am looking for guidelines how to design and build a kitchen were I can hold legally baking classes. I asked at least 10 different people in Italy and I could not get one clear pointer where to find this or really anything intelligent for that matter. Frustrated, I went to go to the Town of Nuernberg and went to the “Ordnungs Amt” (office of order). GOT IT. order Order oRder orDer ordEr ordeR----- Things need to be in order here. I spoke to one lady and she quickly and competently directed me to one floor lower into a room and to a specific man. I asked him if there would be a guideline on how I would have to build a kitchen like this in Germany. Well sure he says. It is EU Verordnung 852/04 Anhang 2 Kap. 1,2,4-12 Read this and you know what you need, he says. But let me give you the gist of it. really easy … 2 minutes of precise and competent explanation made me smile all the way around. I must have said thank you 10 times into his face, I shook his hand with both of mine and really wanted to hug him. A total of 5 minutes in a German government office gave me exactly what I needed.

I LOVE GERMANY

Traffic. The rosary dislike all the busy A-roads  and the Dual carriageway. The constant thundering of cars and lorries reverberate into my being. Tens is my muscles, makes my headache and quickly destroys the purpose of being on a bicycle. If you live in the city No Doubt you would become acclimatized to this constant sound semicolon I have written into this, but I like those mountain bike tires, I'm  out of my normal habitat. I found, however, that the concentration of writing in the environment overwhelmed the distraction of the sound. You become able to predict some drivers Intentions by the sound of the vehicle approaching from behind, or the it is snowing patiently or revving aggressively before squeezing past, or rather it's about to turn across your path. Twice the sound of the driver's intention has allowed me to prepare myself before the car actually came into view and turned a cross me. And when you find those intolerant, impatient drivers blasting their horns and you on a narrow lane, or shouting out of their window and you could get off their way, just stay calm. Don't let and an unappreciative audience for your concert.  If you're riding groups you will be aware of drifts conversation among your fellow writers, punctuated by the occasionaly shouted warning for protein cars. Moving between Riders and friends you experience different sounds, serious discussions, laughter.  And for me, that's all the sound a bike ride should really bring:  Nature's subtle noises, perhaps the odd ring of the Bell, quiet conversations and the hum of those tires along with faintest of mechanical whirring.  A mellow melody, a shooting sonnet.  Let's finish that short ride I was enjoying earlier. I was just about to leave the busy part of town and head around cut a new, beautiful smoother out down by the river. It's with her under these dead trees and Autumn Leaves are no scratching, not crunching, but the overriding sound is that a flowing river on my right it's a soothing background soundtrack occasionally interspersed with the chattering of unseen Birds.  Soon I turn  out onto a quiet Road, a slight Crescendo almost overwhelmed by the sound of my quickening breath,( I usually like to work the orchestra hard at some point).  and so I turn for home the family music of motion marking my way.’ The time is gone, the song is over, thought I had something more to say, as someone once said next time, and every time, a different Journey will bring its own subtle and shifting soundtrack. |

Taormina and Milazzo — The hilly kind of Sicily

Google Pictures [LINK](https://photos.app.goo.gl/FEedeJGF1MaJtu659)

![Taormina](/photos/taormina.png)

So we are driving up from Syracuse to Taormina, not really an eventful drive. As we get closer to Taormina, I look out and see this amazing scene of houses perched upon a hill, like glued on there with Superglue. I told Muriel, I will need to ride up there. This is worth a little drive to get some fun in, on the bike. And we ended up, right in there, sleeping there every night. It is a very touristy place with Tour-Busses coming in by the loads, people streaming in and out, in places it is hard to see your feet. The water is nice, the roads are steep, the landscape is beautiful, the roads are empty. What can a guy do but RIDE and swim? Oh, yes. Then there was the visit of Etna in the midst of the Italian Alpine Club.

Then there was the visit of Etna in the midst of an Italian Alpine club national meet-up. Etna, somehow I never really saw this Vulcano as a “real” Vulcano. I don’t know why. But BOY was I wrong. It’s real, it’s high and it’s beautiful too. At a hight of ~3300m and located really close to the see, the elevation shows, easily. It erupted not too long ago, and you see the lava flow in a  very impressive way. It swallowed hots almost completely, most trees are burnt in its path, some magically survived these temperatures of molten rock. In many areas you see the lava rock starting to break down into sand and dust already, and new vegetation takes root. It’s so destructive and it’s so amazing.

 

\

To get to the north coast of Sicily (Sicily really only has three coastal sides, North, South and East coast) we decided to drive through the center and over the hills. Milazzo is a mid-sized town, we did not expect much of it. The way there was really scenic and rewarding. The views and some of the roads are simply breathtaking. The little town of Novara di Sicilia (mind the double “LL”) is really adorable. Because of the amazing road and scenery, the number of motorcycles went through the roof, as did the number risky maneuvers I had to experience on this road. I just took my time and tried not to kill anyone in the process. Milazzo is a cute town with a lot of character. Some Beach town stuff mixed in with style and fashion love, then some fashion for basic and great food and I met a few cyclists there too. The “Pool of Venus” at the northern end of the peninsula was a treat to get to and swim in. Watching sunset out there was a real treat. Mumu staled at the place as she felt sick that day. That evening we had to take ONE of our most favorite Pizza of the trip. Thin crust, great-tasting ingredients and balanced out to make for an amazing pizza. We went there a total of 3 times in only 2 days. It was that bad. The weighers knew us by the second visit and we got all ready a free 1/2 liter red with our already super cheap meal. There was no way to reject it or even pay for it.

\

The drive to Cefalu was probably the one with the longest time I spent in tunnels so far. At least that is what it felt like. One after the other and there was no end to it. Cefalu is practically a no car town. We had to find out the hard way by being stuck in some TINY streets and having to turn around (after we ignored enough of the “No Cars here” signs). A little town of skinny streets and black cobblestone, lots of tourists and even more shops with trinkets of all kind. If you stay away from that area, it’s a really pleasant town. Right on the 1st day, I rode up into the hills with my little Brompton. I regret I did not get the extra 2 gears for it when I climb hills like these. It just takes a lot more out of you if you face a hill that is just a little steeper than your gear ratio lets you ride with comfort. Tough it out then. As soon as you leave behind the coast, it is mountainous terrain and climate. Great trees and rock formations, then cloud to mix it all up. And there were almost no cars. What a treat. The next day Mumu and I made it up there with the car, hiked a little in this great scenery, then followed a recommendation from our host to a town and known good restaurant. A “Michelin” mention on the door and a down to earth interior as well as staff. Just what I like. The food was good to great, and the price was very reasonable. The bar we went to before was so great, we went back the next day and got the same excellent treatment. We might just go there again tomorrow…..

 

**Our HOME** All this is happening with a background of troubles. Since 3 months I am trying to set up a bank account connection between Germany and the US. I am still not there and I am almost running out of patience. So much paperwork and bureaucracy mixed with incompetence and sometimes “Don’t care” attitude, it drives me up the wall. I now have someone in the US bank that is competent and motivated. She might be the reason why this wiring of money might end up working sometimes. I was VERY disappointed with my German bank and the way it was handled there. I was connected to a branch manager as my personal contact person and I thought this would be a great thing. SO far he has only done something useful today. One time. But some of the data I got from his still was incorrect. From other members of this bank, I get zero response via email, and “not my problem” type answers when on the phone. What in the world is going on with Germany, where accuracy and proper etiquette was important and valued some time ago. The buying process of the home started and was and is also sprinkled with incompetence, but some of the events I trace back to plain fear of being cheated out of your money. It takes a lot of patience to do anything here in Italy.

Well, some advertise it to be the “_End of the World_” and depending on how you look at it, it could be. Or it could be the start of a very different one. Ushuaia is considered the most southern city of this world. There are smaller ones, further and much further south. There are a few congregations of buildings and people close to the South Pole too. Whatever the label you want to put at it. Ushuaia is on the southern tip of South America, Cape Horn is not too far away, so I think it is a significant point on the map. And it most certainly is the most southern point on our trip. And guess what; it’s cold here. At least when we got there it snowed the night before. I counted, it must have been at least 4-5cm of snow. And it is the peak of summer at 4-7C during the day. After contemplating on what to do here and looking at our bodily condition (Bowels) as well as weather and wind forecasts we decided to NOT cross the channel with a little Zodiac and visit the little village of Puerto Navarino, stay a few days, do some hikes there and take the ferry along the glaciers, through the Fiords to Punta Arenas. NO. Instead, we did some light hike up to the Glacier and around town instead and are currently on the bus to Punta Arenas which proofed to be a very scenic bus ride. Amazing trees, huge valleys, incredible meadows and far far planes with just dry grass and lots of wind. All are really huge in size here. What I am really surprised by is the fact how many windows of this bus are drawn closed with curtains, how many are all fogged up and how many people are just sleeping through this journey. Is it just me???? What I see seems like a really fascinating landscape, unique in the world, I can’t think of sleeping or not looking outside, but people are watching Movies behind their phones instead. Even as I am typing this I am doing this without looking at the computer, I am so fascinated by all this. ==> I think I am weird that way.

In the town of Ushuaia, I saw a few Cyclists, the REAL kind, the ones that PUSH the pedals to get places. I am in awe of the determination they seem to have and the drive to do all this, to see all this. Not an easy feat by any stretch, but the rewards are huge. I could probably physically do it, but I am not mentally set up for that kind of ride I think.

[![](/photos/image-3.png)](/photos/image-3.png)

Mumu and I could not really find an angle to this town. I mean, an angle that we really liked. People on the streets, outside, did not seem very open and welcoming. As soon as you stepped inside anywhere it was like flipping a page. The same person would look at you with a smile and can’t wait to talk to you or do something for you. The buildings in town were very utilitarian, practical only and not a whole lot of focus was given to beauty. I was surprised to see buildings with an intricate shape, lots of gables and corners, features that made them pretty hard to build, insulate and seal ==> Heat. I would understand to have a VERY square approach to buildings here, but no, the opposite is what I saw.

\

This looks like a witch house to me.

**German**

Nun, einige werben dafür, dass es das „Ende der Welt“ ist, und je nachdem, wie Sie es betrachten, könnte es sein. Oder es könnte der Beginn eines ganz anderen sein. Ushuaia gilt als die südlichste Stadt der Welt. Es gibt kleinere, weiter und viel weiter südlich. Es gibt auch einige Gemeinden und Menschen in der Nähe des Südpols. Was auch immer das Label sein soll, auf das Sie es setzen wollen. Ushuaia liegt an der Südspitze Südamerikas, Kap Horn ist nicht weit entfernt, daher denke ich, dass dies ein bedeutender Punkt auf der Karte ist. Und es ist sicherlich der südlichste Punkt unserer Reise. Und rate was; es ist kalt hier. Zumindest als wir dort ankamen, hat es gestern Abend geschneit. Ich habe gezählt, es muss mindestens 4-5 cm Schnee gewesen sein. Und es ist der Höhepunkt des Sommers bei 4-7 ° C während des Tages. Nachdem wir uns überlegt haben, was wir hier tun sollen, und auf unsere körperliche Verfassung (Bowels) sowie Wetter- und Windvorhersagen blicken, haben wir beschlossen, NICHT mit einem kleinen Tierkreis den Kanal zu überqueren und das kleine Dorf Puerto Navarino zu besuchen, ein paar Tage zu bleiben, ein paar zu machen Wandern Sie dort und nehmen Sie die Fähre entlang der Gletscher, durch die Fjorde nach Punta Arenas. NEIN. Stattdessen haben wir eine leichte Wanderung hinauf zum Gletscher und in die Stadt gemacht und befinden uns derzeit im Bus nach Punta Arenas, was sich als sehr malerische Busfahrt herausstellte. Erstaunliche Bäume, riesige Täler, unglaubliche Wiesen und weite Flugzeuge mit nur trockenem Gras und viel Wind. Alle sind hier wirklich sehr groß. Was mich wirklich überrascht, ist die Tatsache, wie viele Fenster dieses Busses mit Vorhängen geschlossen werden, wie viele alle beschlagen sind und wie viele Menschen gerade durch diese Reise schlafen. Ist es nur mir ???? Was ich sehe, scheint eine wirklich faszinierende Landschaft zu sein, einzigartig auf der Welt. Ich kann nicht daran denken, zu schlafen oder nicht draußen zu schauen, aber die Leute schauen sich stattdessen Filme hinter ihrem Handy an. Auch wenn ich das tippe, mache ich das, ohne auf den Computer zu schauen. Ich bin fasziniert von all dem. ==> Ich denke ich bin so komisch.

In der Stadt Ushuaia sah ich ein paar Radfahrer, die ECHTE Art, die die Pedale DRÜCKEN, um Plätze zu bekommen. Ich bin beeindruckt von der Entschlossenheit, die sie zu haben scheinen, und dem Drang, all dies zu tun und all das zu sehen. Kein leichtes Kunststück, aber die Belohnungen sind enorm. Ich könnte es wahrscheinlich körperlich tun, aber ich bin nicht mental auf diese Art von Fahrt eingestellt, denke ich.

Mumu und ich konnten nicht wirklich einen Winkel zu dieser Stadt finden. Ich meine, ein Winkel, der uns wirklich gefallen hat. Die Menschen auf den Straßen draußen wirkten nicht sehr offen und einladend. Sobald Sie irgendwo hineingetreten sind, war es, als würden Sie eine Seite umblättern. Die gleiche Person würde Sie mit einem Lächeln betrachten und kann es kaum erwarten, mit Ihnen zu sprechen oder etwas für Sie zu tun. Die Gebäude in der Stadt waren sehr zweckmäßig, nur praktisch, und der Schönheit wurde nicht viel Aufmerksamkeit geschenkt. Ich war überrascht, Gebäude mit einer komplizierten Form, vielen Giebeln und Ecken zu sehen, Eigenschaften, die es ziemlich schwierig machten, sie zu bauen, zu isolieren und abzudichten. Ich würde verstehen, dass ich hier einen sehr quadratischen Zugang zu Gebäuden habe, aber nein, das Gegenteil ist das, was ich gesehen habe.

Das sieht für mich wie ein Hexenhaus aus.

Cela ressemble à une maison de sorcière pour moi.

I want to write about someone very private, very important. I know this person, I know her for a long long time, I know her well and still, there are oceans more to discover about her. 

Grown-up in a very humble and rural family and place, she dealt with a caring but rough upbringing. There was no time nor money for a lot of fluff. She marries out of the house and moves to the city. Everything is new, and adjustments are coming left and right. New friends, kids, family, moving, helping to found a little company is all happening in a very short time. Style is never missed with her around. But the style grows and shrinks with what is possible at that time. I see her life as a life of giving, creating, and then also blazing new trails. 

**\===> Time jump**

* * *

Now I see her leading her living by herself in the apartment I grew up in, not alone, just by herself. The other members of the house become “infected” by the winning nature of her and her communal spirit. People are drawn to her, young and old. The 2-year-old demand to go and see her just as well as the neighbor of the last 40+ years decides to come down for a quick coffee and chat with her. They bounce problems off her with the hope to get a great idea to solve them, want to share some thoughts, or just feel the presence of her. She usually does not disappoint and you walk away feeling better than you walked in. Having received another tool in your toolbelt, another idea in your head, or just the knowledge that there is an open ear and heart that truly cares about you. Cares every time. And you will get to hear what you deserve. Words of care or some words of discipline. All delivered in a way that it can be received, digested, and understood. 

COVID has diminished this stream of people coming for a chat. And over the last year, it proved hard on her not to have these interactions. I now come and visit her pretty frequently because she received some pretty troubling diagnoses from the medical doctors. I am just struck with awe, every time I am with her. She wakes up and smiles at me like “**_THIS_** is a great day”, “**_THIS_** is so good”, “I am so glad **_YOU_** are here with me”. The calm and joy radiate out of her and I get to stand there and receive some of it. She deals with the slowly decreasing physical abilities you get to experience when you get older. She deals with it with the strength of a bull and the attitude of a Budda. Hating some parts of it but she deals with it when she is not working on the recovery from it. When I help her, you could not imagine a more grateful person, so happy to receive the help, hating that she can’t do it herself, but loving that I am there to do it for her. Every time, every time I feel and hear gratefulness radiating out. I want to be like this when I grow up, I want to fight like a bull to get back what I could do yesterday, accept what is truly impossible to get back. I want to be able to have the ability to fight it all and the smarts to know when to let it be the way it is. 

I think you guessed it. I am talking about my Mom. For me, she is and always was amazing. She is not an angle, not without thorns, but no one is. But she does inspire me in so many ways and almost every day. I need to write this, because I need to get it out, just so it is out. I need to express these thoughts and write them down the best way I can. I feel a relief when it is out. It just helps me. I know I will get a verbal beating once she reads it. But what will she do? Let’s find out.

**My Mom - Marita**

DEUTSCH

Ich möchte über eine sehr private, sehr wichtige Person schreiben. Ich kenne diese Person, ich kenne sie schon sehr lange, ich kenne sie gut und trotzdem gibt es noch Unmengen mehr über sie zu entdecken. 

Aufgewachsen in einer sehr bescheidenen und ländlichen Familie und Gegend, erhielt sie eine fürsorgliche, aber rauen Erziehung. Für viel Schnickschnack war weder Zeit noch Geld vorhanden. Sie heiratete und zog von zu Hause aus und in die Stadt. Alles ist neu, und es muss sich links und rechts angepasst werden. Neue Freunde, Kinder, Familie, Umzug, Hilfe bei der Gründung einer kleinen Firma - all das passiert in sehr kurzer Zeit. Der Stil und Style wird nie vermisst, wenn sie dabei ist. Aber der Stil wächst und schrumpft mit dem, was zu dieser Zeit möglich ist. Ich sehe ihr Leben als ein Leben des Gebens, des Schaffens und dann auch des Beschreitens neuer Wege. 

\===> Zeitsprung

* * *

Jetzt sehe ich sie, wie sie in der Wohnung, in der ich aufgewachsen bin, ihr Leben mit sich selbst führt, nicht allein, nur mit sich selbst. Die anderen Mitglieder des Hauses werden von ihrer gewinnenden Art und ihrem Gemeinschaftssinn "angesteckt". Die Menschen fühlen sich zu ihr hingezogen, jung und alt. Der 2-Jährige verlangt danach, sie zu sehen, genauso wie die Nachbarin der letzten 40+ Jahre beschließt, auf einen schnellen Kaffee herunterzukommen und mit ihr zu plaudern. Sie bereden ihre Probleme zusammen, in der Hoffnung, eine tolle Idee zu ihrer Lösung zu bekommen, wollen ein paar Gedanken austauschen oder einfach nur ihre Gegenwart spüren. Normalerweise enttäuscht sie nicht und man geht mit einem besseren Gefühl weg, als man hereingekommen ist. Sie haben ein weiteres Werkzeug in Ihrem Werkzeuggürtel, eine weitere Idee in Ihrem Kopf oder einfach nur das Wissen, dass es ein offenes Ohr und Herz gibt, das sich wirklich um Sie kümmert. Jedes Mal. Und Sie werden zu hören bekommen, was Sie verdient haben. Worte der Fürsorge oder einige Worte der Disziplin. Alles auf eine Art und Weise, dass es empfangen, verdaut und verstanden werden kann. 

COVID hat diesen Strom von Menschen, die zu einem Gespräch kommen, verringert. Und im Laufe des letzten Jahres war es schwer für sie, diese Interaktionen nicht zu haben. Ich besuche sie jetzt ziemlich häufig, weil sie ziemlich beunruhigende Diagnosen von den Ärzten erhalten hat. Jedesmal wenn ich bei Ihr bin bin ich am wundern und am staunen. Sie wacht auf und lächelt mich an; "**_DAS_** ist ein super Tag", "**_DAS_** ist so gut", "Ich bin so froh, dass **_DU_** hier bei mir bist". Die Ruhe und Freude strahlt aus ihr heraus und ich darf dastehen und etwas davon abbekommen. Sie geht mit den langsam nachlassenden körperlichen Fähigkeiten um, die man mit dem Älterwerden erfährt. Sie geht damit um, mit der Kraft eines Stiers und der Einstellung eines Buddas. Sie hasst einige Teile davon, aber sie geht damit um, wenn sie nicht gerade an der Verbesserung davon arbeitet. Wenn ich ihr helfe, kann man sich keine dankbarere Person vorstellen, so glücklich über die Hilfe, hassend, dass sie es nicht selbst tun kann, aber liebend, dass ich da bin, um es für sie zu tun. Jedes Mal, jedes Mal fühle und höre ich, wie die Dankbarkeit herausstrahlt. Ich möchte so sein, wenn ich erwachsen bin, ich möchte kämpfen wie ein Stier, um das zurückzubekommen, was ich gestern tun konnte, ich möchte akzeptieren, was wirklich unmöglich ist, zurückzubekommen. Ich möchte die Fähigkeit haben, gegen alles anzukämpfen und die Klugheit, zu wissen, wann man es so sein lassen sollte, wie es ist. 

Ich denke, Sie haben es erraten. Ich spreche von meiner Mutter. Für mich ist und war sie immer erstaunlich. Sie ist kein Engel, nicht ohne Dornen, aber das ist niemand. Aber sie inspiriert mich auf so viele Arten und fast jeden Tag. Ich muss das schreiben, weil ich es rauslassen muss, einfach damit es raus ist. Ich muss diese Gedanken ausdrücken und sie auf die beste Art und Weise niederschreiben, die ich kann. Ich fühle eine Erleichterung, wenn es raus ist. Es hilft mir einfach. Ich weiß, dass ich eine verbale Tracht Prügel bekomme, wenn sie es liest. Aber was wird sie tun? Lass es uns herausfinden.

**Meine Mutter - Marita**
